# Warum lehrkraefte das schulystem verlassen und wie man sie halten kann

Auch der Wunsch nach einem beruflichen Wechsel ist weit verbreitet. Wie lassen sich Lehrkräfte besser an den Schulen halten? Dieser Frage sind die Bildungsexpertinnen eines Beratungsunternehmens nachgegangen – und haben mehr als 90 Schmerzpunkte im Berufsleben von Lehrkräften identifiziert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.subtitle: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University.

items.articleBody:
Getty Images / Silver Bulletin illustration.

 The latest on QBERT

This is the landing page for QBERT. As with our other landing pages, it’s best viewed on the web rather than over email or in the Substack App. The charts and tables will be updated regularly, and some of the text will change, too.

QBERT has been updated with Week 8 games. Yes, QBERT absolutely loves Brock Purdy.

Here’s what you can expect to see in each week’s update:

QBERT ratings for each QB so far in 2026

A breakdown of each QB’s weekly ratings for 2026, allocating credit between his passing and rushing performance and adjusting for the difficulty of the conditions he faces

An updating lifetime leaderboard of the top QBs in NFL history. (Yes, Tom Brady remains #1.)

A mini-interactive chart where you can compare any two QBs since 1950.

Projected QBERT ratings for each QB’s next start.

And QB depth charts with injury and point-spread ratings.

See also: ELWAY NFL projections.

Who are the best QBs in the NFL?

Up first is our current leaderboard. QBERT is both a historical rating system and a quarterback projection system. The left and middle columns reflect year-to-date performance and can be noisy early in the season. WAR accounts for playing time and, more specifically, the number of “QB plays” (basically passes, QB rushes, sacks, and certain penalties like defensive pass interference1). Projected ratings also reflect data from previous seasons, aging curves, and injuries:

And here is more detailed data on every QB to have thrown a pass in 2026. Our adjusted QBERT ratings are lower across the board than our raw QBERT ratings because the modern NFL is very pass/QB-friendly: an average 2026 season would have been considered extraordinary by 1986 standards. They also account for the strength of the opposing defense, home-field advantage and even the weather:

However, we’ve also broken down performance into two major categories: “pure passing” on the one hand, and rushing and sack avoidance on the other hand. These weekly ratings include various adjustments, such as for the amount of pass pressure a QB faced, with a small bonus for clutch/comeback wins. Ratings in the individual categories are taken relative to league average given the difficulty of the conditions a QB faced. Since an average QBERT rating is defined as a score of 80, you can add 80 to his passing performance grade and his rush/sack performance grade to get his overall adjusted QBERT rating for the week.

The best quarterbacks of all time

Next, here is our mini-interactive allowing you to evaluate and compare any QB who has taken a snap since 1950. This data is based on adjusted QBERT ratings, which put all QBs on a level playing field given the context of their eras. We hope you’ll have a lot of fun with this, but please let us know if you’re having browser-compatibility issues.

Here, meanwhile, is our lifetime QB leaderboard, with active players highlighted. It’s sorted by wins above replacement (WAR), which is heavily dependent on career length; players like Patrick Mahomes are almost certain to continue climbing the list.

Our historical QBERT ratings combine the regular season and the playoffs; there are difficulty adjustments based on the quality of the opposing defense and even weather, so guys aren’t punished for facing tougher postseason defenses. We also have a separate leaderboard with just playoff performance — Mahomes is already #3 on that list — which we’ll restore as the playoffs approach.

items.body:
# 17years

Die Analyse zu „17years“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
Full Page Ad in Conde Nast’s Traveler magazine, March 1988 (via)

I was talking to my friend Jamie about therapy a few months ago and he recommended the “Psychiatry” chapter in Michael Crichton’s 1988 memoir, Travels.

Around 1971, Crichton was separated from his wife. She suggested he see a psychiatrist. “I refused,” Crichton wrote. “I didn’t think psychiatry did any good for people. It was just a lot of hand-holding.”

Then his wife gave him the name of a prominent psychiatrist at UCLA but suggested that the doctor was probably too busy to see him. Crichton took offense at the idea he wasn’t important enough to be seen, and made an appointment. (It’s a very funny chapter.)

“I now found myself in a peculiar situation,” he wrote. “I didn’t really believe in psychiatry, I didn’t want to see a psychiatrist, and I didn’t think there was anything wrong with me, but I was challenged to present myself to Dr. Norton in a fascinating way.”

After a fine performance, Dr. Norton took Crichton on as a patient.

But I still wasn’t sure psychiatry did any good. And it was expensive, sixty dollars an hour. Anything that cost so much must surely be an indulgence. Rich lazy people went to psychiatrists.

I decided to keep track of how much it was costing me to see Dr. Norton, and I assessed each session when it was over to determine if it had been worth the sixty dollars.

I found Dr. Norton puzzling because he was so normal. I’d tell him my story and he’s say things like ‘Time will tell’ or ‘You can’t make an omelet without breaking eggs.’

I thought, Sixty dollars an hour to hear you can’t make an omelette without breaking eggs? What good is this?

But Crichton enjoyed “complaining about my life” and kept going back.

On the fifth session, “three hundred dollars down the drain,” as he put it, they had a breakthrough: it turns out that Crichton was an insecure person.

I felt amazed. Just as amazed as if he had shown me that I had a third arm coming out of my chest, an arm I had never noticed before. How could I not have noticed this before? But I never thought I was insecure. If anything, I saw myself as astoundingly confident.

Could I really have held such an incorrect view of myself?

Dr. Norton tried to soften the blow, and explained that many things about ourselves were difficult to see without outside help. That was the whole point of a therapist. He was an objective outsider.

This was a new idea to me, that there might be some things about myself that I couldn’t see without outside help. But it obviously was true.

I never kept track of how much I was spending again.

Crichton then goes on to tell a funny story about getting involved with several women and how Dr. Norton warns him that things are going to go very badly. Crichton doesn’t think so. He thinks he can handle it.

“Time will tell,” Dr. Norton says.

And it does: things go very badly for Crichton.

“What a mess” I said.

“Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned,” Dr. Norton said.

Crichton gets divorced, goes to a psychic, becomes totally depressed after achieving all his goals in life (it happens!), reads Ram Dass’s Be Here Now, and starts traveling again.

But he never really talks about psychiatry again in that chapter.

So I searched around, seeing if anything came up about Crichton and psychiatry.

The first thing that surfaced was this 1970 clip of his appearance on The Dick Cavett Show to promote his first non-fiction book, Five Patients:

Around 5:26, Cavett asks Crichton about psychiatry.

Cavett: What’s happening in psychiatry these days? There’s always something peculiar going on there. The latest thing I heard about is they’re using computers as psychoanalysts.

Crichton: There is a computer program which I put in the book because it was mostly amusing. It was done as a joke by a fellow named Weizenbaum at MIT several years ago. What he set out to do is to see if you could program a computer to interact in something approaching a conversation with a person. And he did it by a series of kind of tricks. So for example, the computer will pick up something in your sentence and play it back to you. If you mention parents it’ll pop something back, “Can you tell me more?” or “Why do you say that about [blank]?” and put in the parents. But it turns out in practice to be kind of successful, kind of frighteningly successful.

Cavett: It sounds ludicrous to begin with. I mean, it would seem like the idea of therapy would be that the genius of the therapist would be that he treats every person as individual and finds out what this individual’s problems are and he’s unlike any other individual. But how can a machine do that?

Crichton: That particular point is why this thing is kind of frightening the psychiatrist.

Cavett: Because it’s succeeding?

Crichton: Yeah!

There are at several things that are interesting to me about this clip.

This was filmed 56 years ago.

Crichton, seen here, is about one year away from going to therapy himself.

Cavett sort of completely gets wrong what therapy is about, which Crichton later discovers for himself: seen through the eye of an attentive but impartial observer, your problems aren’t actually that unique  at all.

But by far the most interesting is the story of MIT professor and computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum himself, and how his experience ELIZA caused him to turn against AI.

From his MIT obituary:

Weizenbaum was shocked to discover that many users were taking his program seriously and were opening their hearts to it. The experience prompted him to think philosophically about the implications of artificial intelligence, and, later, to become a critic of it.

In 1976, he authored “Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation,” in which he displayed ambivalence toward computer technology and warned against giving machines the responsibility for making genuinely human choices. Specifically, Weizenbaum argued that it was not just wrong but dangerous and, in some cases, immoral to assume that computers would be able to do anything given enough processing power and clever programming.

“No other organism, and certainly no computer, can be made to confront genuine human problems in human terms,” he wrote.

“‘Computer Power and Human Reason’ raised questions about the role of artificial intelligence, and spurred debate about the role of computer systems in decision making for many years,” said Eric Grimson, head of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT.

Weizenbaum’s initial wariness about computers — and humanity’s reliance on them — later evolved into a deep resentment. By the early 1980s, he was railing against the concept of computer illiteracy, saying it was a form of “mass hysteria” drummed up by computer manufacturers as a way to sell more product. The real focus, he said, should not be on computer literacy but literacy itself.

In a 1985 interview with New Age journal, he proudly described himself as a heretic of technology.

“The dependence on computers is merely the most recent — and the most extreme –Â example of how man relies on technology in order to escape the burden of acting as an independent agent,” Weizenbaum told the journal. “It helps him avoid the task of giving meaning to his life, of deciding and pursuing what is truly valuable.”

I was telling this all to my friend Marty on the phone and he was like, “Wait, I just heard a guest talking about this guy while listening to On Point this morning!”

That guest was Sherry Turkle, who’s making the rounds promoting her book Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines.

When Turkle arrived at MIT in the 1970s, she was one of the only psychologists there, and Weizenbaum wanted to meet her because he was trying to figure out why people were so into this ELIZA program he had written.

She told Weizenbaum’s story on The Ezra Klein Show:

He found that the graduate students who had helped him, who knew that this program didn’t know and didn’t understand anything, nevertheless wanted to be alone with it and wanted to be in a closed room with it and wanted to talk to it. His assistant — his secretary, as he called her at the time — wanted to be alone with it, wanted to talk to it. And he was delighted to find me, a psychoanalytically trained psychologist, to try to help him understand what that phenomenon was. And this was really one of the things that drew me into the study of computers and people, because it was really one of the first times that you really saw the seductive power of a machine that talked.

Turkle went on to explain what she calls the “Eliza Effect,” or people’s desire to make the computer seem smarter than it really is.

They wanted so much to believe that it was a thinking creature that they would ask it questions in a way that, with practice, they knew would cause it to give the most humanlike response… And again, that was one of the early things I learned, that it’s not just that we come to a machine and say: “Oh, is this intelligent? Does this understand me?” But we come to these conversations wanting it to be there for us. And that really concerned Weizenbaum because he thought that was a very dangerous road, because the machine really understood nothing.

And that was my afternoon on the internet!

items.articleBody:
A saturated blue sky and cascades of complementary golden-yellow foliage laid the foundation for a vibrant, picturesque Diwali weekend in the suburbs. It wasn’t the most festive Diwali for me — instead of lighting diyas and playing with sparklers, I spent a majority of the weekend hand-feeding a friendly yard squirrel while wearing some bullshit pajamas extracted from the depths of my childhood closet.

Think I’m slumming it? Well, think again! Because those dilapidated pajamas are almost certainly what inspired the theme for next year’s Met Gala and related Costume Institute exhibit: extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday, a program “devoted to the undersung beauty and allure of quotidian garments.” (That’s code for jeans.)

(And t-shirts. And raincoats. Maybe pajamas, but also maybe not.)

It’s an exasperated, last-minute pivot after controversial British fashion designer John Galliano, who was central to the Costume Institute’s original program for 2027, withdrew from participating entirely this August in response to the public backlash toward his racist behavior in the past. Between “elevating” daily wear into runway fashion and exploring how “humble, even ‘disposable’ materials” like paper and aluminum can become wearable, this enormous exercise in putting a positive spin on gentrifying economic recession is at odds with NYC residents who are buckling from profound unaffordability as the city speedruns its transformation into a private equity playground.

I guess I can’t really say which is worse — the current standard of celebrities in bespoke, extravagant garments from elite fashion houses hanging off their GLP-1 frames, or the notion that a Met Gala dress code calling for aluminum foil pants, a shrunken tee, and maybe a jacket made from hole-punched plastic circles is what’ll push people to consider everyday wear in a different light.

However, before we get too pressed, we have to acknowledge that this is a big moment for the Bad Bunny x Zara collection! On the plus side, it might make it easier for some ~lowly civs~ to sneak in and eat all the cheese cubes. Dress for the job you want, right?

Speaking of jobs — Whitney Museum curator Meg Onli returns as a co-curator for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, sharing the stage with director and dancer Zack Winokur, who co-founded the interdisciplinary American Modern Opera Company in 2017. I found the 2026 Biennial to be a textbook case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts. Let’s see how Winokur’s hand in artistic performance direction manifests in this curatorial behemoth; I’m sure he’s used to working with a lot of moving parts.

Back to the here and now, I’m long overdue for multiple museum visits at the peak of the season. The days keep slipping through my fingers before I’ve had a chance to visit the Krasner Pollock show at The Met or the Architects of Liberation at the MoMA. Mayor Mamdani actually paid a visit to the MoMA show before I did, and he’s significantly busier than I am, so there’s really no excuse!

In another nudge for me to make the journey uptown, MoMA recently opened its Brancusi exhibition. With a replica of Brancusi’s studio and a selection of rare media documenting his work environment and the social atmosphere he cultivated between his sculptures and his guests alike, the exhibition spotlights the artist’s labor-intensive process as an art form in itself.

Critic Aruna D’Souza noted that the “sculptures seem to be maintaining COVID-era social distancing protocols,” and chalked that awkward dynamic up to the MoMA’s renovated gallery layout, recalling the previously approachable setup’s capacity to “allow for art objects to talk to each other.”

On Sunday, I bore witness to a conversation that made me think about Brancusi’s glinting buffed bronzes and smooth marbles. The chatter between a yellowing tree branch, an overturned recycling bin, and the white picket fence behind them might have been too maximalist compared to the Romanian sculptor’s sleek, pared-down modernism. Nevertheless, I pulled over to eavesdrop.

Claire Valdez Will Be Your Artist in Congress

Among the historic wave of triumphs for Democrats in yesterday’s midterms, New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, an artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer, was elected to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives. | Anna Lee

Read More

Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company. | Anna Lee

Read More

At MoMA, Brancusi Is Lost in Space

The artist’s work is glorious and resonant, but the Museum of Modern Art has a space problem, or an elegance problem, or a crowd mitigation problem. | Aruna D’Souza

Read More

The Prior Occupants of Westbeth Are Just Beyond Reach

A little more legibility would’ve benefited Alison Nguyen’s fragmented short film about the famed NYC artists’ housing complex. | Rhea Nayyar

Read More

What Else Is Happening?

New York Foundation for the Arts is hosting a free virtual workshop on protecting your art in the age of AI. The discussion will be illustrated with stories in which artists found themselves entangled with the law—and how it all turned out. (Thurs Nov 12) [nyfa.org]

To celebrate Diwali, Studio Oso is hosting a polymer clay workshop. Possible creations include diyas, earrings, trinkets, magnets, and more.  (Sat Nov 14) [studiooso.com]

The 11th annual Brooklyn Cranksgiving is on with a scavenger-hunt-style bike ride that supports food access and equity in our community. (Sat Nov 14) [Brooklyn Cranksgiving]

Filmmaker Ira Sachs just finished reading Chloe Aridjis' new book, The Shadow of the Object. They're going to sit down to talk about it — and you're invited! (Mon Nov 16) [giornopoetrysystems.org]

Pioneer Works and The Yale Review join forces for the only US event for the Life of M, a new — and highly anticipated — novel by Rachel Cusk. (Tues Nov 17) [pioneerworks.org]

items.articleBody:
Gary Marcus:

When a business needs exponentially increasing amounts of capital
to make modest increases in quality in an intensely competitive
market and still owes far more money than it has ever made, there
is a serious problem.

I continue to believe that there is no moat in AI models. None. But the entire premise of Anthropic’s IPO is that they have an enormous gulf of a moat.

I would not be shocked to see Anthropic go out of business. Nor
would I be shocked if the IPO fails. WeWork tried to IPO, 3 times,
and didn’t make it.

I would be surprised if Anthropic does not go out of business. Most cults implode, and Anthropic doesn’t even hide that they’re a cult. And I just don’t see how the math works. Scientology is a long-running cult, but Scientology hasn’t committed $900 billion in spending over the next few years.

(Marcus’s post is on his Substack blog, which, annoyingly, requires you to be logged into a Substack account and to “subscribe”, even though it’s ostensibly a free post. What a rotten oppressive turd of a blogging platform Substack is. Just in case your Substack account isn’t working, here’s a PDF archive.)

items.articleBody:
SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket.

The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13).

During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history.

SpaceX's Flight 15 Starship Super Heavy booster in its assembly bay, before its move to Starbase's launch mount. (Image credit: SpaceX)
Booster 22 therefore "was used for final catch testing upon arrival [at the pad], including a suspended squeeze test at catch height," SpaceX said in an X post today (Nov. 10).

That post shared four photos of the giant booster, which is powered by 33 of SpaceX's next-gen Raptor engines. The first shot showed Super Heavy in one of Starbase's "Mega Bay" assembly buildings before rollout, while the other three depicted it grasped by the tower's arms, held high in the South Texas sky.

SpaceX will try to catch both Super Heavy and Ship during Flight 15 — something it's never done before. (Image credit: SpaceX)
SpaceX has used the chopstick arms during Starship flights before; it has successfully caught Super Heavy on three separate occasions. But the company has never attempted a catch of Ship, which flies higher and farther than the booster and is therefore a more challenging target. And SpaceX only reached orbit with Starship for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.

So Flight 15 will break new ground. And, if all goes to plan, it will give us a look at the future: SpaceX plans to catch Super Heavy and Ship on all operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will allow the company to boost the megarocket's launch cadence.

And SpaceX wants to fly Starship incredibly often, so that it can build out its Starlink V3 broadband constellation and even bigger Starmind AI data-center network. Indeed, Elon Musk has said the company is eyeing 10,000 Starship flights per year by 2030.

The launch tower's "chopstick" arms giving the Flight 15 Super Heavy a loving squeeze. (Image credit: SpaceX)
If all goes to plan, Flight 15 will launch from Starbase on Friday during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time).

Super Heavy will return to Starbase for its catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. Ship will follow suit much later — about 22 hours later, in fact, after it has deployed 26 Starlink V3 spacecraft into LEO and completed 14 circuits of our planet.

You can watch all the action live here at Space.com and get updates about the mission here.

Senate Democrats today opposed President Trump's nominee for an open Federal Communications Commission seat, and criticized Republicans for moving to confirm a new commissioner during the period before Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027. Democrats also plan to use their majority next year to launch probes of FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

"After the American people last week overwhelmingly rejected the MAGA agenda, there is no justification for this committee to advance partisan nominees during the lame-duck period," Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) said today at the Commerce Committee's nomination hearing for Danielle Thumann Severs, Trump's pick to fill an empty commissioner's seat.

Thumann Severs, an attorney and senior counsel to Carr, faced questions from Democrats about whether she supports Carr's attacks on TV broadcasters.

items.articleBody:
Im vergangenen Monat kündigte Apple Arcade bereits an, dass Football Manager 27 Touch ab November auf dem Spiele-Abo-Dienst erhältlich sein wird. Am heutigen Tag ist es endlich soweit und das große Update steht bereit. Darüber hinaus gibt es einen Ausblick auf vier Spiele, die im Dezember auf Apple Arcade debütieren.

Football Manager 27 Touch startet auf Apple Arcade

Ab sofort steht Football Manager 27 Touch auf Apple Arcade zur Verfügung. Das Spiel bringt die Rolle des Fußballmanagers direkt in eure Hosentasche. So könnt ihr von überall wichtige Entscheidungen für eure Mannschaft treffen. Die neue Version bietet eine verbesserte Match Engine und damit neue Möglichkeiten, das Geschehen auf dem Spielfeld zu gestalten. Neue Tools für die Spielersuche und Spielvorbereitung erleichtern das Scouting und die taktische Planung, während eine neu gestaltete Benutzeroberfläche für iPhone dafür sorgt, dass alles bequem mit dem Daumen erreichbar ist.

4 Spiele-Neuheiten im Dezember 2026

Am 03. Dezember geht es mit vier Spiele-Neuheiten auf Apple Arcade weiter. Konkret warten in rund 3 Wochen Plants vs. Zombies: Replanted, solitaire(ish),  Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown und LEGO® DUPLO Playtime auf euch. Blicken wir etwas näher auf die Neuheiten.

Plants vs. Zombies: Replanted bringt die beliebten Charaktere, den typischen Humor und das strategische Gameplay zurück, die das Original zu einem Klassiker gemacht haben. Neben neuen Leveln und Spielmodi bietet das Spiel auch die Möglichkeit, gemeinsam mit Freunden im lokalen Koop- oder PvP-Modus auf demselben Gerät anzutreten. Der exklusiv auf Apple Arcade verfügbare Partymodus verpasst dem heimischen Hinterhof zudem einen völlig neuen Look.

Mit solitaire(ish) präsentiert Playstack eine ungewöhnliche Neuinterpretation des klassischen Kartenspiels. Spieler stapeln Karten zu immer höheren Türmen, um zunehmend anspruchsvolle Punktevorgaben zu erfüllen. Dabei sammeln sie seltene Bonuskarten und optimieren ihre Decks mit mehr als 150 Spezialkarten. Tägliche Herausforderungen, Bestenlisten und freischaltbare Sammelkarten sorgen dafür, dass jeder Durchlauf neue Überraschungen bereithält.

In Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown+ kommen mächtige Zeitkräfte, akrobatische Fähigkeiten und präzise Schwertkampftechniken zum Einsatz. Damit erkunden ihr die miteinander verbundenen, von Zeitverzerrungen geprägten Tiefen des Berges Qaf und stellen sich zahlreichen Gefahren. Die Apple-Arcade-Version umfasst das vollständige Spielerlebnis des von der Kritik gefeierten Originals sowie sämtliche zusätzlichen Download-Inhalte. Darüber hinaus warten neue Herausforderungen, Quests und kosmetische Anpassungsmöglichkeiten.

Abgerundet wird das Dezember-Lineup durch LEGO DUPLO Playtime. Die entspannte, offene Spielwelt richtet sich an kleine Baumeister, die ihre Kreativität frei entfalten möchten. Mit den beliebten LEGO DUPLO Steinen können sie nach Belieben experimentieren, verschiedene Elemente kombinieren und ihre ganz eigene, lebendige Spielwelt erschaffen.

items.articleBody:
walking through a tidal landscape at Powerhouse Parramatta

Tyrrell Studio transforms a naturally lit gallery at the recently opened Powerhouse Parramatta, Australia, into a shifting landscape of water, sandstone and reflected light with Overflow, a large-scale installation grounded in the living principles of First Nations Water Country. Conceived by Wiradjuri woman Emily McDaniel, the First Nations-led exhibition brings together stories from seven Aboriginal organizations across New South Wales, with films by Kamilaroi filmmaker Ivan Sen. The project makes water the physical medium through which visitors encounter these stories, inviting them to remove their shoes and walk barefoot across a changing tidal landscape.

Occupying a gallery measuring approximately 60 × 40 meters, the installation takes the form of a shallow pool flowing across an abstracted sandstone rock shelf. The stone references the geological terrain beneath Parramatta, where the river has shaped the landscape over tens of thousands of years. As water rises and recedes, different sections of the sculpted surface emerge and disappear, transforming the gallery throughout the day.

Reflections of the building’s structure and surrounding sky appear on the surface of the pool, while natural daylight creates shifting patterns across the space. As the water level rises, the installation becomes a broad reflective plane; as it retreats, the sandstone outcrops become visible again.

all images by Mark Tyrrell

water country beyond the riverbank

The artwork by the team at Tyrrell Studio draws on a broader understanding of the Parramatta River as a changing landscape. Before European settlement, the river occupied an extensive terrain shaped by tidal movement, sediment and the meeting of freshwater and saltwater. Its banks were not the definitive boundaries that contemporary infrastructure suggests but part of a much larger system extending through sand, stone, groundwater and floodplains.

European settlement gradually changed this relationship. Weirs, built-up riverbanks and concrete channels were introduced to control the flow of water, turning a naturally changing river into a more contained and controlled waterway. Tyrrell Studio’s design responds to this history, reconsidering what lies beyond the visible channel.

Overflow allows some of the underlying processes of the former landscape to become perceptible. Water gathers, spreads and withdraws across the stone and changing light and reflections introduce an element of unpredictability. The installation brings attention to the forces that continue to shape the terrain beneath the contemporary city.

a film projection illuminates the water and sculpted sandstone in Overflow

making space for country

The cultural foundations of the exhibition come from Emily McDaniel’s original concept, which places Aboriginal cultural practices at the center of the experience. Seven participating organizations contribute knowledge and stories connected to Water Country across New South Wales, including Baramadagal Community, Gamay Rangers, The Goondee Aboriginal Keeping Place and Museum, Jagun Alliance, Joonga Land and Water Aboriginal Corporation, Moogahlin Performing Arts and Naru Aboriginal Corporation.

Their work encompasses caring for species, fishing, water monitoring, flood mitigation, language and cultural water rights, practices that enter the gallery through films by Ivan Sen. Sen’s films bring different waterways, communities, and forms of knowledge into conversation with the physical environment in Parramatta, projected onto and reflected across the water, where ripples fragment their images before they reform across the sandstone and the bodies of visitors.

bringing landscapes from across New South Wales into the gallery

from the riverfront into the museum

Overflow is closely connected to Tyrrell Studio’s work outside the museum, particularly its permanent 3,000-square-meter riverfront landscape, Ngurra Budyari Ngalawagulang. Developed with Baramadagal elders and Dharug community representatives, the public space draws on the cultural and natural history of Water Country. The landscape is made up of sandstone paths, vegetation and rain gardens. Water collects in shallow hollows, plants grow through the paving and the stone gradually changes with exposure to the elements. Τhe design lets nature become part of how the space looks and feels. It is a landscape that changes with the weather, the seasons and the passage of time.

Inside the museum, Overflow picks up where the riverfront leaves off. The same materials and ideas continue into the gallery, where water moves across sculpted sandstone instead of being contained within a pool. The connection can even be felt in the morning, when mist from the Parramatta River rises toward the upper floors of the museum.

a visitor faces a large-scale film projection

visitors move through the changing landscape of water, stone and projected imagery the structural framework of the museum is mirrored in the still water walking beside the water and exposed sandstone

a river appears above the installation’s sculpted sandstone surface

items.articleBody:
A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.

The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in St Louis, USA, is one of five Best of Globe winners. Designed by CannonDesign and photo by Nic Lehoux

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

The We Labo 2F office, Okamura Corporation in Japan, which was designed by the company, is another winner. Photo by Takuya Yamauchi

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.

“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.

“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”

The Diageo Gurugram Workplace office interior in India also won the prize. Design by M Moser Associates and photo by Shubham Sharma

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and new elements, as well as the important social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.

Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a new layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The Diageo Gurugram Workplace was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” design. Design by M Moser Associates and photo by Shubham Sharma

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.

Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.

Another US project to win was the Missouri Athletic Club based in Missouri, USA. Designed by HOK and photo by Alise O'Brien

The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.

We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.

Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

It was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” interiors, which combine a wide range of workspaces with shared hospitality areas. M Moser Associates dedicated more than half of the building to community spaces.

Finally, DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects is a large workplace for a legal company. It was designed to cater to different work styles.

The third office to win Best of Globe was DLA Piper in Leeds, UK. Design by |Sheppard Robson and photo by Adrian Lambert

According to Shaw Contract, it won the prize for providing a broad range of workspaces suited to different needs, as well as wellbeing, dining and meeting areas.

The jury particularly enjoyed how materials had been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”.

DLA Piper's office materials have been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”. Design by |Sheppard Robson and photo by Adrian Lambert

The Best of Globe winners are selected from the programme’s Best of Region winners. Winners receive global media exposure and a donation to a charity of their choice.

Shaw Contract’s ambition for the award programme is to encourage discourse within the international creative community.

To learn more about Shaw Contract and the awards programme, visit its website here.

items.articleBody:
Takumi Kama, “The First Appearance KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L162×W130.3×H3.5cm(F100)

In Japanese pop culture, a kaiju is a mythical monster of great proportions. They have long been symbols of chaos and destruction, serving society as cathartic vehicles to dealing with difficult times and challenging situations. In media, they could symbolically manifest as World War II and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, or natural disasters that make humankind feel powerless in the face of nature. More than anything, though, kaiju represent the consequences of human actions—or inactions.

These fantastical creatures inspired Japanese artist Takumi Kama to tackle a more recent and universal topic. In his aptly titled KAIJU series, these towering beasts aren’t made of flesh and blood. Instead, their bodies are an accumulation of the things we consume and quickly discard, whether physical or digital. “In other words,” the artist says, “it exists like a mirror reflecting us—the very people who are looking at this work—and perhaps it could even be described as a self-portrait of us as human beings.”

These kaiju loom in dark alleys and the morning fog, for which they can be accidentally run into. Some feature imagery from the Edo period, as the artist wonders how these creatures would have looked in that time, while others are more contemporary, made up of pixels or pop culture, junk food, and plastic trinkets.

Kama recently presented his work at Art Taipei, where he was one of the most talked about creatives for his unique approach to modern culture and our increasingly digitalized lives. As such, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery, which represents the artist, will offer plenty of chances to check out the artist’s work from up close. From late December 2026 through early January 2027, the gallery will present many of Kama’s works in an annual exhibition centered on the theme of the Chinese zodiac, spotlighting the artist’s charming and playful style.

Next year, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery will open a dual exhibition featuring Kama and fellow Japanese painter Hisashi Matsumoto in March. Before that, his work will be exhibited at Osaka International Art 2027, taking place January 29-31, 2027 (VIP Preview on January 28, 2027).

We had the opportunity to talk to Kama about the story behind the kaiju motif, his creative process, and what he hopes people will take away from his work. Read on for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview with Takumi Kama.

Takumi Kama, “Ishibe-Koji KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L116.7×W91×H3.2cm(F50)

How did your art journey begin?

My journey into art began with my childhood environment. I grew up in a single-parent household and spent much of my time at my grandparents’ home. Drawing became a way for me to escape feelings of loneliness and boredom.

When my grandparents saw my drawings, they were genuinely impressed. Their reactions made me incredibly happy, encouraging me to draw even more enthusiastically. This was my earliest formative experience with art.

Takumi Kama, “Shrine and KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic on cotton mounted on wood panel. 53 × 45.5 cm (F10)

What’s your creative process like?

I don’t usually sit down with the intention of deliberately coming up with an idea for an artwork. Instead, as I go about my daily life with my family, I take note of things that feel unusual or strike me as interesting. I repeatedly reflect on why these particular things have affected me, and as they gradually become connected to concrete imagery in my mind, they eventually develop into artworks. As a result, I have no shortage of ideas. However, only a relatively small number of them ultimately develop into finished works.

Takumi Kama, “Digital KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L91×W72.7×H3.2cm(F30)

What inspires your compositions?

My approach to composition and the arrangement of elements within an image varies from one artwork or series to another. This is because each work has its own focal points and themes, and the composition needs to communicate them as effectively as possible.

To achieve this, I don’t limit myself to the conventional principles of pictorial composition. I also draw inspiration from a wide range of visual expressions, including cinema, video games, and manga.

Takumi Kama, “THE Anatomy of KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L162×W130.3×H3.5cm(F100)

What is the inspiration behind the KAIJU series?

It began one morning when I was taking out the rubbish. As I stood before a large pile of discarded waste, I suddenly sensed something in it. Looking around the neighborhood, I noticed that rubbish was scattered everywhere. The sheer quantity of it suddenly sent a chill down my spine.

I began imagining all these discarded objects piling up higher and higher, eventually merging into something enormous that was slowly stirring and moving. That real-life experience became the initial concept for the KAIJU series.

Takumi Kama, “Morning Mist KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L116.7×W91×H3.2cm(F50)

Can you explain more about the decision to depict kaiju made of many things?

The kaiju are formed from vast quantities of discarded objects. These are things that were once needed by someone, but eventually became unwanted and were thrown away. Today, however, waste is no longer limited to physical objects. We also constantly generate and discard enormous amounts of digital information, images, and data. Even when these things are no longer visible or actively used, they leave behind a kind of virtual residue. I am interested in how this less tangible form of accumulation might also be understood as a contemporary form of waste, and how kaiju could embody the things we produce, consume, and eventually forget in our increasingly digital lives.

In Japan, there has long been a belief that spirits or deities reside in all things in the natural world. There are also traditional stories about tsukumogami (付喪神), in which spirits or divine beings inhabit not only natural elements such as mountains, rivers, and stones, but also objects made by human hands. Perhaps each of the countless discarded objects that make up the kaiju’s body also contains its own spirit or deity.

I sometimes wonder whether the kaiju has appeared in order to communicate something to us, as we continue to pursue a mass-consumption society while forgetting these traditional beliefs.

Takumi Kama, “Vending Machine and KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic on cotton mounted on wood panel. 53 × 45.5 cm (F10)

Do you remember your earliest encounter with kaiju imagery? How has your perception of it evolved?

For me, the existence of kaiju is closely connected to the act of drawing itself. As I mentioned in my first answer, the very subjects I was passionately drawing as a child were monsters. To keep me entertained, my grandparents repeatedly showed me television programs featuring Godzilla, Gamera, and Ultraman. I was fascinated by these enormous monsters and became absorbed in drawing them. I believe it was my encounter with these monsters that first made me so passionate about drawing. As a child, I admired monsters almost as heroic figures. However, as I grew older, my perception of them gradually changed.

I became increasingly interested in questions such as why Japan, a relatively small island nation, has repeatedly produced such enormous threats in its cultural imagination. Attack on Titan, for example, is another work that touches on this fascination. Today, I am drawn not only to the monsters themselves, but also to the human imagination that has given rise to them.

Takumi Kama, “Utopia,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L72.7×W60.6×H2.4cm(F20)

From your perspective, how does it connect to your larger body of work?

Until now, I have created works that reconsider human activity through the relationship between people and animals. I primarily chose animals as my subjects, depicting them in ways that brought them closer to human activities. Through this approach, I sought to reveal the true nature of human beings as animals belonging to the primate family.

However, as I continued working, the scale of the issues and the sense of urgency I felt around mass production, mass consumption, and environmental problems grew increasingly significant. I gradually realized that depicting the relationship between humans and animals alone was no longer sufficient to express these concerns. It was in this context that I encountered the idea of kaiju.

Kaiju are not animals. Unlike my earlier works, they do not depict lions, elephants, or polar bears. Yet, to me, these kaiju are beings that encompass even those wild animals. I see them as something resembling the Earth itself, possessing both a physical form and a will of their own.

My longstanding interest in the human being as an animal remains at the heart of my work. However, through my encounter with kaiju, I feel that my focus has expanded to another level: from examining human beings as animals to contemplating the very existence of humanity itself.

In some of my more recent works, I have introduced settings inspired by the Edo period. By placing kaiju within a historical landscape, I wanted to explore the relationship between humans, nature, and the environment from a different perspective. Looking back at a time when people’s lives were more closely connected to the natural world also offers a way to reflect on how our relationship with nature has changed through modernization, mass production, and consumption. Although the works are set in a historical context, the questions they raise are very much about the present.

Takumi Kama, “Polar Bear in a Bear hoodie,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L41×W31.8×H2.1cm(F6)

What materials and media do you work with, and what do you like about each of them?

My materials are quite traditional: I paint on wooden panels covered with cotton canvas, using acrylic paint. The technique itself is relatively simple.

At university, I studied the fundamentals of oil painting, tracing its techniques back to classical methods. I initially worked with oil paint, but gradually became interested in issues associated with its aging over time, such as yellowing and cracking. This led me to explore acrylic paint, a relatively modern medium. Although acrylic painting has a shorter history and its techniques are not as fully established as those of oil painting, I find the process of exploring and developing its possibilities appealing. I am also attracted to its potential for long-term durability.

Takumi Kama, “Penguin Snow Globe,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L41×W31.8×H2.1cm(F6)

What do you hope people will take away from your work?

I don’t intend to present viewers with a single definitive answer through my work. I want to avoid simply imposing my own concerns on viewers from the position of an artist. Instead, I would rather stand alongside them and invite them to consider these questions together, as if saying, “Shall we talk about this?”

To me, an artwork is like a table around which we sit together to have that conversation. Even as we enjoy convenient and comfortable lives, there are moments when we experience a sense of unease about something. Normally, it is easy to turn away from these feelings and forget about them. But I believe art can give us an opportunity to pause and reconsider the things that might otherwise go unnoticed. If someone who encounters my work happens to experience a similar sense of unease at some point in their future, and my work comes back to mind, perhaps prompting them to think differently or imagine an alternative future, I could not be happier.

Takumi Kama, “The Monkey King,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L33.3×W24.2×H2.1cm(F4)

items.articleBody:
Did President Donald Trump make a post calling Vice President JD Vance "Judas Disloyal Vance" following the 2026 midterm elections? No, that's not true: The president did not make such a post on his official Truth Social account, and a search of an archive of his posts found no such entry. Lead Stories found no reports from established news outlets of Trump using the phrase.

The claim appeared in a post (archived here) on X where it was published by @miribobs on Nov. 10, 2026. The post's caption read:

Aww, the Bromance is over, do you think Vance with [sic] start calling him 'America's hitler' again?

This is what the image included in the post looked like on X at the time of publication:

(Image source: post by @miribobs on X.)

The text in the image read:

I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally
changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!
Nobody gave JD more than President Trump. I took him
from the sidelines and gave him the biggest job of his
life-and now he thinks he can DOUBLE CROSS THE
BOSS and run for President in 2028 without my blessing?
EHHH!
WRONG!
You don't walk into the Trump Family, eat at the table,
kiss the ring, and then decide you're the new Boss!
There is only ONE person who can make America Great
Again the RIGHT WAY, and everybody knows who that is.
JD, you may have forgotten who made you-but I NEVER
forget!
THE PRESIDENT HAS SPOKEN.

There is no evidence that Trump ever made this post. The details in the supposed screenshot -- such as the username being @realDonaldTrump and the inclusion of the repost metric "ReTruths" -- suggest that the post would have been made on Trump's official Truth Social account (archived here). However, some of the details do not exactly match the appearance of the platform, such as the colors of the Truth+ Premium badge icon and the format of the date of the fake post. The date included on the image showed that the post was allegedly made on Nov 5, 2026, just a couple of days after the 2026 midterm elections (archived here). Lead Stories manually reviewed Trump's account for posts made from Nov. 4, 2026, to Nov. 10, 2026. There was no post calling Vance "Judas Disloyal."

An archive of Trump's Truth Social posts, Trump's Truth (archived here), keeps a record, including deleted posts, from the president's official account. A search of the archive for "JUDAS DISLOYAL" (archived here) did not return any results.

Had Trump made such disparaging comments about Vance, would likely have been widely reported by news outlets. Searches of Google News (archived here) and Yahoo News (archived here) for the claim did not return any matching results from established news outlets.

items.articleBody:
Today, the Literary Arts Fund announced the inaugural winners of a new major literary prize: The Stylus Award, which recognizes nonprofits making essential contributions in the literary world.

This award is designed to highlight the many literary organizations that keep the industry honest and lovable. In accordance with this mission, the awardees were culled from writers’ nominations; to make their shortlist, the Literary Arts Fund queried dozens of authors across the U.S. about the groups that have fueled their writing.

This year’s three big winners represent respectively a small publisher, a prestigious literary magazine, and a beloved community. They are Graywolf Press, One Story, and The Porch Writers’ Collective.

Each of these nonprofits will receive an unrestricted cash award of $250,000 to further their work. In a season of slashed budgets and disappeared arts funding, this is welcome news.

As One Story founders wrote in a collective email sent this afternoon, “this is a transformational moment” for the magazine.

As a nonprofit dedicated to supporting short story authors—providing them publication, education, and mentorship—we see this award as an affirmation of our mission and the profound impact of the literary arts field on writers’ creative lives. It is also a catalyst for a broader investment in One Story’s next chapter: raising the strength, resources, and capacity that will allow us to do our best work and think beyond immediate needs toward a more ambitious, long-term vision.

Give it up for the literary orgs that make great writing—and great writing community—possible.

Release: llm-gemini 0.36

Gemini 4 Carbon was announced two weeks ago for "a subset of cyber defenders", but today it's available to everyone else.

This is Google's best ever Gemini, priced at $2/million input and $10/million output at launch (that's GPT-6.1 Sol / Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices) but scheduled to double in price to $4/$20 on December 1st (same as Opus 5.5).

Here are three pelicans for the low, medium and high thinking efforts (it defaults to medium). This is the pelican I got for high:

Gemini pelicans have all been great for a while now, so I also tested it out using Google's Antigravity IDE with a prompt I first tried with Claude Fable 5.2 yesterday:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the HTML result (I had to prompt "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies). I then screen-captured that as a video:

Update: Huh, just saw this on YouTube:

Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music.

items.articleBody:
Maybe so:

We study the statistical credibility of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in development economics and the optimal allocation of resources to replication. Using 745 principal-hypothesis tests from 190 articles in leading economics journals, we find that actual t-statistics peak well below the theoretical benchmark of 2.8 expected under 80 percent power, though above values associated with p-hacking. This suggests many RCTs are underpowered. Estimating an empirical Bayes mixture model that accounts for selective publication, we find that approximately 30 percent of published rejections are false discoveries, with average directional power at only 40 percent. At conventional significance thresholds, the posterior probability of a false discovery reaches 66 percent. Doubling original sample sizes lowers the average false discovery rate by five percentage points, whereas tightening the significance threshold to 0.005 yields a larger reduction at the cost of total discoveries. Finally, we characterize a funder’s optimal replication policy under a fixed budget and an evidence standard. Under standard regularity conditions, replications concentrate in an intermediate interval of original test statistics, and the optimal replication sample size is single-peaked in the original t-statistic. Illustrative calibrations show that successful replications reduce aggregate false discovery rates to 1.8–7.8 percent, depending on the evidence standard.

That is from a new paper by Qingyuan Chai, Kevin Lang & Liang Zhong.

The post Are RCTs underpowered? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

items.articleBody:
Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare.

So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player?

Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025, on the pod today:

In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models.

Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday.

The developer gets there before the model

Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email

Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question.

80 tools, or two?

When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server, which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute().

Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs.

What happens after “send”?

Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment

Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use.

Show notes

Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013.

Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions.

Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion.

Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window.

Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes.

items.articleBody:
For most animals, plants, and other life forms, fire is the worst thing that can happen. It's deadly, and even if you escape, your environment is ruined. But wildfires have always been a part of earth's activities, and some species have evolved to use it to their benefit. For example, the fire lily bulb stays dormant in the ground until after a wildfire rages through. Then it grows and blooms without competition from other plants!

Plants that grow in the ashes of a wildfire attracts bugs, and then bugs attract birds. It's almost as if there's a system to heal and renew the environment after it is devastated by fire. There are other species that are attracted to wildfires, as strange as that seems, and even one that will actively spread a fire. SciScow introduces us to how all this works. items.articleBody:
Namit Arora at Shunya’s Notes:

My first time with psilocybin turned out to be a dazzlingly vivid, emotionally intense and deeply joyous experience, surpassing all expectations based on my pre-reading. I felt an intense outpouring of love and a profound sense of oneness with the natural world—an experience commonly reported by psilocybin users. I have learned that many articulate people, too, find themselves at a loss for words when trying to describe their psilocybin experiences. I now understand why.

I’m still processing this powerful experience, but I’ll nevertheless try to put some of it into words, however inadequately. I’m aware that in doing so, I run the risk of looking ridiculous, certainly to those who have never ventured or desired to see the truths and realities of their world from anything other than the ‘default settings’ of their contingent brain chemistry—one that evolution has arguably optimized for survival, rather than for apprehending truth or reality.

More here.

Preis und Verfügbarkeit:

Links

Plugin Schmidt Vi ist erhältlich

Auf der Superbooth 26 wurde das Plugin Schmidt Vi vorgestellt. Jetzt ist der Software-Klon des Schmidt Eightvoice endlich erhältlich. Schmidt betont, dass sämtliche Funktionen des Originals vollständig in das Plugin übernommen wurden und es sich um eine erstklassige Emulation handelt. Die Umbenennung vom Eightvoice Analog Synthesizer zu Schmidt Vi ist nachvollziehbar: Als Plugin kann die Software deutlich mehr Stimmen berechnen als die Hardware. Bei der Klangerzeugung selbst sollen laut Schmidt jedoch keinerlei Kompromisse gemacht worden sein.

Schmidt Eightvoice wird eingestellt

Das Erscheinen des Schmidt Vi Plugin bedeutet das Aus für die Hardware. Der Schmidt Eightvoice wird nach 15 Jahren nicht mehr hergestellt. Schmidt kündigt an, noch 20 Exemplare in einer limitierten Auflage mit dem Namen „Final Series“ bauen zu wollen. Wenn ihr also noch einen Schmidt-Synthesizer haben möchtet, ist jetzt die letzte Gelegenheit zuzuschlagen.

Hier geht es zum Schmidt Eightv)oice Test

Schmidt Vi und Deck (Bildquelle: Schmidt )

Schmidt Vi (Mai 2026)

Bei Schmidt Vi handelt es sich dabei um eine virtuelle Version des Schmidt Synthesizers. Entwickelt wurde das Plug-in in Zusammenarbeit mit UJAM. Das Plugin wird in den Formaten VST3, AU und AAX verfügbar sein.

Schmidt Vi Plug-in (Bildquelle: Schmidt)

Wie Schmidt erklärt, ist der originale Schmidt Synthesizer seit rund 12 Jahren auf dem Markt und wird von zahlreichen Musikern und Studios weltweit eingesetzt.

Mit dem neuen Schmidt Vi bringen sie diesen nun erstmals als Plugin heraus. Entwickelt wurde die Software in Zusammenarbeit mit UJAM. Das Plugin wird in den Formaten VST3, AU und AAX verfügbar sein.

Schmidt Deck

Zusätzlich wurde die Software Schmidt Deck vorgestellt. Mit dieser lassen sich Sounds spielen, die auf dem Hardware Schmidt-Synthesizer erstellt wurden. Von diesen Sounds können laut Hersteller mit den Bedienelementen des Plug-ins Variationen hergestellt werden.

Pressemitteilung (Bildquelle: Schmidt)

Schmidt Synthesizer (Mai 2026)

Wenn es um Superschlachtschiff-Synthesizer der absoluten Luxusklasse geht, denken viele sofort an den Schmidt Synthesizer. Umso spannender ist es, dass Schmidt für die Superbooth offenbar eine Überraschung vorbereitet.

Hier geht es zum Schmidt Synthesizer Test.

Der Schmidt Synthesizer (Bildquelle: Schmidt)

Schmidt Deck Teaser (Mai 2026)

Schmidt präsentiert auf der Superbooth einen neuen Synthesizer namens „Deck”, von dem bis jetzt nur ein Teaser Bild bekannt ist.

Dass das Unternehmen dort seinen bekannten Schmidt-Synthesizer präsentiert, ist wenig überraschend. Interessant wird es jedoch durch ein Teaser-Bild, auf dem ein bislang unbekanntes Gerät mit der Bezeichnung „Deck“ zu sehen ist. Worum es sich dabei genau handelt, bleibt bislang ein Geheimnis.

Das Werbebild ist zudem mit der Unterschrift „C Vi – The Virtual Recreation of a Dream“ versehen. Das lässt Raum für Spekulationen: Möglicherweise arbeitet Schmidt an einem Software-Synthesizer oder sogar an einem Plug-in für den Schmidt-Synthesizer, sofern sich ein solches Konzept überhaupt sinnvoll und realistisch umsetzen lässt.

Teaser mit Deck (Bildquelle: Schmidt auf Facebook)

Fest steht: Das „Deck“ wirkt deutlich kompakter als der große Schmidt-Synthesizer. Zu erkennen sind unter anderem ein Joystick, etwa 17 Regler sowie rund 22 Taster. Besonders auffällig ist ein schräg eingebautes Touch-Display, das sich scheinbar über die gesamte Breite des Desktop-Geräts erstreckt. Auch ein Holzgehäuse scheint wieder Teil des Designs zu sein.

Was Schmidt hier genau vorstellen wird, bleibt abzuwarten. Bis dahin lohnt sich ein Blick auf den Schmidt Synthesizer Test, um ein Gefühl dafür zu bekommen, auf welchem Niveau dieses Unternehmen arbeitet.

Schmidt Vi Plug-in (Bildquelle: Schmidt)

Preis und Verfügbarkeit:

items.articleBody:
An artist’s concept depicting a Voyager spacecraft.

Launched nearly 50 years ago in 1977, NASA’s Voyager 1 on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will have traveled one light-day from Earth, which is more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, and any light from Earth would take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. NASA will highlight this historic milestone with two events.

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, NASA invites the world to participate in “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day” by creating a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset. NASA has created a website that enables smart phones and tablets to flash “VGR”, Voyager’s call sign, in morse code.

For more information about how to participate in “Shine Bright for Voyager Light-Day,” visit:

go.nasa.gov/shinebright

Everyone is encouraged to capture photos or videos of their light-day signal and share it on social platforms, tagging @NASA.

On Thursday, Nov. 19 at 12 p.m. EST (9 a.m. PST), NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with mission members and NASA leadership about the status of Voyager 1 and 2, the unique science the twin probes continue to gather in interstellar space, and the challenges of keeping the spacecraft operating for so long over such vast distances. A Q&A with media and other audience members will follow. In addition, there also will be a preview of the upcoming NASA+ Voyager documentary, planned for release in 2027 for the mission’s 50th anniversary.

The event will take place in NASA JPL’s von Kármán Auditorium, where JPL hosted Voyager briefings during the spacecraft’s grand tour of the outer planets.

The participants will be:

Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, Washington

Jonathan Lunine, chief scientist, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Southern California, and professor of planetary science, Caltech

Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, NASA JPL

Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager, NASA JPL

Jamie Rankin, Voyager deputy project scientist, Princeton University

Learn where to watch online at:

https://www.nasa.gov/live

U.S. media interested in attending the event in person must RSVP by Monday, Nov. 16 to Josh Smooha at: josh.smooha@jpl.nasa.gov. To be considered for onsite credentials, foreign national media must RSVP no later than Thursday, Nov. 12. Media interested in participating virtually must RSVP no later than two hours before the event. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online.

For almost half a century, the agency’s Voyager mission has blazed a trail through space. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 were designed to explore the outer planets by taking advantage of a planetary alignment that occurs once every 176 years. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. Following a different trajectory, Voyager 2 entered in 2018. Both spacecraft continue to provide unique scientific observations of the environment beyond the heliosphere, the protective bubble created by the Sun.

Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, NASA JPL built and operates the Voyager spacecraft. NASA’s Deep Space Network, also managed by NASA JPL, enables communication with the distant probes. The Voyager mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington.

For more information about NASA’s Voyager mission, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/

-end-
