items.articleBody:
Bishnu Saroop Atal
Acoustics and signal processing pioneer
Life Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

Bishnu Saroop AtalNokia Bell Labs

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.
Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois Section
Senior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold Richter
Telecommunications engineer
Life senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. Giordano
Former RCA engineer
Life member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. Wilson
President of Power Technologies
Life Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.
Electronic packaging engineer
Life Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

items.articleBody:
Israel Putnam, affectionately known as “Old Put,” was a prominent figure in American history. He served as a colonial American military officer and a Patriot hero during the American Revolutionary War. Putnam also played a significant role in the French and Indian War.

In 1775,  Congress  appointed Putnam as one of the first four major generals of the Continental Army. He commanded the New England militia forces at the Battle of Bunker Hill in June of that year. He helped organize the “Sons of Liberty” Traditionally, Putnam is credited with giving the famous order, “Don’t fire until you see the whites of their eyes.”

Tragically, Putnam suffered a stroke in 1779 and subsequently retired from military service. He passed away on May 29, 1790, in Brooklyn, Connecticut and is buried there under a large monument.

items.articleBody:
A collage showing a diagram of the key parameters of the proposed terminal, a photo of a U.S. Navy exercise in the Beaufort Sea in 2022, and two vantage points on the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System. Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Photos by Lance King/Getty Images, Justin Yarborough/U.S. Navy.

To an outsider, the research boats bobbing in the frigid and stormy Beaufort Sea off Alaska would seem little cause for alarm. Oil and gas companies have regularly explored the area for decades.

For this project, businessmen from the United Arab Emirates were touting a plan to tap the vast natural gas reserves that lay beneath the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope. They promised the operation would eventually be American-owned. No one could dispute Alaska’s dire energy needs — not to mention the potential for lucrative exports.

The surveyors last year used specialized equipment to map the depth and shape of the seabed, collect samples of shallow marine sediments and conduct sonar scans to check for obstructions such as shipwrecks. Documents show that their work was not far, as the crow flies, from the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System — a cornerstone of U.S. energy production. An Air Force long-range radar station sat just to the west. More than 100 miles off the coast, the Navy’s fast-attack nuclear submarines sometimes practiced surfacing through the thick Arctic ice.

But this project was far from routine. While the contractors performing the work were American, the UAE company paying for the surveys was actually being steered by Russia’s liquefied natural gas giant, Novatek — a company under partial U.S. sanctions, documents and interviews show.

The proposal to create an LNG processing plant on Alaska’s coast has already put reams of scientific data about the strategically critical region within reach of Novatek’s leader, an oligarch who is close to President Vladimir Putin, a ProPublica investigation found.

The Financial Times and The New York Times reported on the Russian ties to the venture last month. But the extent to which the company gathered detailed information about sensitive areas of Alaska has not been previously disclosed.

Such information is highly valuable in the ever-changing and unpredictable Arctic, with its potential routes for both naval ships and missiles. Norwegian security services and U.S. lawmakers have expressed concerns this year about the danger of increased spy and sabotage operations by Russia in the Arctic.

Russia-backed information gathering so close to the U.S. shoreline can be seen as “a direct challenge to sovereignty and security,” said Heather Conley, a former State Department official who is now a senior fellow with the American Enterprise Institute.

“It’s super, super sensitive,” she said, adding, “Any scientific data, it immediately is dual use,” meaning it can serve both military and civilian ends.

Information on changing sea ice and other conditions off the North Slope could help Russia plan activities that undermine U.S. security, said Troy Bouffard, director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The fact that the surveys were given permits and done without interference could be seen as an intelligence failure, he said.

Bouffard added that it’s “highly unlikely” that intelligence personnel didn’t learn of the effort because any work in the austere, remote and militarily sensitive North Slope area stands out.

“All this is really surprising,” Bouffard said. “Should not have happened.”

The surveys were conducted in the second half of 2025, paused during harsh weather, then restarted in mid-2026, documents and sources say. By late August 2026, dozens of contractors were stationed on three large vessels — the Annika Marie, the Ukpik and the Uŋalaq — loaded with equipment for tasks such as monitoring waves, testing currents, and tides, and drilling core samples in the mud, according to a person familiar with the situation.

Then, in September, the CEO of the project’s U.S. arm, Polar Train LNG, resigned, questioned the operation’s legality and asserted it was a Russian ploy to gain control of a strategic U.S. asset, Alaska’s natural gas reserves.

In 2025, the survey work was focused on an area just west of Prudhoe Bay, which is near where the pipeline originates, documents and sources say. The next year, as the area thawed, Polar Train’s CEO, Joel Riddle, and his team told his financiers that location was not ideal for an LNG operation because of the high cost of dredging that would be needed and the potential to interfere with whaling by local residents. They urged the company’s UAE parent to focus on a site more than 250 miles to the west.

A page from a Tech Wave presentation on plans to locate a liquified natural gas operation in Alaska. Polar Train LNG is a subsidiary of UAE-based Tech Wave. Reviewed by ProPublica

But the UAE company asserted its control over the purportedly American outfit Riddle led in late August and ordered the contractors offshore to head back to a site closer to Prudhoe Bay. Riddle resigned the next month, on Sept. 19, warning that Polar Train’s “investments” were “very likely sooner or later to trigger” a federal inquiry.

Polar Train had applied to the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control the month before, seeking a waiver of U.S. sanctions to allow it to purchase a partially built LNG plant sitting in a Murmansk, Russia, shipyard and transport it to Alaska.

“Deploying this technology in Alaska serves not only to unlock U.S. LNG resources in the Pacific basin closer to key export markets in Asia,” said the application, which ProPublica obtained, “but also to ensure this cutting-edge equipment is deployed primarily to the benefit of the United States rather than Russia.”

The six-page application did not make clear who was behind the effort, steering the financing and decision-making needed to get the venture off the ground. The document’s digital properties held a clue: Many computer applications include what is known as metadata in a document that can reveal who has previously worked on it. In this instance, the OFAC application was signed by a lawyer in Washington, D.C., but the author’s name was listed in the metadata in Cyrillic: Evgeniya Kononova, a lawyer whose LinkedIn profile says she is deputy head of legal for Novatek in Moscow.

Novatek said in a statement to ProPublica that it “provided technical and other information” about its equipment for the waiver request, providing “comments to the draft application.” The company did not answer a list of specific questions, including inquiries about Kononova’s role.

It’s not clear whether the Russian natural gas executives backing the project hope to operate an LNG plant in Alaska or have a more immediate goal in mind — like finishing the incomplete plant that sanctions had stranded in Russia or gathering intelligence for the Kremlin in a strategically important region.

In a statement to ProPublica, Novatek denied it is gathering intelligence through the project, saying: “We state clearly and categorically: any such claims or implications are false.”

Novatek said it is “focused on utilizing its technology in Alaska and views this opportunity as a standalone and self-sufficient project.” The company said decisions about the project’s surveys “and other operational matters” were made by Polar Train and its UAE parent, Tech Wave Industrial Project Management.

The revelations about the Alaska LNG project come as the Trump administration has scaled back rules requiring U.S. companies to report their true owners, cut back counterintelligence squads in the FBI and disbanded a Department of Justice task force aimed at seizing Russian oligarchs’ assets.

Reduced staffing makes counterintelligence more difficult, said Emily Harding, a former CIA analyst and former deputy director of the Senate intelligence committee under Republicans.

“It’s not just that you need people knowledgeable about the counterintelligence mission, but you need people knowledgeable about highly technical topical areas,” she said. “That’s a big problem in normal times, but especially hard when staffing is down.”

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment last week.

ProPublica’s account of the Polar Train LNG project is drawn from interviews with a dozen people and documents that include corporate records, correspondence, and memos, as well as presentations detailing the survey work, budgets, a wire transfer receipt, and loan agreements.

On Saturday, Polar Train LNG said its research in Alaska “involved a standard set of surveys routinely conducted by companies worldwide.” The data collected is not classified, it said, and “all activities complied with applicable laws.” The purpose of the work was to find an appropriate site for the LNG project, the company said.

The White House has sought to leverage energy deals involving Russia as an incentive to negotiate an end to the war with Ukraine. Putin has spoken publicly about his desire to cooperate with the U.S. in the Arctic, potentially through Novatek.

“We are discussing with our American partners the possibility of working together in this field, not only in our Arctic zone but also in Alaska,” he said in August 2025, days after meeting with Trump at a summit in Anchorage.

In September, Putin talked about Polar Train LNG’s project with President Donald Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, The New York Times reported last month. Polar Train’s U.S. parent has also filed an application with the Treasury Department in hopes of importing LNG to Alaska directly from Russia, according to a person familiar with the request.

When he resigned as CEO, Riddle accused Novatek of “financing and ultimately controlling the strategic direction” of the supposedly American-led Polar Train.

Polar Train, now under new leadership, denied that Novatek is “secretly financing” the project, in a statement it posted on its website.

All three companies said Novatek had agreed to buy a minority stake in the Alaska operation and had paid Tech Wave an undisclosed amount of money. The deal, they said, is contingent on Tech Wave attracting American investment totaling more than 50%. Novatek simultaneously said it “did not provide any funding to the Project.”

”We would like to note, however, that provision of debt financing, including to U.S. persons, is not prohibited.” Novatek did not answer questions from ProPublica about whether it has provided debt financing to the Alaska project.

In its website statement, Polar Train called Riddle “a disgruntled employee” and said he was “recently terminated from the company for cause.”

“You can’t legally terminate someone who’s already resigned,” Riddle said. Tech Wave’s termination notice, which accused Riddle of announcing plans to launch a competing LNG project, was dated six days after his resignation, copies of both documents show. The notice was signed by a new acting CEO, Tim Talkington.

In a statement to ProPublica on Saturday, Talkington said that the U.S. has “a generational opportunity to advance U.S. energy dominance, unlock profound benefits for the state of Alaska, and strengthen American Arctic navigation.”

An Audacious Plan

A schematic drawing of the liquified natural gas processing facility Polar Train LNG is asking to bring to Alaska Polar Train OFAC waiver application

The audacious LNG project was launched in 2025, when a half dozen executives with ExxonMobil sat down with representatives of Abu Dhabi-based Tech Wave Industrial Project Management, which was eyeing Alaska for an LNG facility, according to a person familiar with the project.

Tech Wave was 95% owned by Norwegian Bjorn Gundersen. He’d served as a deputy director for Novatek and played a key role in developing one of the most technologically ambitious LNG projects ever, known as Arctic LNG 2, on the Gydan Peninsula in Russia’s Far North. Gundersen and Tech Wave’s CEO, Rajeev Lehar, assured Exxon and others that no Russian money was involved in their project, the person said.

Tech Wave said in a statement Saturday that “Novatek offers the only proven technology suited to Arctic conditions” that also meets the project’s timeline. The company’s expertise is “informed in part” by Gundersen’s experience working on Arctic LNG 2, the company said.

Reached in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, Gundersen declined to comment. Exxonmobil did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech Wave’s plan was to seek permission to buy state-of-the-art natural gas equipment from Novatek that was meant for Arctic LNG 2 before U.S. economic sanctions prevented the company from finishing the work. The incomplete apparatus, built atop a concrete platform that is the size of nearly 10 football fields, was sitting in a Russian shipyard. Tech Wave wanted to bring the equipment by sea to Alaska’s North Slope, where it could begin processing and selling millions of metric tons of liquified natural gas that had been trapped in the ground for decades. The project would need to reach an agreement with the oil and gas companies already working in the area, since the natural gas it wanted was a byproduct of their extraction work.

Tech Wave had been exploring possible sites for the plant in the summer of 2025, before its leaders met with the Exxon executives, according to documents obtained by ProPublica and interviews.

It also dispatched the first group of surveyors who worked off the coast near Prudhoe Bay, collecting detailed information about the seabed.

Riddle was hired in March 2026 as Polar Train LNG’s CEO. Documents show his employment agreement was signed by Gentry Beach, a Texas investor who was a college friend of Donald Trump Jr. and helped raise money for President Trump’s campaign in 2016. Beach, who took part in meetings about the Alaska project, later told The Financial Times that he had an “incredible relationship” with oligarch Leonid Mikhelson, the Novatek founder and CEO.

Beach did not respond to requests for comment. Novatek said “Gentry Beach has no connection” with the company.

Riddle previously led the Australian fracking operation Tamboran Resources, where he developed a business relationship with Chris Wright, who was confirmed as Trump’s energy secretary in February 2025. Wright had been CEO of the fracking giant Liberty Energy, which partnered with Tamboran in 2023.

Leonid Mikhelson, the founder and chief of Russia’s largest private gas group, Novatek, on July 20, 2023 Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images

It wasn’t long before the actions of the UAE leaders made Riddle suspicious about who was behind the company and what their motives were.

Early on, Riddle said he and his team sought information on how Tech Wave spent tens of millions of dollars before he came on the project, including doing the surveys. “They were very hesitant to provide details around the cost or origin of the money that supported the company before I was hired,” Riddle said.

Riddle said Gundersen wanted to locate the LNG plant just off the coast near Prudhoe Bay, an area that includes the largest oil field in North America, the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and operations by companies that include Exxon, ConocoPhillips and Hilcorp. The site is near, too, to the Oliktok Long Range Radar Site. Such installations watch for inbound missiles and aircraft and play a critical role in national defense because satellites don’t have good visibility over the poles. Prudhoe Bay is a key location, as well, for communications infrastructure supporting the military and residents in northern Alaska, through a subsea fiber optic cable that originates there and stretches to Nome.

Riddle advised Tech Wave to consider a different site, near Wainwright, saying it would require less dredging and would not interfere with whaling by Alaska residents. He hired another team of surveyors for about $10 million to scope out that area, records and interviews show.

At the time, Riddle was becoming concerned that the operation was not truly the work of Abu Dhabi-based investors, but instead was controlled by Novatek, and its CEO, Mikhelson, who has close ties to Putin.

In meetings throughout the summer, Riddle and other Polar Train executives met with Novatek executives including Mikhelson, according to documents reviewed by ProPublica and interviews with Riddle. Tech Wave also employed several others who had worked for Novatek besides Gundersen, according to social media profiles and documents.

On Aug. 14, Polar Train formally requested permission from the Treasury to import parts into Russia to complete construction of the LNG processor, and then to allow Polar Train to buy the plant and bring it to Alaska.

Riddle said his efforts to secure U.S. backing for the project met resistance from his funders. “For months now, there has been no engagement on productively achieving substantial US shareholding,” he told Gundersen in a September letter.

Riddle and his team consulted lawyers on how to handle sanctions issues related to the project — including concerns from Treasury personnel that Gundersen “may be acting on behalf” of Novatek. In an Aug. 3 letter, the firm Baker Botts told Riddle those concerns “could result in heightened regulatory scrutiny of the Project even absent a direct sanctions prohibition.”

Records show Polar Train’s funding, on paper, came in the form of loans from Tech Wave and Gundersen.

In late August, however, Riddle asked Gundersen and Lehar for more funding for Polar Train. In response to his request, he said, an employee connected him via WhatsApp to Denis Solovyov — a deputy of Mikhelson’s at Novatek. Solovyov — who has been lobbying in Brussels and Washington against tougher sanctions on Russian energy — promised Riddle he would send money. Solovyov did not respond to a request for comment.

Joel RiddleDenis – in our meeting on Tuesday, you committed to facilitating the new funding by the end of this week. Can you please let me know the status? Thanks. 9:03amDenis SolovyovThe initial funds are already on their way; for stable financing, I need an approved budget and a weekly payment schedule.10:40 amAugust 21, 2026

Messages show Solovyov and Riddle discussed unpaid bills, payroll, budgets and loan proceeds sent to Polar Train, which were routed through as many as three other companies, records show.

Joel RiddleDenis – I have now received confirmation that all information requested by Rashid and Catherine has been provided. It is critical that the new funding agreed is wired on the morning of Aug 27th. If funding is not received, Polar will not be able to make payroll for its employees and pay critical bills, which will negatively impact the reputation of the company.1:07amDenis SolovyovJoel, Katerina confirmed to me that the funds should be in your account on the morning of August 27. We are doing everything we can.1:46amJoel RiddleThanks Denis 1:47amDenis SolovyovHow did your meeting in Alaska go?1:52amJoel RiddleDinner just finished, Secretary Wright is very supportive. I also have a 1:1 planned with him tomorrow1:54amAugust 27, 2026

In the meantime, Riddle had dispatched boats to survey his preferred project site near Wainwright. But Tech Wave pushed to move the operation back to Prudhoe Bay, which it said would be quicker and cheaper. Lehar, Tech Wave’s CEO, sent Polar Train orders Aug. 20 to tell contractors to “cease and suspend works and services related to the Wainwright site.”

That day, Tech Wave also asserted its control over Polar Train’s spending, directing Riddle to follow a budget it provided. The plan allocated $13 million for summer field surveys near Prudhoe Bay that included studies of the seabed, weather and oceanographic conditions, records show. The UAE company also barred Riddle from obtaining any financing for Polar Train without Tech Wave’s approval.

Tensions between the American executives and their backers in UAE and Russia culminated in a meeting in a lavish private suite at the Four Seasons Hotel in Abu Dhabi between Riddle and Mikhelson on Aug. 31. Riddle said he tried again to convince Mikhelson and Tech Wave that Wainwright was the only location that made sense for the project. Mikhelson told Riddle that a Prudhoe Bay area site was non-negotiable. Riddle told him he’d consider their position and do what was in the best interest of the company.

In the days that followed, Riddle again became concerned about making payroll.

“Denis please confirm the new funding that was agreed last Monday will be transferred no later than Monday 7th,” Riddle wrote on Sept. 6 to Mikhelson’s deputy. In Solovyov’s next message to Riddle in the chat the following day, he wrote that “the first 5 million were supposed to arrive by today.”

Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank on Sept. 7 wired $5 million from Tech Wave to a holding company called Polar Eagle, the U.S. parent company of Polar Train, records show. A Tech Wave employee messaged Riddle the next day saying that “PE is making a wire transfer to PT.”

Tech Wave’s funding came via a loan from a UAE financial services company, records say.

In statements, Tech Wave and Polar Train LNG said the company has been “funded exclusively by Tech Wave, through both personal investments by Mr. Gundersen and borrowed funds.”

Joel RiddleDenis – I just had calls with both EDF and State – this was to introduce the potential Murmansk trip in late Sept. I noticed from both of these calls there was a material uptick in anti-Russia sentiment. I’ll continue to push on the trip but wanted to just share this feedback – how should I respond?9:59amDenis SolovyovJoel, thanks for the information. How is this anti-Russian sentiment manifesting itself? Positive news should be coming our soon. Besides, the Graham Act is currently on hold.12:39pmSeptember 3, 2026

The Graham Act, which was named for the late South Carolina Sen. Lindsay Graham and expanded the sanctions on Russia, was signed into law Sept. 18. Riddle resigned the next day, and several others followed.

“They wanted to have Russian technology controlling the resource and the North Slope,” Riddle said. “I just felt like that was not in the U.S. interest.”

In meetings with energy and state officials, Riddle said he told them what he’d learned about Novatek’s backing for the project. Energy officials said they would alert the FBI, Riddle said.

With Riddle gone, Polar Train tapped Talkington, who was formerly CEO of Goldman Sachs Bank Russia in Moscow and sits on the board of Rusal, one of the world’s largest aluminum producers. The Russian company was founded by oligarch Oleg Deripaska, who is under U.S. sanctions.

Lehar said in a statement that the company is “ready to work with the Trump administration” and the state of Alaska. He said the LNG project will, among other things, “deliver jobs, tax revenue, and more affordable, reliable energy for Alaskans.”

The status of Polar Train’s application to the Treasury Department is unclear. On its website, the company says, “LNG deliveries to the market are expected in 2030.” A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment on the status of the sanctions waiver, saying the department does not comment on “specific licenses or applications, including on the existence or lack of any application.”

Arctic Spying

Russia is keenly aware of the power of information in the Arctic: In January, Russian authorities arrested an Arctic public health and environmental researcher whom they accused of treason, saying his work could help Norwegian intelligence. (He has denied the charges through a family member.)

The Trump administration’s stance on Russia is in flux. The president and his representatives have signaled that they hope to use business deals as a carrot to bring Putin to the negotiating table and end the war in Ukraine. In October, Trump signed a waiver exempting Russia from the new sanctions laid out in the Graham Act.

But other U.S. policymakers have been less sanguine. In June, U.S. Sens. Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah, and Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire, introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at stopping spy ships from countries like China and Russia from conducting research and espionage operations in U.S. waters.

“This legislation shuts the door to foreign adversaries attempting to commit espionage and exercise influence at our doorstep in the Arctic,” Lee said then, “affirming the sole right of the American people to determine who may approach their shores, from the Aleutians to the Beaufort Sea.”

The Senate has not acted on the bill.

items.articleBody:
Apple hat gestern iOS 27.2.1 für alle Nutzer veröffentlicht.

Dieses Update fürs iPhone behebt eine Reihe nicht unerheblicher Sicherheitsschwachstellen.

Sie stecken unter anderem in iMessage, Bluetooth und der AirPlay-Funktion.

Apple hat Details zu den Sicherheitskorrekturen seiner jüngsten Betriebssystemupdates veröffentlicht. Neben iOS 27.2.1 und iPadOS 27.2.1 betreffen die Aktualisierungen auch macOS, watchOS und visionOS. Unter den behobenen Schwachstellen befinden sich Probleme in iMessage, AirPlay und Bluetooth, die unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen unbefugte Zugriffe ermöglicht haben könnten.

Die Sicherheitsupdates stehen für zahlreiche aktuelle und ältere Apple-Geräte zur Verfügung. Da mehrere Betriebssysteme gemeinsame Softwarekomponenten verwenden, betreffen einige Schwachstellen unterschiedliche Geräteklassen.

iMessage-Sicherheitslücke ermöglichte möglicherweise unbefugten Gruppenzugriff

Eine der von Apple dokumentierten Schwachstellen betrifft die Nachrichten-App und insbesondere die Verwaltung von iMessage-Gruppenchats.

Nach Angaben des Unternehmens hätte ein entfernter Angreifer unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen einer bestehenden iMessage-Gruppenunterhaltung beitreten können, ohne zuvor eingeladen worden zu sein.

Ein solcher Angriff könnte die Vertraulichkeit privater Kommunikation beeinträchtigen. Welche technischen Voraussetzungen für die Ausnutzung der Schwachstelle erfüllt sein mussten, geht aus den vorliegenden Informationen nicht hervor.

Mit den aktuellen Sicherheitsupdates hat Apple das zugrunde liegende Problem nach eigenen Angaben behoben.

AirPlay und Bluetooth ebenfalls betroffen

Eine weitere Sicherheitskorrektur betrifft AirPlay und die Absicherung von Kopplungsvorgängen.

Demnach hätte ein Angreifer innerhalb der Bluetooth-Reichweite eines betroffenen Geräts eine Begrenzung für die Anzahl zulässiger Eingabeversuche bei Kopplungscodes umgehen können.

Solche Beschränkungen sollen verhindern, dass Angreifer durch wiederholtes Ausprobieren unterschiedlicher Codes unbefugt eine Verbindung herstellen.

Durch die Schwachstelle hätte diese Schutzmaßnahme unter bestimmten Bedingungen umgangen werden können. Das hätte die Möglichkeit eröffnet, Kopplungscodes mit einer größeren Zahl von Versuchen zu erraten.

Apple hat das Problem mit den aktuellen Aktualisierungen adressiert.

Weitere Sicherheitsverbesserungen betreffen nach Unternehmensangaben zusätzliche Komponenten der Betriebssysteme, darunter auch Bluetooth-Funktionen.

Auch ältere iOS-Versionen werden gepatcht

Die Sicherheitskorrekturen werden nicht ausschließlich für Geräte mit der aktuellen Betriebssystemgeneration bereitgestellt.

Apple hat insgesamt sechs Aktualisierungen für iPhones und iPads veröffentlicht beziehungsweise dokumentiert:

iOS 27.2.1 und iPadOS 27.2.1

iOS 26.7.3 und iPadOS 26.7.3

iOS 18.7.12 und iPadOS 18.7.12

Damit erhalten auch Geräte, auf denen ältere Betriebssystemversionen eingesetzt werden, weiterhin wichtige Sicherheitskorrekturen.

Welche Schwachstellen im Einzelnen für welche iPhone- und iPad-Modelle relevant sind, führt Apple in den jeweiligen Sicherheitsdokumenten auf.

Auch macOS, watchOS und visionOS erhalten Aktualisierungen

Neben den mobilen Betriebssystemen hat Apple Sicherheitsupdates für mehrere weitere Plattformen bereitgestellt.

Für Mac-Computer stehen macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 und macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 zur Verfügung.

Auch die Apple Watch wird berücksichtigt. Hier hat Apple watchOS 27.2.1 und watchOS 26.6.1 veröffentlicht.

Für die Apple Vision Pro steht visionOS 27.2.1 bereit.

Die Sicherheitskorrekturen überschneiden sich teilweise zwischen den verschiedenen Plattformen. Das liegt daran, dass Apple zahlreiche technische Grundlagen und Softwarebibliotheken in mehreren Betriebssystemen verwendet.

Eine Schwachstelle in einer gemeinsam genutzten Komponente kann deshalb beispielsweise sowohl iPhones als auch iPads oder Macs betreffen.

Apple veröffentlicht technische Details zu den Schwachstellen

Wie bei Sicherheitsupdates üblich, hat Apple für die einzelnen Betriebssystemversionen gesonderte Dokumentationen bereitgestellt.

Darin beschreibt das Unternehmen die behobenen Sicherheitsprobleme, nennt die betroffenen Geräte und erläutert die möglichen Auswirkungen der jeweiligen Schwachstellen.

Zudem werden Sicherheitsforscher und andere Personen genannt, die Apple auf die Probleme aufmerksam gemacht haben.

Die Dokumentationen ermöglichen es insbesondere Administratoren und Sicherheitsexperten, die Relevanz der einzelnen Korrekturen für ihre Geräte und IT-Umgebungen zu bewerten.

Ob die jetzt geschlossenen Sicherheitslücken bereits aktiv für Angriffe ausgenutzt wurden, geht aus den vorliegenden Angaben nicht hervor.

items.articleBody:
On the eve of a House impeachment vote, self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made a rare appearance before the Pentagon press corps. Over half an hour, he declared every military operation he has overseen “lawful” and claims of civilian harm “slander.” He said the Iran war was a great victory and only 18 Americans have died in the conflict. He also claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.”

None of it is true.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Democrats are overwhelmingly expected to join Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide. “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the presumed next House speaker.

Massie wrote on X that if his impeachment resolution advances Tuesday evening, he will request a separate vote on each of the eight articles. “I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them,” Massie wrote. “If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately.”

As Hegseth steels himself for a vote that could see him put on trial in the Senate and sink his chances of serving for the rest of Trump’s term, The Intercept is dissecting his self-defense and examining Hegseth’s false claims about his disastrous war-making.

Everything Was “Lawful” and “Notified to Congress”

“Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen — every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs.”

Related

“Trump Has Appointed Himself Judge, Jury, and Executioner”

Experts in the laws of war, a Pentagon official, and members of Congress from both parties say Hegseth’s boat strikes against “cartels,” which have now killed upward of 240 people, are illegal extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians — even suspected criminals — who do not pose an imminent threat of violence.

Sarah Harrison, who previously advised Pentagon policymakers on issues related to human rights and the law of war, said that the attack on Venezuela was also a clear violation of international law and that the administration’s justifications for the raid were baseless.

Of the Iran war, Air Force Lt. Col. Rachel VanLandingham, a former chief of international law at U.S. Central Command, said the opening strike “clearly violates the U.S. Constitution and the War Powers Resolution,” which requires the president to seek congressional approval to start a war in most cases. Harrison Mann, a former U.S. Army officer and intelligence official and now the associate director for campaigns and policy at Win Without War, drew specific attention to the attacks on the bridges and water reservoirs in Iran. It is “quite dangerous to be conditioning the U.S. military to carry out orders that are clearly war crimes,” he warned.

Hegseth’s claims about notifications are also spurious. Congress never authorized the Iran war, and a call to the congressional “Gang of Eight” the night before is not the formal report experts say the law requires. Following the January attack on Venezuela, Republicans privately complained they were not told in advance.

“The Terrorists That We Hunt”

“As to the claim that the American military targets civilians, well, that is a lie and that is a slander against every professional who flew, sailed, and fought on these missions. The only people who target civilians are the terrorists that we hunt.”

The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians. The summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs, in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and brought them to trial on criminal charges.

A U.S. military investigation also found U.S. forces attacked an elementary school in Minab, Iran, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. One official called it “colossal negligence.”

For months, Central Command has failed to answer questions about additional civilian casualties, including eight members of a family — the youngest, a 20-day-old infant — killed in an attack documented in an Intercept investigation.

These attacks came after Hegseth conducted a comprehensive campaign to undermine efforts to prevent and mitigate civilian harm. The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, for example, slashed its staff from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just nine by the end of the year, according to the report.

“Dead Where They Should Be”

“More than 70 narco vessels sunk. 218 narco-terrorists dead where they should be. Maritime smuggling down at least 65 percent and dropping even further.”

Hegseth misstates the toll of his own boat strike campaign. The Intercept’s tracker counts 72 strikes and at least 243 dead. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., after reviewing classified material, wrote that the evidence suggests the military killed people not involved in drug trafficking. A top Pentagon Joint Staff official told lawmakers in a classified briefing that victims of human trafficking could be among the dead of the first strike.

The drug claims fare no better. Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Americas Security Affairs Joseph Humire, for example, offered completely different numbers to Congress, telling the House Armed Services Committee in March that there “has been a 20 percent reduction of movements of drug vessels in the Caribbean and an additional 25 percent reduction in the Eastern Pacific.”

The Pentagon’s latest civilian casualty report, meanwhile, claims no civilians were killed in the boat strikes. One U.S. official said it had “absolutely no credibility.”

Read Our Complete Coverage

License to Kill

Iran Was a “Historic Military Victory”

“By every measure, we achieved a historic military victory. Under 40 days of sustained combat…”

The Iran war, by all objective measures, is an abject failure. The conflict undermined the decades-old U.S. security framework, as well as America’s archipelago of bases, in the Middle East. Iran determined how to overwhelm U.S. air defenses, offering up a playbook for U.S. adversaries around the world. This, in turn, damaged U.S. military security across the globe. From Jordan to Kuwait to the United Kingdom, U.S. outposts are now increasingly vulnerable to attack. As a result, the Iran war has left the military on the brink of a “breakdown.”

Related

Pentagon Fears Drone Attacks on U.S. and Foreign Bases

The Trump administration’s attempt to rebrand its faltering forever war hasn’t slowed the mounting toll of U.S. casualties, either. While Hegseth focused on the conflict’s first 40 days, the U.S. has suffered more casualties as a result of the conflict since the war formally ended and, in July, underwent a name change to “Overseas Operations.”

Voters did not see a victory either: About 6 in 10 told The Associated Press the war was the wrong decision, and Vice President JD Vance agreed, writing of the GOP’s crushing defeat in last week’s midterms: “The reason we lost is the war.”

18 Americans

“Eighteen Americans have given their lives in Operation Epic Fury.”

Hegseth spent his rare press conference using the troops under his leadership as a shield, claiming that indictments of him were actually indictments of them. When not using them for cover, Hegseth praised them. “They are the best of our nation. Like the president, I will defend them with every fiber of my being every single day,” he crowed.

What he didn’t care enough to do was offer an accurate count of the war’s toll. The official Pentagon count of deaths during Epic Fury is 15, not 18 — but that’s misdirection at best and a lie at worst. At least 23 military personnel have died in Operation Epic Fury and “Overseas Operations,” the new moniker for the war introduced in July, according to the Pentagon’s official count. (This includes 11 killed by hostile fire.) The actual number of troop deaths in the region since the war began is higher.

“One Disgruntled Congressman”

“This is one disgruntled guy who drew up some really flimsy articles.”

In Hegseth’s telling, Massie is pursuing his impeachment out of resentment over the loss of his Kentucky congressional seat to Trump-backed far-right candidate Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL. But Massie’s impeachment effort has strong bipartisan support. The entire House Democratic caucus is widely expected to vote in favor of the impeachment effort. While no House Republicans aside from Massie have openly committed to voting yes, the outgoing congressman said Monday that he believes “several” Republicans will vote for the measure.

Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz agreed. So did Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight.

Related

Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement

Discontent with Hegseth is widespread within the military establishment as well. The Intercept recently spoke with six current and former defense officials who said Hegseth had undermined the rule of law; irreparably harmed the U.S. military through purges of top commanders; spurred religious extremism; and diminished the department he leads due to an almost endless raft of scandals and culture-war clownishness. In fact, 64 percent of active-duty service members, veterans, and military families disapprove of Hegseth, according to a recent poll conducted by Common Defense, a grassroots veterans organization.

The American people, writ large, appear to agree with Ansari, Massie, the U.S. officials, and those in the military’s orbit. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove, according to a Quinnipiac University poll in September.

The post Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense appeared first on The Intercept.

items.articleBody:
Die Navigations-App Waze kann Autofahrer künftig auf Radfahrer aufmerksam machen, die sich in ihrer unmittelbaren Umgebung befinden. Die Grundlage hierfür schafft eine Kooperation zwischen Waze und Garmin. Radfahrer, die einen kompatiblen Fahrradcomputer oder eine Smartwatch von Garmin verwenden, können ihren Standort während einer Tour automatisch für die Warnhinweise in Waze freigeben. Die neue Funktion wird ab sofort weltweit für iOS und Android eingeführt und soll damit auch in Deutschland verfügbar sein.

Die Standortübermittlung erfolgt über die bereits vorhandene Garmin-Funktion LiveTrack. Damit können Nutzer ihren Standort während sportlicher Aktivitäten schon seit längerer Zeit mit Freunden oder Familienmitgliedern teilen. Für die Nutzung wird ein kompatibler Fahrradcomputer der Garmin-Edge-Reihe oder eine entsprechende Garmin-Smartwatch benötigt.

Garmin Connect steuert die Standortfreigabe

Für die Zusammenarbeit mit Waze wird LiveTrack um eine zusätzliche Freigabemöglichkeit erweitert. Radfahrer können in der Garmin-Connect-App festlegen, ob ihr Standort während einer aufgezeichneten Radtour auch für die Warnhinweise in Waze verwendet werden darf.

Autofahrer, die Waze zur Navigation verwenden, sehen daraufhin bewegliche Symbole auf der Karte, die auf Radfahrer in ihrer Nähe hinweisen. Zusätzlich sollen Warnmeldungen eingeblendet werden, die Autofahrer ausdrücklich auf Radfahrer in ihrer unmittelbaren Umgebung aufmerksam machen.

Autofahrer erhalten keine persönlichen Daten

Die Teilnahme ist freiwillig und muss von den Radfahrern ausdrücklich aktiviert werden. Garmin und Waze zufolge erhalten Autofahrer dabei keine persönlichen Informationen, anhand derer sich einzelne Radfahrer identifizieren lassen. Auch die gefahrene Route soll für Autofahrer nicht einsehbar sein.

Die Standortfreigabe erfolgt zudem nur während der jeweiligen Radtour und ist damit zeitlich begrenzt. Sobald die Aktivität auf dem Garmin-Gerät beendet wird, sollen auch die zugehörigen Warnhinweise in Waze automatisch verschwinden.

Waze Navigation und Verkehr (Kostenlos, App Store) →

★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★

Der Beitrag Waze macht Autofahrer künftig auf Radfahrer aufmerksam Wurde zuerst auf iphone-ticker.de veröffentlicht.

items.articleBody:
Verbindung ohne Begegnung: Erstmals wurden Lichtteilchen aus zwei getrennten Halbleiter-Quantenpunkten miteinander verschränkt, obwohl sie nie direkt wechselwirkten. Die Messungen erreichten eine Zustandsübereinstimmung von bis zu 0,71. Damit ist ein wichtiger Schritt zu Quantenrepeatern gelungen, die einzelne Quantenverbindungen zu einem größeren Netzwerk verknüpfen sollen.

Paderborn (Deutschland). Für ein Quanteninternet reicht es nicht, verschränkte Lichtteilchen nur an einem Ort zu erzeugen. Quantenverbindungen müssen vielmehr zwischen weit entfernten Stationen aufgebaut werden, obwohl Photonen auf langen Übertragungswegen zunehmend verloren gehen.

Quantenrepeater sollen dieses Problem lösen, indem sie kürzere Verbindungsabschnitte zu einer längeren Quantenstrecke verknüpfen. Dazu müssen zwei zunächst voneinander unabhängige Photonenpaare ihre Verschränkung sozusagen weiterreichen, ohne dass die beiden verbleibenden Lichtteilchen direkt aufeinandertreffen.

Verschränkung ohne direkte Begegnung

Forscher der Sapienza Università di Roma um Giuseppe Ronco haben ein solches Entanglement Swapping mit Photonen aus zwei separaten Galliumarsenid-Quantenpunkten demonstriert. Jeder Quantenpunkt erzeugt zunächst ein verschränktes Lichtteilchenpaar, das unabhängig vom zweiten Paar entsteht.

Anschließend treffen jeweils ein Photon aus jedem Paar an einem Strahlteiler aufeinander und werden gemeinsam einer Bell-Zustandsmessung unterzogen. Bei einem geeigneten Messergebnis sind die zwei nicht gemessenen Photonen miteinander verschränkt, obwohl sie einander nie begegnet sind.

„Bei diesem Verfahren wird die Verschränkung zwischen zwei ursprünglich getrennten Photonenpaaren neu verknüpft“, erklärt Prof. Dr. Klaus Jöns von der Universität Paderborn (UPB).

Warum die Lichtquellen zusammenpassen müssen

Die Schwierigkeit: Gewöhnlich strahlen unterschiedliche Quantenpunkte Photonen mit leicht verschiedenen Energien und Eigenschaften ab. Für die gemeinsame Messung müssen die beiden eintreffenden Lichtteilchen jedoch möglichst ununterscheidbar sein, damit sie quantenmechanisch miteinander interferieren.

Deshalb wurden die Galliumarsenid-Quantenpunkte präzise in kreisförmige Bragg-Resonatoren integriert, die das ausgesandte Licht effizient sammeln und seinen zeitlichen Verlauf beeinflussen. Zusätzlich veränderten piezoelektrische Bauteile die mechanische Spannung der Halbleiterstruktur und stimmten die Photonenenergien aufeinander ab.

„Heute können wir ihre Eigenschaften so präzise kontrollieren, dass Photonen aus zwei unterschiedlichen Quantenpunkten nahezu ununterscheidbar werden. Das ist essenziell, damit sie miteinander interferieren und wir Verschränkung übertragen können“, sagt Klaus Jöns.

Der Nachweis liegt über der Grenze

Die Messungen ergaben eine sogenannte Fidelity von bis zu 0,71 ± 0,02, also eine Übereinstimmung des gemessenen Zustands mit einem ideal verschränkten Zustand. Der Wert liegt mehr als zehn statistische Standardabweichungen über der Schwelle von 0,5, die für unverschränkte Zustände nicht überschritten werden kann.

Allerdings wurde der Spitzenwert erreicht, indem nur Nachweise innerhalb eines engen Zeitfensters berücksichtigt wurden. Ohne diese zeitliche Auswahl blieb die Verschränkung ebenfalls messbar: In einer der untersuchten Messkonfigurationen erreichte sie eine Fidelity von 0,60 ± 0,01.

Die beiden Quantenpunkte arbeiteten in getrennten Kühlapparaturen, und der Aufbau enthielt eine 150 Meter lange Glasfaserstrecke. Erfolgreiche Ereignisse traten bislang nur wenige Male pro Sekunde auf, sodass das Experiment noch keine praxistaugliche Übertragung über große Entfernungen darstellt.

Noch kein fertiger Quantenrepeater

Der entscheidende Vorteil der Quantenpunkte liegt in ihrer gezielten Anregbarkeit: Sie können verschränkte Photonenpaare auf Abruf aussenden. Im Unterschied zu herkömmlichen zufallsbasierten Lichtquellen vermeiden sie dadurch einen grundlegenden Zielkonflikt zwischen der Rate erzeugter Photonenpaare und ihrer Verschränkungsqualität.

Die Verknüpfung selbst hängt dennoch vom Ausgang der Bell-Messung ab und gelingt nicht bei jedem Versuch. Für ein größeres Netz müssen zudem Verschränkungsqualität und Ereignisrate steigen und geeignete Quantenspeicher integriert werden.

„Genau diese Fähigkeit brauchen wir, um einzelne Quantenverbindungen zu größeren Netzwerken zusammenzuschließen“, betont Klaus Jöns.

Eine einsatzfähige Verbindung mehrerer entfernter Knoten ist damit noch nicht verwirklicht. Der Versuch zeigt aber, dass sich zwei unabhängig anregbare Quantenlichtquellen für den entscheidenden Zwischenschritt eines solchen Netzes nutzen lassen.

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin Science Advances, doi: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh7797

items.articleBody:
Der Milliardenmarkt der Online-Werbung schadet nicht nur Verbraucher:innen, sondern auch Werbetreibenden und Publishern. Europäische Digitalgesetze bekommen die Probleme nicht in den Griff. Das zeigt eine umfangreiche Studie im Auftrag der EU-Kommission.

Auf dem Markt der Online-Werbung gewinnen nur die Mittelsmänner. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: Erik Mclean
Online-Werbung ist ein riesiges Geschäft: Knapp 800 Milliarden Euro sollen Werbetreibende im letzten Jahr dafür ausgegeben haben, davon 63 Milliarden Euro in der EU. Europa bildet nach den USA und China damit den drittgrößten Online-Werbe-Markt der Welt, Tendenz steigend. Ein Markt allerdings, der ziemlich kaputt ist und den auch die umfangreiche Tech-Regulierung der EU nicht in den Griff bekommt, wie eine neue Studie im Auftrag der EU-Kommission darlegt.

Die 570-seitige Untersuchung der Beratungsfirma AWO dürfte eine der umfassendsten Analysen der Werbeindustrie überhaupt sein. Sie zeichnet ein detailliertes Bild einer Branche, die von extremer Komplexität und Undurchsichtigkeit geprägt ist, in der heute schon sehr viele Prozesse automatisiert ablaufen und in der Künstliche Intelligenz bestehende Probleme weiter verschärfen könnte.

Es ist eine Branche, die laut der Studie wenige zentrale Player dominieren, allen voran Google und Meta. Diese setzen jährlich hunderte Milliarden Dollar mit Werbung um, weil sie selbst einerseits geschlossene Ökosysteme betreiben, in denen sie umfangreiche Daten über Milliarden Menschen sammeln und ihnen Werbung ausspielen können, und weil sie andererseits gleichzeitig wichtige Infrastrukturen für die Online-Werbung im offenen Netz betreiben. Dort wiederum sind tausende unterschiedliche Firmen an dem Ökosystem beteiligt, die kaum ein Menschen kennt – von Auktionsplattformen für Werbeplätze bis zu Datenhändlern.

Die Studie bleibt nicht bei der Beschreibung dieser Industrie stehen, sondern zeichnet auch zahlreiche Probleme nach, die mit ihrer heutige Funktionsweise einhergehen. Ausführlich beleuchtet werden zudem Initiativen, die angesetzt haben, um diese Probleme zu lösen – von technischen Standards über Industrie-Vorschläge bis zur Tech-Regulierung der EU.

Das bittere Fazit ist, dass bislang nichts richtig fruchtet, weshalb die Autor:innen der EU-Kommission zahlreiche Vorschläge für neue Maßnahmen unterbreiten. Der Moment könnte günstig sein: Am morgigen Mittwoch will die Kommission ihren Vorschlag für einen Digital Fairness Act vorstellen, mit dem sie Lücken im digitalen Verbraucherrechte schließen will. Ein kürzlich öffentlich gewordener Leak des Entwurfs deutet jedoch darauf hin, dass dabei wohl kein einziger Vorschlag aus der Mega-Studie umgesetzt wird.

Eine lange Liste an Problemen

Grundlage der Untersuchung sind zahlreiche Studien aus Wissenschaft und Industrie sowie eigene Erhebungen und Interviews mit Branchenvertreter:innen und Expert:innen.

Allein die Liste der dargestellten Probleme, die durch Online-Werbung verursacht werden, ist so lang, dass ihre Behandlung leicht den Rahmen dieses Artikels sprengen könnte. Sie umfasst unter anderem „Fragen des Datenschutzes und der Privatsphäre, ausbeuterische Praktiken zulasten schutzbedürftiger Personen, die Verbreitung von mit systemischen Risiken verbundenen Inhalten, Risiken für den Medienpluralismus und den Wettbewerb sowie Fragen der Fairness“.

Die meisten dieser problematischen Auswirkungen haben den Autor:innen zufolge „ihre Ursache in der Abhängigkeit des Marktes von personenbezogenen Daten“. Über das Manipulationspotenzial, das der umfassenden Erfassung und Analyse menschlichen Verhaltens für Online-Werbung innewohnt, wurde in den vergangenen Jahren viel geschrieben. Auf netzpolitik.org berichteten wir unter anderem über 650.000 detaillierte Kategorien, in die die Werbeindustrie Menschen einsortiert. Die Studie geht hier unter anderem auf Gefahren für Heranwachsende und Suchtkranke sowie durch politische Manipulation ein.

Immer deutlicher ist in den vergangenen Jahren zudem geworden, dass die kommerzielle Überwachung für Werbe-Targeting auch ein Sicherheitsproblem darstellt, weil die angeblich nur für Werbezwecke erhobenen Daten im großen Stil bei Datenhändlern landen. Die Studie erwähnt in diesem Zusammenhang auch eine 2025 erschienene Recherche von netzpolitik.org und dem Bayerischen Rundfunk mit der belgischen Zeitung L’Echo im Rahmen der Databroker Files, die gezeigt hatte, dass sich mit solchen Daten auch hochrangiges EU-Personal ausspionieren lässt.

Ein Markt, der fast nur Verlierer kennt

Interessant ist, dass die Untersuchung neben Problemen für Nutzer:innen, Verbraucher:innen und Bürger:innen auch intensiv die negativen Konsequenzen des aktuellen Systems für Werbekunden und Publisher in den Blick nimmt, also beispielsweise für Apps oder Websites, auf denen Werbung ausgespielt wird.

So könnten Phänomene wie betrügerische Werbung (Scams), mit Werbung ausgespielte Schadsoftware (Malvertising) oder unpassend platzierte Werbung an der Reputation sowohl von Medien als auch von Marken kratzen (Brand Safety). Wenn Verbraucher:innen Werbe-Targeting als zu invasiv wahrnehmen (Exploitative Personalisation), könne dies laut Untersuchungen zudem dazu führen, dass Werbung den gegenteiligen Effekt habe und bestimmte Marken und Produkte gemieden werden.

Richtig ins Geld gehen grassierende Betrugsmaschen (Ad Fraud), bei denen beispielsweise mit Bots gefälschte Klicks auf Anzeigen generiert und so die Preise in die Höhe getrieben werden, obwohl niemand die Werbung gesehen hat. Die Autor:innen zitieren eine Untersuchung, der zufolge ein Viertel aller Werbeausgaben in der EU im Jahr 2025 durch Ad Fraud verloren gegangen sein könnte, also etwa 15 Milliarden Euro.

Problematisch sowohl für Werbekunden als auch für Publisher sei, dass sie sich bei der Preisgestaltung und der Erfolgsmessung von Online-Werbung oft komplett auf die vielen AdTech-Plattformen verlassen müssten, die die Infrastruktur dafür bereitstellen. Insbesondere die Abhängigkeit von Google und Meta, aber auch anderer wichtiger Gatekeeper wie TikTok, Amazon, Microsoft und Apple sei hier ein Problem.

Am Ende entsteht das Bild eines Marktes, auf dem es mit Ausnahmen der AdTech-Mittelsmänner nur Verlierer gibt.

Reform statt Abkehr vom aktuellen System

Die Studie kommt zu dem Schluss, dass die Probleme der Online-Werbung nicht ohne weitreichende regulatorische Maßnahmen zu lösen sind. Die Vorschläge setzen teilweise bei bestehenden Verordnungen an, gehen jedoch weit darüber hinaus.

So könnten den Autor:innen zufolge beispielsweise Privacy- und Sicherheitsrisiken durch Werbe-Auktionen vermieden werden, indem Werbe-Auktionen ohne Übermittlung personenbezogener Daten an potenziell tausende Firmen stattfinden. Targeting sei auch möglich, indem die Zuordnung zu Zielgruppen-Kategorien dezentral auf den Geräten der Betroffenen geschehe.

Einer der wichtigsten Vorschläge zielt darauf ab, Nutzer:innen mehr Kontrolle über ihre Einwilligungen zu ermöglichen, indem sie diese zentral im Browser oder Betriebssystem verwalten. Möglich wäre dies unter anderem über sogenannte Privacy Signals, also technische Übermittlungen der Nutzer:innen-Präferenzen, die AdTech-Firmen akzeptieren müssten. Genau dies hatte die EU-Kommission im Rahmen der Digital-Omnibus-Reform der DSGVO vorgeschlagen, die Mitgliedstaaten der EU haben sich gerade dagegen ausgesprochen.

Andere denkbare Maßnahmen zielen eher auf den Abbau der Informationsasymmetrien zwischen unterschiedlichen Akteuren im Werbe-Ökosystem ab. Dazu zählen etwa Vorschläge zur Nachschärfung des Digital Markets Act, die die Transparenz über Werbeauktionen und Performance-Messungen für Werbekunden und Publisher erhöhen. Auch Transparenz-Vorschriften des Digital Services Act sollten den Autor:innen zufolge verschärft werden, etwa mit Blick auf die Transparenz von Targeting-Prozessen und die Werbe-Bibliotheken.

Weiter gehen würden kartellrechtliche Eingriffe in die Rolle von Werbe-Infrastruktur-Betreibern wie Google. Diesen könnte etwa untersagt werden, gleichzeitig Werbedienstleistungen und Marktplätze zum Versteigern von Werbeplätzen anzubieten, weil sie sich dabei selbst bevorteilen könnten.

Gemein ist allen Vorschlägen, dass sie nicht auf eine radikale Abkehr vom derzeitigen System der zielgerichteten Werbung auf Basis von Interessen und Verhalten abzielen, sondern lediglich auf eine Reform dieses Systems. Gar nicht thematisiert wird etwa ein weitreichender Vorschlag, den zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen immer wieder ins Spiel bringen: Ein grundsätzliches Verbot von Tracking und Profilbildung zu Werbezwecken. Vor mehreren Jahren hatte auch eine parteiübergreifende Initiative von Europa-Parlamentarier:innen einen entsprechenden Vorschlag eingebracht, dafür jedoch keine Mehrheit erhalten.

Verbrauchschützer: Vorschläge „reichen nicht aus“

Zivilgesellschaftliche Experten begrüßen auf Anfrage von netzpolitik.org die Untersuchung mit ihrer umfassenden Problemanalyse, kritisieren jedoch, dass die darin enthaltenen Vorschläge nicht weit genug gehen.

„Die Studie zeigt erneut, dass personalisierte Werbung erhebliche Risiken für Verbraucherinnen und Verbraucher birgt und trotz der bestehenden Vorschriften große Schutzlücken verbleiben“, schreibt etwa Florian Glatzner vom Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband. Vorschläge wie bessere Risikoberichte, Werbearchive und Sorgfaltspflichten seien sinnvoll. „Sie reichen jedoch nicht aus, solange die umfassende Verfolgung von Verbraucherinnen und Verbrauchern, die Zusammenführung von Datenbeständen und die Ableitung individueller Schwächen zulässig bleiben.“

Glatzner begrüßt explizit, dass die Studie „automatisierte Datenschutzsignale“ als Lösung vorschlägt, damit „Verbraucherinnen und Verbraucher Tracking nicht mehr bei jedem Besuch einer Website ablehnen oder zustimmen müssen.“ Dass die Mitgliedstaaten einen entsprechenden Vorschlag der EU-Kommission im Rahmen des Digital Omnibus gestrichen haben, sei bedauerlich. „Nun ist das Europäische Parlament gefragt, diese Möglichkeit wieder aufzunehmen und die Rechte der Verbraucherinnen und Verbraucher zu stärken.“

Tracking-Forscher: „Die Online-Werbung ist kaputt“

Noch deutlicher wird der renommierte Tracking-Forscher Wolfie Christl, der seit mehr als einem Jahrzehnt mit unabhängiger Forschung die Datenpraktiken der Werbeindustrie beleuchtet. „Die Studie bietet eine detaillierte Analyse von Regulierungslücken und liefert eine Reihe von fundierten Vorschlägen“, schreibt er auf Anfrage von netzpolitik.org. „Dennoch habe ich den Eindruck, dass auf den fast 600 Seiten der Kern der Problematik etwas untergeht: Die Online-Werbung ist kaputt und braucht einen kompletten Neustart.“

Seine jahrelange Forschung zeige, dass DSGVO-konforme Datenverarbeitung im Bereich der Online-Werbung eher die Ausnahme als die Regel sei. „Kaum ein Website- oder App-Betreiber und auch nicht die beteiligten Werbe- und Datenhandelsfirmen wissen, wohin die Daten wirklich fließen.“ Und weiter: „Die angebliche informierte Einwilligung ist unter diesen Bedingungen eine reine Farce.“ Die unkontrollierten Datenflüsse seien nicht nur ein Problem für Grundrechte, sondern auch ein großes Sicherheitsrisiko „für Staaten, den privaten Sektor, Zivilgesellschaft und für alle anderen.“

Es brauche deshalb mehr Klartext, fordert Christl: „In unserer schönen neuen digitalen Konsumwelt gibt es eine gewaltige Lücke zwischen gesetzlicher Regelung und Praxis. Das ist Gift für das Vertrauen in die Digitalisierung und die Zukunft einer demokratischen Informationsgesellschaft.“

More than 15,300 submissions made their way to the judges for this year’s Close-Up Photographer of the Year, setting a record for the highest number of entries in the competition’s history. From uncanny insects to slime molds to unexpected animal interactions, photographs captured by amateur and professional photographers alike highlight the diverse and sometimes surreal flora and fauna all around us.

The contest winners will be announced in January. In the meantime, a photography challenge on the theme of “Close to Home” is open for submissions through the end of the month. Explore some of our favorites from the shortlist below, and learn more on the contest’s website.

items.body:
# Dfb fuellkrug klopp nationalmannschaft li.3578459

Die Analyse zu „Dfb fuellkrug klopp nationalmannschaft li.3578459“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.
