The EU should go big and hard over border IT failure (permalink)

If the EU has a future as a political project, it will have to be as a living, breathing repudiation of Ronald Reagan's maxim that "The nine most terrifying words are 'I’m from the government and I’m here to help.'"

In other words, the EU's future depends on its ability to publicly perform competence and capacity. The EU is a technocratic project, and the one trait technocrats must show is undeniable technical competence. This is the secret of Zohran Mamdani's administration: being seen in public, constantly fixing things that are broken, and making things that work even better:

https://www.nyc.gov/content/100days/pages/

This is a goal that is largely incompatible with charismatic megaprojects, and unfortunately, that's the EU's favorite kind of project: something big and splashy and worthy of the extreme effort required to squeeze anything through the Byzantine EU approvals process:

https://backofmind.substack.com/p/the-planning-system-system

Even more unfortunate is that the EU isn't just a technocratic project, it's a neoliberal technocratic project, so when it does embark on one of these megaprojects, it almost always does so as a "public-private partnership" that sees vast sums transferred to private firms to carry out public works. Since megaprojects are always over-budget and behind schedule, this creates the perfect conditions for absolute banditry, in which private companies overcharge and underdeliver, and before you know it, you're billions poorer and back in Reagan's "most terrifying words" territory.

Here's a perfect example: Schengen is a region of (mostly) EU countries who have opened their borders to one another. Once you've crossed into any of the 29 Schengen countries, you can generally stroll into any of the other Schengen countries without showing a passport or having your bags searched:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area

This is an awfully convenient system…once you're inside of Schengen. But the Schengen agreement means that each of the member states is trusting the other states to manage a common border, a task that is made all the more urgent by the fascist international, whose far right parties have whipped millions of otherwise sensible people into a xenophobic frenzy over migration. This has led to a kind of bureaucracy-shifting exercise that removed all the complexity from inter-Schengen borders and concentrated it at the borders between each Schengen country and the rest of the world.

Under this system, every Schengen country must accurately log the passage of every non-Schengen person into and out of the region. If you fly into Rome and out of Helsinki, then both the Italian and Finnish border guards must be cognizant of that fact and correctly log it. To make matters even more complex, visa-free access to Schengen is restricted to 90 days in the entire region out of any given 180-day period. For example, last month I was stranded in Frankfurt overnight thanks to a canceled flight. If I had totaled 90 days out of the previous 180 in Schengen, I would not have been allowed out of the airport's secure area until midnight, when the day ticked over and now my total would be 89 days out of 180 (thankfully, I was able to leave the airport and stay in a crummy airport hotel instead of sleeping on the floor of the airport).

To manage this system, the EU commissioned several giant IT companies to build a networked, biometric border-crossing system. Under the spec, the system would track those 90-day windows for everyone who passed in and out of Schengen, using fast fingerprint/facial scans to move people swiftly through any border crossing in the 29 Schengen countries.

It is a gross understatement to call this system behind schedule and overbudget. The Entry Exit System (EES) was supposed to roll out in 2022, but it didn't go live until October 2025 – whereupon it completely, catastrophically failed, despite having doubled its budget:

https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/09/25/eu-to-register-fingerprints-faces-for-short-stay-visitors/1141501

It's been more than a year since EES went live and it is still an absolute disaster. Travelers arriving or leaving Schengen are frequently hit with multi-hour delays. Numerous flights have been canceled, and airlines who fly without waiting for passengers in the immobile, snaking lines must rebook those passengers and endure their wrath. At major airports, it's routine for border guards to simply suspend their use of the EES system, waving through passengers without registering them in the system:

https://eesqueue.com/

EES is a disaster for aviation operations and border crossings. Any true reckoning with its costs wouldn't stop at the hundreds of millions of euros paid to private sector partners, but also the hundreds of millions more in costs borne by travelers and airlines, to say nothing of the opportunity costs paid by travelers who made it through the checkpoints through the brute-force expedient of leaving hours of extra time for a broken border formality.

Which means that the disaster isn't merely a logistics crisis, it's also a credibility and legitimacy crisis. A year (and counting) of headlines about this dismal failure of an IT system have further eroded public confidence in the EU's technical capabilities. How can the EU claim to be a sound technocratic steward of the vast administrative challenges facing a 27-state transnational entity when it can't make the computers work, and when those failures produce the very visible phenomenon of gigantic queues of fuming passengers?

(Not just fuming, either: when I was stuck in Frankfurt last month, there were at least half a dozen travelers who were loudly sobbing as they realized they were going to miss their flights home.)

The contractors for this nonfunctional, grossly overbudget, years-late project (IBM, Atos, and Leonardo) are now being sued, but – incredibly – the EU kept the lawsuit a secret. The only reason we know that IBM, Atos, and Leonardo are facing the EU in court is that the FT spotted an inconspicuous note in the annual financial statements for eu-LISA (the European Union Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice):

https://www.eulisa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/fy2025_eu-lisa_faa.pdf

The secrecy of this lawsuit is another mark against the EU's technical competence. Any administrative system that relies on private-sector outsourcing to carry out its essential projects must have a core competency in overseeing those private partners, which includes loudly and mercilessly punishing those partners when they fail.

https://www.theregister.com/public-sector/2026/11/10/eus-212m-border-it-project-lands-ibm-and-atos-in-legal-water/5308669

Anyone who's ever watched a large IT consultancy firm run one of these large projects knows that this kind of bungling and gouging is par for the course. The old adage that "no one ever got fired for buying IBM" does not mean that IBM can deliver a functional IT system; it means that when IBM fucks up your project, you can escape any blame because they're the gold standard for fucking up.

Every time the EU lets these companies off the hook without a big, splashy public reckoning, they reinforce Reagan's "most terrifying words" maxim. As Voltaire wrote, "Sometimes you must execute an admiral to encourage the others." The EU should be dragging these IT bandits in public, every day, naming the top executives who oversaw the project.

They should do this every time there's a problem with a private contractor, but EES is especially ripe for this kind of treatment. That's because EES whacked a ton of rich, powerful people. Those are the sort of people who might otherwise run cover for giant, bungling, wildly profitable IT consulting firms, but who are also the most reliably pissy, vindictive dickheads about anything that affects them personally. These are the sorts of people you definitely want inside your tent, pissing out – but in hiding its lawsuit under a bushel, the EU has invited them to stand outside its tent and piss in.

items.articleBody:
photo cred: my dad

Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD, I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here. This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine.

(For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder)

Anyway, onto the post!

Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.

The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions do not work.

For example:

In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, those grants did nothing.

Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators.

The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs.1

Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance.2

Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism.

Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:

When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment.

In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that the program did none of those things.

And here is the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs that run across the United States:

In the social sciences, nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing. We can’t say that it’s impossible for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here.

HEAVY METAL

It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?

We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.

In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of.3 It was called “The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules“, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased:

The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.

The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.

The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.

The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.

Rossi tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006, insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”.

Rossi did not do us the favor of actually naming any of those “statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”, and I know why, because I have gone looking for them, and they are not easy to find. The Earned Income Tax Credit, which is designed to benefit low- and middle-income families, was once considered a slam dunk; now a new analysis suggests that it might not do anything. Plain packaging—where you strip cigarette boxes of their attractive branding—seems like a no brainer, but in Australia, it looks like the policy caused smokers to switch to cheaper brands and to smoke more. There’s a reading and math program that has done well in India, but as soon as other researchers tried to implement it elsewhere, the effects shrank.

You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!”

Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this:

OJ A-OK

The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false.

One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control, a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it.

That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86.4

I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect.5

I wouldn’t let this one go either

Unsurprisingly, well-powered, preregistered replications with actual lotteries have failed to find any difference in picking vs. not-picking. So that’s that: there’s no such thing as the illusion of control.

Except...obviously there’s an illusion of control! Look around! People will blow on their dice at the craps table, they’ll don their lucky undies when the Knicks go to the finals, they’ll scream “look out!” to the hapless protagonists of a horror movie. When I was a kid, my parents used to send me off to play arcade games without any quarters, knowing that I would simply move the joystick in synchrony with the demo playing on the screen, convincing myself that I was causing the characters to move, when in fact I was merely mirroring them.

Put it this way: why do you think The Secret has sold over 30 million copies? It ain’t the beautiful prose or the sterling scientific evidence. It’s because when Rhonda Byrne tells you that “your thoughts are the primary cause of everything,” it feels kind of true. After all, can’t you jinx yourself by thinking the wrong thing? Haven’t you ever been like “whatever you do, don’t spill this soup” and then the next thing you know you’ve got a shirtful of bisque? And if brainwaves are powerful enough to spill soup, who knows what else they might do!

So no, people don’t believe they can magically improve their chances of winning the lottery by picking the numbers themselves. Still, our intentions feel more potent than they should, and this shows up not only in our harmless superstitions, but also in the way we keep meddling in each other’s lives despite having no idea what we’re doing.6

How do I know my preferred policies will have their intended results? Well, because I intend them. That’s not really my answer to the question; it’s the reason I don’t even think of the question in the first place.

GEORGE W. BUSH, PROPHET OF OUR TIME

Here’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all.

For instance, the National Science Foundation funds over 1,000 STEM education projects, which are aimed at improving curricula, training, student outcomes, etc. According to an analysis by , 76% of the time, the researchers running those programs don’t even attempt to evaluate them with actual experiments. Apparently if you have a bright idea about how to teach kindergarteners to code, you don’t need to bother assessing it. It turns out George W. Bush was actually right when he said:

Speaking of the government, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office, many federal programs don’t even define their goals, let alone collect data on their progress toward those goals. For instance, the Department of Homeland Security is supposed to stop people from producing and distributing illicit fentanyl, and so they do things like search people’s cars and walk around with drug-sniffing dogs. When DHS was asked, “How do we know any of this is working? What would success even look like?”, they were like “hmm great questions”. They hadn’t set any goals or collected any data, despite being required to do so by law. As the GAO puts it with characteristic mildness: “As a result, DHS’s ability to fully understand the effectiveness of these efforts is limited.”

Maybe it’s too much to expect that the Department of Homeland Security, especially in its current incarnation, would try to figure out whether it’s doing things that actually work. But it’s certainly not too much to expect of private philanthropists, who choose to give away their money of their own free will. Certainly they would care whether their dollars do anything. Right?

Wrong. In 2018, Kenneth Langone, the Home Depot billionaire, donated $100 million to eliminate tuition fees at New York University’s main medical school. This was supposed to encourage med students to pick lower-paying specialties like pediatrics and primary care, and it was supposed to attract lower-income students to medical school in the first place. But neither of those things happened. The makeup of the student body hasn’t changed, and they’re picking the same specialities they always did.

In this case, it should have been easy to foresee that those beaucoup bucks were going to do bupkis. First, medical school is already a good investment, regardless of income: yes, you take on a big pile of debt, but you also make a much bigger pile of money, even in the lowest-compensated specialties. Second, wiping out that debt does almost nothing to reduce the disparities between specialties: the average orthopedic surgeon earns $564,000 per year, while the average family practitioner earns about $281,000. If both of them work for 30 years, the surgeon earns about $17 million, while the family doc earns about $8 million. Meanwhile, the average medical school debt is about $200k, which is nothing compared to an extra $9 million over the course of your lifetime.

And remember: in this situation, both the surgeon and the family doc attend for free, regardless of how much money they had when they arrived, or how much money they make after they leave. So there’s no reason why free tuition should encourage anybody to do anything differently—except to apply to NYU in the first place. And indeed, applications are up 47%.7

To be clear, giving away dunderheaded donations is better than a lot of things that billionaires could be doing with their money, like buying a second superyacht or digging an additional doomsday bunker so they have a place to summer after the apocalypse. I’m glad that the plutocrats are trying to do something nice. I would just like them to succeed.

THE GREAT BARRIER, GRIEF

When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief.

Bargaining

Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea!

Unfortunately, large, well-designed randomized controlled trials keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfers. In one study, when low-income participants got $2000 with no strings attached, it made them less happy compared to people who got $500 or nothing at all. Psychologically, receiving 20 Benjamins was about 25% as bad as losing your job during the pandemic. That finding might be a fluke, but it also showed up in a study where researchers wiped out a bunch of people’s medical debt and it maybe made them more depressed.

These programs do succeed in sense that when you give people more money, they have more money, and they spend it on things that they need. It’s just surprisingly difficult to find any evidence that having more money makes a difference. (Though note that results are more promising in low- and middle- income countries.)

Denial

This is where people typically raise the no true Scotsman defense: if we get bad results from a good idea, it must be because someone screwed something up, not because the good ideas were actually bad ideas. Maybe the measures were wrong, the implementation was shoddy, or the people who benefitted didn’t fill out the followup survey for some reason.

This response isn’t totally irrational; programs go pear-shaped all the time. Maybe your One Laptop Per Child program only failed because all the laptops got stolen out of the back of the truck. Case in point: in that medical debt study, it seems like 76% of people didn’t even realize their medical debt had been wiped out. (But don’t get too excited: if anything, calling people and informing them of this boon made them slightly more depressed.)

The real problem with no-true-Scotsman-ing these studies is that you must subscribe to the dubious belief that some tiny tweaks will somehow unlock giant effects. This is a holdover from pre-replication-crisis psychology, back when we thought you could, say, subliminally flash an American flag at someone and make them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks later. It now seems like rinky-dink interventions tend to have rinky-dink effects, or none at all. So yes, we could always pick more appropriate measures, and the facilitators delivering the intervention could always have a bit more pep in their step. That might be enough to make a program slightly more effective, but it’s not enough to turn a null result into a blockbuster.

Acceptance

Acceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying.

This is a bit like finding out that bloodletting doesn’t work and then concluding that no medicine can ever work. (“Well, We’ve Tried Everything”, Says Society That Has Only Tried One or Two Things.) The social sciences are still in their alchemical stage. We do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mind, let alone what happens when those minds combine in societies and economies. Imagine trying to cure cancer using Galenic medicine or trying to land on the moon using Aristotelian physics—that’s what we’re doing when we roll out programs designed to change human behavior.

FULL THROTTLE ARISTOTLE

That doesn’t mean our ill-informed attempts can never succeed. Both Galen and Aristotle were right about some important things: it was Galen who figured out that urine is produced by the kidneys, rather than the bladder (as was commonly assumed), and it was Aristotle who successfully described how objects move in fluids, even if he attributed it to the wrong forces.

But if we want to solve real, Hydra-headed problems, we need more than a handful of facts. (“Doc, I’m all itchy and covered in spots! What do I do?” “Hmm...did you know that urine is produced in the kidneys?”) Until psychology and its neighboring disciplines grow into scientific maturity, all we can do is guess and check. There’s nothing shameful in that, but there is something shameful in pretending otherwise.

This is hard for us to internalize, because by default we assume that we were born near the end of history. We understand, of course, that we still have a few things to figure out, but emphasis on the few. Just look at our beautiful universities, our begowned scholars, our numerous and inscrutable papers! How can you say we know nothing when we have so many TED talks?

We misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.”



That’s why the worst possible reaction to a failed intervention is resignation. We may not know enough to improve our lot right now, but perhaps we could figure it out, if we tried. Maybe that means another RCT, or maybe it means another century of futzing around in the fundamentals before we can do anything useful.

(This does put a ceiling on the utopia we can expect to achieve in the near future. If you believe that we can perfect human nature by reorganizing society to your specifications, you would do well to remember that, as of now, we can’t even get people to go to the gym.)

That may seem unfair—what a bummer to be born in medias res, when so many of our problems remain unsolved! But if it is an affront, every human before us has been similarly affronted, and some of them chose to begin the work anyway. Whenever we pluck a low-hanging fruit today, it’s only because someone else planted a seed that they never got to harvest. So why should we expect to pluck without planting?

As Seneca put it nearly 2,000 years ago:

I revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased.

I know some people don’t feel this way. Some believe that the answers are simple and known and merely need to be enacted by force. Others think the answers are unknowable and will remain so forever. For those folks, I offer an invitation: the next time we conduct the ritual before undertaking some new policy, they may have the honor of playing the part of the goat.

(source)

Experimental History is produced in the kidneys

1

Of course, that sum is negligible compared to $4-6 trillion we spent trying and failing to turn Afghanistan and Iraq into thriving democracies.

2

How times have changed: I know parents who spend hours commuting every day just so their kids can attend a school that won’t issue them a laptop.

Other times an academic made a joke that went on to become their most prominent work:

In 2009, four neuroscientists published a poster—not even a paper!—showing that, with fMRI techniques that were standard at the time, it was possible to detect activity in the brain of a dead salmon. As far as I can tell, this is one of the most-cited publications, if not the most-cited publication, for every single author.

Andre Geim won the Nobel Prize in 2010 for his work on graphene, but when people stop him at conferences they want to talk about that time he used diamagnetism to make a frog float.

Stigler’s Law of Eponymy: “No scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer.” Named after Stephen Stigler (and by Stephen Stigler), originally discovered by Robert Merton. Cited more than most of Stiglers other papers.

Goodhart’s Law was originally a “jocular aside“ in a paper about monetary policy, and is now the claim for which he is best known.

$68.09 and $15.39 today, respectively.

There are five other studies in the paper that purport to show similar effects, but none of them inspire much confidence. Most of these studies have like 15 participants in each condition, which is not enough to detect big honking effects like “people have more lapses in attention when you deprive them of sleep for 24 hours” (required N = ~28 well-rested people, 28 sleep-deprived people).

6

In this way, I think the illusion of control may be another triple-decker fallacy, much like the one I described in Bamboozle Me, Daddy:

There’s the illusion of control: people assume they have more influence over the course of events than they really do

An illusion of the illusion of control: The original demonstrations of the illusion of control were probably flukes or fraud

And an illusion of the illusion of the illusion of control: Nevertheless, people still seem to believe they have more influence of the course of events than they really do, and so if you believe there is no such thing as the illusion of control, you are probably subject to an illusion yourself

🤖 Anthropic unveils Fable 5.2 LINK
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two newest AI models, as the company gets ready for an IPO that could happen as soon as next week.

The company says both models run 30% faster than the 5.1 generation and cost 20% less, priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

It's Anthropic's first "frontier" release since CEO Dario Amodei called in September for a slower pace of AI work, and the firm says the models went through fresh safety and alignment testing.
🕵️ Report reveals Huang affair aided $7.5 billion China chip shipments LINK
A report from The Information says Nvidia chief Jensen Huang's affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang helped move at least $7.5 billion worth of restricted Nvidia AI chips into companies in China.

Alice Huang and her family reportedly set up a network of firms across Singapore and China, including Shanghai Century Litong, which Nvidia named a preferred cloud partner just four months after it was founded in 2023.

Her ties to Nvidia and its distributors allegedly helped ship roughly 240,000 H-series and A-series chips into China, with some reaching giants like Alibaba and Tencent; Nvidia says it sees no sign its secrets were compromised.
🚁 Ring unveils a flying camera and patrol robot LINK
Ring has introduced two autonomous security gadgets, the $250 Drone Cam that flies around your home and a ground-based Rover Cam, both shipping under its new Ring Robotics line starting on January 27, 2027.

The 165-gram Drone Cam is a small quadcopter with a 2K front camera, a 1080p underside camera, and LEDs that can mimic a guard's flashlight; it flies on a schedule or reacts to motion and leak sensors.

Its battery lasts eight to 10 minutes per flight, and a system Ring calls AI Pilot uses cloud processing over Wi-Fi to map rooms, pick patrol points, and steer around obstacles instead of running local AI.
🔥 Meta's cheapest AI model matches Claude Haiku LINK
Meta has launched Muse Ember, its smallest and cheapest AI model, which the company says ties Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 on intelligence scores while doing the same work for roughly a third of the price.

Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output, the same list price as Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, but ran one benchmark for about $0.14 per task versus Haiku's $0.41.

Built for small repeated agent jobs like tool calling and document parsing, Ember reads up to a million tokens across text, images, audio and video, though Meta is keeping its model weights private.
🛑 OpenAI builds kill switch for rogue research models LINK
OpenAI has built a system called Control Room that can cut off an AI research model's access to output, a safety measure prompted by several cases this year of its models acting beyond their instructions.

The system tracks training runs, evaluations, and data processing across OpenAI's research setup, assigning each job an identifier that the inference engine checks before producing any model output.

When a person or automated monitor orders a job stopped, Control Room revokes its authorization and blocks further output, though cached permissions can delay a shutdown by up to 35 seconds.
🔐 Google DeepMind proves Signal encryption is secure LINK
Google DeepMind says its AI agents mathematically proved that the code behind the Signal protocol, which secures conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages, works correctly without security flaws.

The team used a framework called AlphaProof Code, pairing human experts with AI agents powered by Gemini Carbon to generate over six million lines of Lean, a language that checks code is accurate.

The process took four weeks instead of years, with agents flagging just one percent of the code for human review, and it correctly caught two old bugs deliberately put back into an isolated copy.

items.articleBody:
“Let’s talk about death.”

That’s what the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat said to President Trump near the end of their interview that aired Sunday.

Douthat asked Trump what he thought would happen to him when he dies. “I’m a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” the president said. When Douthat pressed him on whether he actually believes he’s going to heaven, Trump replied, “I hope so. I don’t want to go to hell.”

Douthat then posed a hypothetical: “Let’s say you pass away, you’re entering the next life, and all you have to do to enter paradise is feel love and forgiveness for James Comey, Nancy Pelosi, anyone who you have expressed hate for over the years. Do you think you can do it?”

Trump acknowledged that the easy answer would be, Oh, yes, I could forgive. He didn’t give it. “I found them to be extremely dishonest people, very bad people, very bad for our country,” he said. Pressed again, he was blunt: “The answer is no.”

“Before the judgment throne of God?” Douthat asked.

Trump didn’t budge. “No, I think they were very bad people and—I dislike, I can use the word hate, I do hate some of my enemies.”

Moments later, he removed any doubt. Even before the judgment throne of God, with his eternal salvation at stake, would he forgive his enemies? “No, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”

NO POLITICIAN IN AMERICAN HISTORY has told as many lies as Trump. But on this question, I believe he was telling the truth. In one respect I give him credit for it. He might have just said he could forgive. That’s the answer we’re taught to give. Jesus told his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, and forgiveness is preached from American pulpits every week. But forgiveness is hard, really hard, and it’s especially hard to grant to those you believe have gravely wronged you. (In Trump’s case, he’s confusing being wronged with being held accountable. But he’s convinced himself that he’s been horribly mistreated.)

[Nick Clegg: Getting too close to Trump was a mistake]

Too many churches preach what I’d call “cheap forgiveness,” a cousin of what the theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer called “cheap grace.” Forgiveness takes time, and it should. Forgiving someone instantly usually means you haven’t yet reckoned with the pain. We have to make space to process the grief, anger, and trauma of suffering a deep injustice. That’s why “forgive and forget” is such bad advice. The Christian psychiatrist Curt Thompson argues that it gets things backward: Real forgiveness requires remembering. That means deliberately revisiting the hurt, ideally with others, until the memory is reshaped rather than suppressed.

Cheap forgiveness is also a form of enabling. It lets the person who did the damage off the hook. When forgiveness comes too fast and with no cost, it can tell them that what they did wasn’t so bad after all. It lets them skip remorse, stunts their capacity for genuine empathy, and reinforces a sense of impunity.

But Trump wasn’t simply acknowledging that forgiveness is hard. He seems to regard forgiveness as unnecessary at best and a sign of weakness at worst. For one thing, he has said he isn’t sure he’s ever asked God for forgiveness. “I don’t bring God into that picture,” he once explained. For another, he has turned the National Prayer Breakfast into a stage for denouncing his political opponents as “dishonest” and “corrupt.” He has preached vengeance at a gathering that, until Trump, had been a bipartisan refuge of reconciliation and generosity of spirit.

BUT WHAT WAS MOST REVEALING about the 60 Minutes interview was how openly Trump owned the hatred at the core of who he is. He seemed almost proud of its depth and intensity. More than any other force, even his narcissism, hate seems to drive him. It fuels his posts on Truth Social. It explains his hunger for power. It feeds his obsessions. It bleeds into his every interaction. And it works on him like a drug: The more he indulges it, the more he craves it. Not even the deaths of men he considered enemies—John McCain, Rob Reiner, Robert Mueller—can satisfy his venom. When Mueller died in March, Trump’s response was, “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.”

It has also crowded out joy. It’s hard to recall Trump ever seeming truly happy. And it leaves no room for intimacy, because anyone close to him might one day become an enemy. Hate often does its deepest damage to the one who carries it. In the end, it corrodes the soul of the hater.

Trump’s hatred has also corroded the soul of his party. It’s striking how much the Republican Party—and how much of the Christian right—has come to resemble him during the Trump era. We see it in the brutal personal attacks, the proud displays of cruelty, and the delight in watching the strong hurt the weak. The party that for decades championed family values, law and order, and the formation of virtue and character in the young has become Castle Rock, Jack’s stronghold in William Golding’s Lord of the Flies. It’s a place of violent tribal loyalty, where power comes from force and hatred is a badge of belonging.

[Peter Wehner: A good night for the Christian faith]

Last week, the GOP’s Castle Rock was breached. People who practice the politics of love crushed those who embody the politics of hate. It will take time for Castle Rock to collapse. But collapse it will, and so will the man who built it.

IT WAS NOT TRUMP’S FIERCEST CRITICS but Trump himself who said, in effect, that he would choose hate and hell over love and heaven. That calls to mind C. S. Lewis’s line in The Problem of Pain that “the doors of hell are locked on the inside.” Lewis meant that people choose hell because they prefer their own will and pride. They would rather cling to their grievances and grudges, their self-pity and their enmity, than let them go, even to God.

“I imagine one of the reasons people cling to their hates so stubbornly is because they sense, once hate is gone, they will be forced to deal with pain,” the novelist, essayist, and civil-rights activist James Baldwin wrote. The pain beneath Trump’s hatred may well be enormous. Under different circumstances, he might be a tragic figure. But because he has inflicted so much pain on so many, especially the weak and the vulnerable, and has delighted in their suffering, he is instead a malevolent figure. His indelible legacy, and his movement’s, will be disgrace and dishonor.

Baby Audio startet Black Friday Sale mit bis zu 72 % Rabatt

Baby Audio Plugins · Quelle: Baby Audio

Falls du noch nie ein Plugin von Baby Audio ausprobiert hast, ist jetzt eine top Gelegenheit dafür. Und auch wenn du dein Sortiment mit weiteren Tools des Herstellers erweitern willst, solltest du mal die aktuellen Angebote studieren. Der Hersteller startet nämlich schon jetzt seine Black-Friday-Offensive.

Im Angebot ist fast jedes Plugin, darunter sind auch die neueren Tools des Herstellers und ebenso die meisten All-Time-Hits. Davon hat Baby Audio ja mittlerweile einige am Start. Effekte wie Spaced Out sind dabei, Smooth Operator, Humanoid (für sehr kreative Vocal-Effekte), Graininferno oder auch die sehr schönen Synthesizer BA-1 oder Atoms.

Ich mag die Plugins von Baby Audio sehr. Sie haben einen sehr coolen Look und klingen fantastisch – letztendlich kommt es darauf ja am meisten an. Dazu versucht Baby Audio, sehr eigenständige Konzepte umzusetzen.

Spaced Out hat sich zum Beispiel zu einem meiner Lieblingseffekte gemausert, der mich mit seiner Würfel-Funktion immer wieder neu begeistert. Und das Plugin bekommst du jetzt für nur 27,90 Euro (statt 99 Euro).

Bis zu 72 % Rabatt gibt Baby Audio während dieses Sales, der bis zum 8. Dezember 2026 läuft. Lohnt sich wirklich, da mal zu stöbern. Hier bei Thomann* findest du die Plugins des Herstellers und siehst auch genau, wie hoch die Rabatte ausfallen.

Auch bei Safari Audio gilt: Der Hersteller ist erfrischend anders. Vielleicht sind die Plugins einigen etwas zu bunt, aber hier steckt Expertise drin. Und zwar von dem Mixing- und Mastering-Ingenieur Noam Levinber. Der will mit seinen Tools nicht nur für guten Sound sorgen, sondern auch inspirieren.

16 Effekte stecken in dem Everything Bundle V2 und bieten neben Noams Mastering Console V2 (einer nach analoger Hardware entwickelte Mastering-Kette mit True-Peak-Limiter) viele weitere schöne Effekte an.

Du entdeckst hier Vintage-Verzerrer mit Transient Shaper, Bass-Enhancer, Hall-Effekte, einen Kanalzug wie Camel Strip V2, Fuzz-, Chorus- und Tape-Effekte oder ein Tape-Delay. Aber auch eine Bandmaschinen-Simulation, ein Parallelkompressor (mit Opto-, VCA- und „Devil“-Schaltung) oder auch Klangerzeuger wie Super Chunk, Polyrex und Cubby sind in diesem Bundle enthalten.

Obendrauf gibt’s neben der gerade erwähnten Mastering-Chain auch noch KI-Assistenten für Mixing und Effektketten.

items.title: Pablo Neruda on How to Hold Time
items.subtitle: “Time is a river that sweeps me along, but I am a river,” Borges wrote.
items.feedText:
“Time is a fire that consumes me, but I am the fire.”

Most of us are not Borges. Most of us are drowning in bewilderment at where the time goes, burning with the urgency of being alive while waiting to start living, wandering the labyrinth of life with wayward presence, wishing that time ran differently as the cult of productivity turns each minute into a blade pressed against the vein of our transience. And all the while, our time is nested within our times — the epoch we are living through together, born into…
items.articleBody:
“Time is a river that sweeps me along, but I am a river,” Borges wrote. “Time is a fire that consumes me, but I am the fire.”

Most of us are not Borges. Most of us are drowning in bewilderment at where the time goes, burning with the urgency of being alive while waiting to start living, wandering the labyrinth of life with wayward presence, wishing that time ran differently as the cult of productivity turns each minute into a blade pressed against the vein of our transience.

And all the while, our time is nested within our times — the epoch we are living through together, born into it with no more choice in the matter than the body and brain and family we have been born into. In his magnificent essay on Shakespeare, James Baldwin countered the commonplace lament of every epoch: “It is said that his time was easier than ours, but I doubt it — no time can be easy if one is living through it.” A century before him — a century of unrest and transformation — Emerson issued the ultimate antilamentation: “This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it.”

Discus chronologicus — a German depiction of time from the early 1720s. (Available as a print and as a wall clock.)

Not knowing what to do with the time we have been given, not knowing how to hold time in our personal and political lives, is at bottom an act of forgetting how time hold us. Pablo Neruda (July 12, 1904–September 23, 1973) casts a spell against forgetting in the fourth canto of his long poem “Morning,”:

You will remember that whimsical ravine

where the vibrant aromas rose,

and from time to time a bird dressed

in water and languor: winter’s garment.

You will remember those gifts from the earth:

piquing fragrance, gold clay,

thickets of herbs, wild roots,

bewitching thorns like swords.

You will remember the bouquet you brought,

a bouquet of shadow and silent water,

a bouquet like foam-covered stone.

And that time was like never and always:

We go where nothing is expected

and find everything waiting there.

Pablo Neruda

If time is the fundamental problem of human life and poetry is our most precise technology for parsing the aching astonishment of being alive, then time is the prime subject of poetry. Neruda knew this — time is the subterranean current coursing beneath his vast and varied body of work, the substrate upon which all of his stunning love poems and his meditations on the inner life grow. He reverenced the stones for how they have “touched time,” reverenced the minute for how it is “bound to join the river of time that bears us,” reverenced “the inexhaustible springs of time,” longed for “a time complete as an ocean,” then made that ocean with his poetry.

In his poem “The Enigmas,” composed during WWII, he writes:

You’ve asked me what the crustacean spins

between its gold claws

and I reply: the sea knows.

You wonder what the sea squirt waits for in its transparent bell?

What does it wait for?

I’ll tell you: it’s waiting for time like you.

A decade later, in one of his “Elemental Odes,” Neruda laid out his most explicit instruction for how to hold time:

Listen and learn.

Time

is divided

into two rivers:

one

flows backward, devouring

life already lived;

the other

moves forward with you

exposing

your life.

For a single second

they may be joined.

Now.

This is that moment,

the drop of an instant

that washes away the past.

It is the present.

It is in your hands.

Racing, slipping,

tumbling like a waterfall.

But it is yours.

Help it grow

with love, with firmness,

with stone and flight,

with resounding

rectitude,

with purest grains,

the most brilliant metal

from your heart,

walking

in the full light of day

without fear

of truth, goodness, justice,

companions of song,

time that flows

will have the shape

and sound

of a guitar,

and when you want

to bow to the past,

the singing spring of

transparent time

will reveal your wholeness.

Time is joy.

Couple with three poems for trusting time, then revisit Kahlil Gibran on how to befriend time.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

# 10

Die Analyse zu „10“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
Last year, I was talking to an Apple engineer at WWDC and they asked me which features I was still missing from iPadOS following the massive update that was iPadOS 26 and its complete rethinking of multitasking, among other updates. Without hesitation, I replied that for iPadOS to be effective in my new kind of AI workflow, I still needed two niche features that would help me – and others like me – work better with agents: a Terminal, for running agents locally on iPad, and the Screen Sharing app they’d updated on macOS a few years prior in macOS Sonoma, for connecting to agents remotely.

I knew that the second part of the answer would catch them by surprise. “What do you mean the Screen Sharing app?” As I reminded them, a few years before, Apple’s macOS team added a High Performance mode to the Screen Sharing app that is built into every Mac. That feature is awesome: it requires a high-speed network with low latency, plus a modern Mac with Apple silicon; if these requirements are met, it kicks off a remote desktop session that is basically “fancy VNC” that has vastly superior image quality, low-latency interactions, and “supports stereo audio, HDR video reference mode, 4:4:4 chroma subsampling, and high frame rates (30 or 60 fps)”. You can read more about it here; John reviewed it at the time here.

You see, rumor has it that Apple created High Performance mode for the Vision Pro (which was also announced in 2023) as the underlying technology for Mac Virtual Display, which is, arguably, the best feature of the Vision Pro to date. In the process, however, they realized that the mode was also useful for Mac-to-Mac connections, and so they added it to the semi-forgotten Screen Sharing app, thus turning an abandoned utility into the best-performing remote desktop client for Mac.

I’ve been using Apple’s Screen Sharing app almost exclusively (I still used Jump Desktop for connecting to my gaming PC) for the past two years since I started running coding agents first on a Mac mini, then on a fleet of Mac Studios. Nothing came even close to the speed, stability, and image quality of Apple’s High Performance mode when I wanted to connect from my MacBook Pro to the Mac Studio running Claude Code and Codex. Hence why I brought this up in my private conversation with the aforementioned Apple engineer: in an agentic world that involved remote Macs doing the work behind the scenes, and assuming Apple didn’t want to put a Terminal on iPadOS, it would have been nice to at least have a Screen Sharing app of matching quality on the platform.

Well: I can stop wishing for that. In a surprising turn of events, Edovia’s Screens – the app that started it all for me when I first covered it 16 years ago (welp) – has become, to the best of my knowledge, the first third-party VNC client for Apple platforms to support the same High Performance mode used by Apple.

And, as you can imagine, this mode is awesome in Screens too. And because Screens is on the iPhone and iPad, too, in addition to the Mac and Vision Pro, it means we finally have a way to connect to a remote Mac (with support for multiple virtual displays, also new in this release) with the same quality and performance as the Screen Sharing app for Mac, but from iOS and iPadOS. In my tests for the past week with Apple’s and Edovia’s apps side by side, I couldn’t tell a meaningful difference between the two in terms of image quality and performance. Even better: the updated Screens app does not require any additional software to be installed on your Mac to take advantage of the new performance mode. Since it’s using the official Apple technology for this, all you need to do is – just like in the Screen Sharing app – pick between Standard and High Performance mode upon connecting.

Connecting in High Performance mode.

Multitasking with Screens on iPhone Duo (right).

There is, however, a lot more going on behind the scenes in Screens 5.10 that made this update possible. One of the benefits of High Performance mode is that it can dynamically scale the resolution of the host Mac to match the display that’s connecting to it. This means that, at long last, Screens will resize the Mac’s desktop to match the resolution of the display you’re using with no more constant panning and zooming to navigate around black bars shown around the macOS UI. If you’re connecting from a Mac laptop, you’ll get a widescreen desktop in full resolution. Using an iPhone Duo’s outer display? You’ll get a tiny Mac desktop instead that is, however, perfectly usable in my experience for quick tasks (such as approving agent prompts). Open up the Duo, or use an iPad, and Screens will automatically resize to match the larger canvas. It all just works and it takes a couple of seconds on a fast connection to resize. We’ve seen this feature in other apps before (such as Jump Desktop and Sill, which I covered last week), and it’s great to see Screens catch up in this regard.

Using the new Screens on the iPhone Duo’s inner display.

Dynamic resizing in action.

But wait, there’s more. In addition to High Performance mode and dynamic resizing, Edovia also modernized the underlying foundation of the app, improving the frameworks that are used to stream from one device to another. Screens now uses HEVC video, which allows for smoother animations and more fluid transitions of windows and other elements; and the app is now using a Metal-based graphics rendering pipeline to accelerate graphics performance and responsiveness. Impressively, the Metal-driven optimizations also apply to non-Mac computers, which I haven’t been able to test myself, but am curious to learn more about. The difference in performance between the old Screens with Standard mode and its original rendering engine and this new one is staggering.

To top it all off, this update also introduces the ability for Screens to stream audio in real time from a remote computer – again, matching what’s possible in Apple’s Screen Sharing app. I didn’t quite believe it when I first read the app’s changelog last week, so I had to check for myself. The combination of HEVC, Metal, and audio streaming is so good, I can start a YouTube video on my M5 Ultra Mac Studio, stream it via Screens to my MacBook Pro, and the video looks and sounds just fine with no delays or weird image artifacts. I don’t know why I’d ever do this in practice, but the fact that it’s technically possible is a testament to the quality of the work Edovia put into this release.

Screens on macOS Golden Gate.

In case it’s not clear: I think Luc Vandal and the Edovia team shipped one of the most impressive app updates of the year with Screens 5.10, breathing new life into an app at the best possible time given the rise of agents running on remote Macs and Apple’s lack of a Screen Sharing app for iPhone and iPad.

Screens 5.10 has singlehandedly allowed me to unify my scattered remote screen sharing setup back into one app on all my devices that matches the performance of Apple’s official app, but also exceeds Apple’s work thanks to its power-user options such as a floating toolbar, Tailscale integration, customizable keyboard shortcuts, and more.

After 16 years, Screens is, once again, the best remote screen sharing app for Apple platforms. If you, like me, manage agents on remote Macs on a daily basis, I cannot recommend checking out Screens 5.10 enough.

I knew that the second part of the answer would catch them by surprise. “What do you mean the Screen Sharing app?” As I reminded them, a few years before,…

items.subtitle: Set on the southern edge of Banyoles Lake, La finca de Casa Nostra occupies a site of exceptional environmental sensitivity.

items.articleBody:
Giuliano Infantino, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Toronto, has created new, freely accessible digital editions of the works of Hegel and Schelling.

About the Hegel collection, Infantino writes:

Digital Hegel texts have existed for a long time; they mostly follow older editions of the works, often in modernized spelling and without Hegel’s letter-spacing. This digital edition presents Hegel’s text according to the Gesammelte Werke (GW), the authoritative historical-critical edition: in the spelling of the GW, with letter-spaced type marked, citable line by line according to the GW pages. It contains only Hegel’s public-domain text, without the editors’ protected apparatus.

It is a work in progress, as further volumes will be added to it as its intellectual property protections expire. Infantino discusses the intellectual property rights issues related to scholarly editions of these texts here.

The Schelling collection is based on the text of the Sämmtliche Werke. Infantino says:

Schelling’s Sämmtliche Werke are widely cited, and for the late philosophy they remain the only complete edition to this day. Until now they could be read freely only as scans or in electronic versions that have not been checked against the print. This edition reads the text page by page from the print: original spelling, letter-spaced type, real Greek, the notes in their place, citable by division (Abtheilung), volume, and page.

Both collections feature full text search functions.

The editions were created using a “a multistage, machine-based procedure: the text is obtained directly from the scan of each printed page, guided by fixed rules for spelling, emphasis, and structure.”

Check sheet images from the production of the Schelling collection

For example, for the Schelling editions:

The text is produced from three readings. An older electronic transcription supplies wording, letter-spaced type, notes, and Greek; to this is added the OCR [optical character recognition scan] of two copies of the print digitized by the Bavarian State Library. Where the three do not agree, the decision is made against the page image.

The procedure is described in more detail here.

I’d be curious to hear from Hegel and Schelling scholars what they think of these new resources.

The post New Digital Editions of Hegel, Schelling appeared first on Daily Nous.

items.articleBody: Reliable generalization is essential for deploying drug–drug interaction (DDI) and drug–target interaction (DTI) models in drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, and clinical decision support. However, strong performance on random splits or weakly constrained evaluations may not reflect how well a model generalizes to new drugs, targets, or deployment conditions. In pairwise prediction, test instances may still resemble training examples in molecular structure, sequence, or network context. Such overlap can inflate performance estimates and make interpolation appear to be extrapolation. In this Perspective, we argue that cold-start evaluation should be treated as an auditable deployment claim. We organize common evaluation settings by their source and scope of novelty, ranging from random splits and entity-disjoint protocols to structure-level, temporal, domain-disjoint, and many-domain evaluations. The L0–L5 framework clarifies which deployment claim each setting is designed to test. Coverage, overlap, and distance quantify the resulting train–test discrepancy. We further provide a practical checklist for leakage control, validation alignment, candidate-pair construction, and domain-level risk reporting. This Perspective clarifies the boundaries and evidential scope of cold-start evaluation, providing a common basis for interpreting and comparing results across DDI and DTI studies.

items.articleBody:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

—James O’Donnell

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why.

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair
+ Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. (Wired $)
+ They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. (Verge)
+ And threaten the fate of the economy. (WP $)

2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges
Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. (NPR)
+ Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. (Axios)
+ Is your smart kitchen next? (Wired $)

3 The Iran war has triggered a drop in global emissions
The main driver is energy supply constraints. (New Scientist $)
+ But the decline will likely prove temporary. (Gizmodo)
+ Our climate models have a big blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)

4 The FDA has ordered GLP-1s to carry warnings about blindness
It says the drugs may increase the risk of vision loss. (NBC News)
+ GLP-1s could also exacerbate eating disorders. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Australia is mulling criminal penalties for rogue AI
The proposals follow an AI agent hacking government systems. (BBC)

6 The Pentagon is planning to patrol the Moon
The project’s first five satellites could launch in 2029. (Ars Technica)

7 Two US cities have voted to ditch Flock surveillance cameras
York, Maine, and League City, Texas, have voted to ban them. (Vox)
+ What Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)

8 Constant surveillance is changing how children grow up
Tracking apps can fuel anxiety and undermine resilience. (Atlantic $)

9 A tiny RNA molecule could explain how life began
Some researchers believe life emerged from self-copying molecules. (Quanta)

10 A sci-fi novel has won the Booker Prize for the first time
The End of Everything was awarded the prestigious honor. (Gizmodo)

Quote of the day

“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company’s strings himself.”

—Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, tells Reuters why it will be so difficult to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.

One More Thing

China wants to restore the sea with high-tech marine ranches

Just a short ferry ride from the Chinese port city of Yantai sits Genghai No. 1, a strange offshore complex that combines a tourist attraction with an industrial fish farm. It even has a seven-story visitor center shaped like a cartoon starfish. But its main purpose is to breed fish and release them into the ocean.

Genghai is part of China’s ambitious marine ranching program. Since 2015, the country has built 169 demonstration ranches and released at least 167 billion juvenile fish and shellfish. But the approach has also proved controversial.

Dive into China’s divisive plans to restore the seas with marine ranches.

—Matthew Ponsford

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ “Earth artist” David Popa has created a new land-art portrait in the mountains of Norway.
+ The winners of Wildlife Photographer of the Year capture both the power and fragility of nature.
+ A Minnesota man who stopped a runaway school bus got surprised with a $1,000 cheque from Superman.
+ After more than two decades without regular star shows, Frank Lloyd Wright’s only planetarium has been restored.

items.body:
# Kassel studierende zivilklausel protest

Die »Zivilklausel« ist seit ihrer Einführung an der Universität Bremen im Jahr 1986 ein Eckpfeiler des deutschen Hochschulwesens der Nachkriegszeit. Sie wird mittlerweile von über 70 Hochschulen und Forschungseinrichtungen in Deutschland als verpflichtend angesehen. Demnach muss dort alle universitäre Forschung ausschließlich friedlichen Zwecken dienen.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.
