items.articleBody:
What Is Regret?

“Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all, – the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.” – Seneca, from Letters from a Stoic

After a long day at work and terrible traffic, you finally make it home. The stress has taken its toll, and you’re exhausted, bored, and frustrated with the day’s events all at once. You walk into your kitchen to find a heaping pile of dishes–something you asked your spouse to take care of this morning! Yet, they’re relaxing in front of the TV as if nothing’s wrong.

You feel the anger rising up, and unable to control yourself, you yell at your spouse. You don’t hold back. You’re out to make a point, to prove that what happened is a really big deal.

Your spouse is frightened and embarrassed. They’re worried–you’ve never yelled at them like this before. They were going to do the dishes later, but you never gave them that opportunity. The day’s been long for them too, yet you didn’t care. They just wanted to have a nice night with you, but now that’s ruined.

Later that night, you finally start to understand what losing your temper has cost you. You know you shouldn’t have said what you said. You should have been more considerate. You should have acted differently–you regret your choices.

Maybe for you it wasn’t a pile of dishes that set you off. Maybe it was your kids using markers on the wall. Or your boss dumping that report on you before your vacation. Regardless of the scenario, we’ve all lost it at some point, and we’ve all felt the pang of regret.

The Stoics would define regret as the moment when past events consume our present lives. When we dwell over things we have no control over. When we resist our fate. Marcus Aurelius argued that we must be “satisfied with what [we] have, and accept the present–all of it.” Regret is the contrary–when we’re not satisfied with what we have, when we reject what we’ve been given.

Seneca said “we often suffer more in imagination than in reality.” He was saying that regret is no more than an emotion of our imagination. We believe that had we said something (or held our tongue), had we acted differently, the outcome would have been different.

Marcus Aurelius carried a similar mindset, and provided a solution to this problem. “External things are not the problem. It is your assessment of them. Which you can erase right now.”

Let’s take another look at that “fight” you had with your spouse. Your regrets are not about the actual dishes or your spouse–it’s about your perception of expectations. You expected your spouse to have the dishes done when you got home. So you believe it should have been different, and had it been different, you would be better off.

So does that mean it’s your spouse’s fault? Maybe for leaving the dishes in the sink. But certainly not for your overreaction. And definitely not for the regret you felt later that night. Regret is an internal problem, to be both diagnosed and treated by ourselves. We must learn to look past these “self-focused emotions” and master our feelings of regret. This post aims to help you understand your emotions, use the past to your advantage, and conquer your biggest regrets.

Why Do I Feel Regret?

“Life is very short and anxious for those who forget the past, neglect the present, and fear the future” – Seneca

We’ve all told ourselves, “no regrets.” There are countless memes, inspirational quotes, and videos reminding us online. Poets, singers, painters, and writers have been creating art about it for millenia.  We’ve practically been conditioned to live by it.

But no matter how many times we read about it, sing along to a song about it, or tell ourselves not to, we all have something we regret. We all have that nagging feeling that comes back to us. That hits us exactly when we thought we forgot about that time, that place, those people. It comes back at the very worst time. It sucks. It hurts.

The power of regret is not to be understated. Bestselling author and founder of the American Regret Project Daniel Pink found that 82 percent of Americans experience regret at least occasionally. Pink describes regret as “an indispensable emotion,” yet also claims it can be “a positive instrument for improving your life.”

If we truly want to improve our life, we can’t run away from these negative feelings. We can’t hide them. But should we just accept this despair? Should we just come to terms living with regret?

This is what the great writer Samuel Johnson must have been wondering near the end of 1775. With 1776 on the horizon, Johnson wrote in his diary:

“When I look back on resolutions of improvement and amendment which have year after year been made and broken, either by negligence, forgetfulness, vicious idleness, casual interruption, or morbid infirmity; when I find that so much of my life has been stolen unprofitably away, and that I can descry by retrospection scarcely a few single days properly and vigorously employed, why do I yet try to resolve again? I try because reformation is necessary and despair is criminal.”

Johnson came to terms with his past, but not with his regret. He chose to reflect upon his hardships in order to better himself, to avoid making those same mistakes in the future. He chose to fight regret–not to wallow in it.

If there’s one thing we can learn from Johnson, it must be that experiencing regret is inevitable–but our actions and our mindset are not. Thus, the question is not ‘Why do I feel regret?’, but rather ‘How do I deal with it?’ ‘How do I move on?’ ‘How can I make myself better because of this?’ In order to answer these questions, the Stoics practiced the following strategies to help them build their mental toughness and resilience–starting with examining what they controlled.

Focus On What You Control

“Every event has two handles, one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can’t. If your brother does you wrong, don’t grab it by his wronging, because this is the handle incapable of lifting it. Instead, use the other—that he is your brother, that you were raised together, and then you will have hold of the handle that carries.” – Epictetus

One of the most important practices in Stoic philosophy, which was introduced by Epictetus, is determining what we control and what we don’t. What we have power over and what we don’t. What we can change and what we can’t.

There are two ways in which we can look at the past–two handles we can grab, to use Epictetus’ quote. The first handle forces us to perceive the past as an inevitable experience, destined to wrong and hurt us from the beginning. The opposite handle, however, allows us to extract the good parts, and use our experiences to benefit ourselves.

In looking at past decisions, we must grab them by the latter handle. We must understand that what happened, happened. We must see that we can’t change the past, no matter how much it hurt us or someone else. So what good does regret do?

Absolutely nothing, as Holocaust survivor and author Dr. Edith Eger explained to Ryan Holiday on an episode of The Daily Stoic Podcast. Ryan was discussing a relationship he regretted messing up, and Dr. Eger offered him one gift that would solve the guilt right then. “I give you a sentence,” she said, “One sentence—if I knew then what I know now, I would have done things differently.” That’s the end of that, she said. “Guilt is in the past, and the one thing you cannot change is the past.”

As a society we’ve become disillusioned by the idea of what we control. We all believe we have some control over the outcome of whatever we encounter. We all believe that if we keep thinking about what happened, somehow we’ll be able to change what happened.

Yet, we must come to terms with the fact that some things simply can’t be changed. We must understand that some things are in our control and some that aren’t. Say, if you regret getting a haircut, you’re in control. You can style it, cover it, or just wait for it to grow out again–you command your situation. But if you regret cursing out your boss before quitting your job, you’re not in control–you can’t take back your words.

As Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself—and by extension, to us:

“Remind yourself that past and future have no power over you. Only the present—and even that can be minimized. Just mark off its limits. And if your mind tries to claim that it can’t hold out against that…well, then, heap shame upon it.”

The past is done. We can’t linger in our insecurities. We can’t ponder over our regrets. We must learn that what happened is out of our control now–we must let go.

“Letting go is a necessary, if sometimes heart-wrenching gateway to genuine transformation,” is how the always-zen basketball coach Phil Jackson put it. The Stoics called it the “art of acquiescence”—the giving up and the assenting of whatever things are so that they can be what they are to become.

In one way, regret is just wishing things went the way we wanted them to. But by letting things become what they must, we are less likely to regret what we’ve done. In accepting that some things are simply out of our control, we are less likely to wish for a different outcome.

The past is something we can’t control anymore. We can’t change what we said, what we did, or how we felt.

We can, however, control the present. We control how we grow from our experiences. We control how we respond to adversity. We control how we can use our regret to our advantage.

We control how we act right now. We must.

To learn more on this topic, check out “You Control How You Play”, where Ryan speaks to the Cleveland Browns about the importance of perspective, staying motivated, and knowing what they control.

Love Your Fate

“A blazing fire makes flame and brightness out of everything that is thrown into it.” – Marcus Aurelius

After we sort out what we control, we must find how to respond–regardless if we control what’s happening or not. We must determine how we handle ourselves. We must determine how we overcome obstacles. We must determine how to move forward.

In the first book of his Discourses, Epictetus envisions himself being executed by Roman guards, his life out of his control. In a display of tranquility and wisdom, he lays out his thoughts:

“I must die. But must I die bawling? I must be put in chains–but moaning and groaning too? I must be exiled; but is there anything to keep me from going with a smile, calm and self-composed.”

Though the term was first coined by German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, the practice of amor fati–loving your fate–dates back to Epictetus and the Stoics. Often by means of reflection and meditation, the Stoics would use this practice to settle past trauma and help them achieve a greater sense of inner peace. “The Fates guide the person who accepts them,” Cleanthes said, “and hinder the person who resists them.”

Amor fati is more than just understanding what happens to us. It’s understanding that our perception doesn’t always have to be negative. It’s understanding that accepting the present circumstances will make us better. It’s understanding that we must be grateful for the cloudy weather sometimes–and that there’s always a way through the storm.

We all face hardships. We all get stuck in traffic. We all deal with slow WiFi, or bad cell service, right when we need to send that important message. As rational people, we tend to think that these hardships were made specifically for us. That the world is out to get us. That we can’t win.

But this couldn’t be farther from the truth. Everybody goes through obstacles. Everybody gets tripped up sometimes. As we talked about in the first section, we can’t control some things in life. And these hardships, no matter how hard we try, will always be out of our control.

When we accept what happens to us, after understanding that certain things— particularly bad things—are outside our control, we are left with this: loving whatever happens to us and facing it with unfailing cheerfulness and strength. As bestselling author Robert Greene (48 Laws of Power, Mastery) put it, we need to, “accept the fact that all events occur for a reason, and that it is within your capacity to see this reason as positive.”

Marcus Aurelius portrays this concept perfectly in Meditations through the image of an artisans shop:

“There are thorns on the path, then keep away! Enough said. Why ponder the existence of nuisance? Such thinking would make you a laughing-stock to the true student of Nature, just as a carpenter or cobbler would laugh if you pointed out the sawdust and chips on the floors of their shops. Yet while those shopkeepers have dustbins for disposal, Nature has no need of them.”

Why get tripped up by the thorns? Why ponder over the sawdust on your floor? It’s simply part of nature! As long as you have the capability to see them, you have the capability to move past them.

In practicing amor fati, we’re also less likely to have regrets in the future. By embracing the challenges that lay ahead of us, we’re less likely to regret the decisions we make to conquer them – regardless of the outcome. We’re able to tackle the future with confidence, conviction, courage, and so much more.

Amor fati is more than just a mindset–it’s a way of life. Incorporating amor fati into your life will take time, effort, and sacrifices that probably won’t feel comfortable. But we must. We must move past this existential angst. We must move forward, away from our regret, and towards our future.

Love what’s happened to you. Love who you’ve become, and how much you’ve changed. Love your fate–amor fati.

Carry this reminder with you every day with our amor fati medallion from the Daily Stoic Store. Carry this in your pocket as a reminder to treat each and every moment–no matter how challenging–as something to be embraced, not avoided.

Look Ahead

“We should project our thoughts ahead of us at every turn and have in mind every possible eventuality instead of only the usual course of action.” – Seneca

Before Ryan Holiday gets on stage for a big speech, he runs through everything that could go wrong: trouble with the microphone, the clicker not advancing a slide, the audience not reacting as anticipated. He is able to see potential problems before they arise, and come up with solutions before anything actually happens. He is able to prevent himself from being overwhelmed if a problem arises by being prepared.

“Rehearse them in your mind: exile, torture, war, shipwreck,” Seneca said. “All the terms of our human lot should be before our eyes.”

This practice, called premeditatio malorum, is one of the oldest and most common practices in Stoic philosophy. It literally means the “premeditation of evils.” The Stoics used this practice to help them prepare for life’s inevitable hardships, and remain calm and confident in turbulent times.

The world isn’t fair. We all know this. We don’t always get what is ours, even if we’ve earned it. We don’t always win, even if we play hard.

But we can’t be surprised when we don’t win. If it comes as a constant surprise each and every time something unexpected occurs, you’re not only going to be miserable whenever you attempt something big, you’re going to have a much harder time accepting it and moving on to attempts two, three, and four. You’re going to have a much harder time living in the present instead of lingering in the past. You’re going to have a much harder time trusting your instincts–and fighting regret.

There’s perhaps no better personification of premeditatio malorum than the great Booker T. Washington. Washington ran a school with 1,500 students, all while advising politicians and activists and traveling across the country to give speeches. But how? How did he maintain this lifestyle, and with such striking success?

“When I begin my work in the morning, I expect to have a successful and pleasant day of it, but at the same time I prepare myself to hear that one of our school buildings is on fire, or has burned, or that some disagreeable accident had occurred, or that someone has abused me in a public address or a printed article, for something that I have done or omitted to do, or or something that he had heard that I had said—probably something I had never thought of saying.”

He envisioned the worst possible things that could happen to him throughout his day. Not only envisioned, but he expected them to happen. In doing this, Washington was more prepared for the hardships of the day. A canceled train couldn’t be as bad as his school burning down. Being late to dinner couldn’t be as bad as someone verbally abusing him in public.

In preparing himself for challenges, Washington was simultaneously preparing himself for regret. Since he saw his fears right in front of him, and anticipated them happening, he was less scared of the outcomes of his choices–and he was less likely to regret them.

In the same manner, Epictetus used this to help him foresee all of the dangers that came with a seemingly easy decision–bathing:

“If you are going to bathe, represent to yourself the incidents usual in the bath—some persons pouring out, others pushing in, others scolding, others pilfering…. For thus, if any impediment arises in bathing, you will be able to say, “It was not only to bathe that I desired, but to keep my will in harmony with nature; and I shall not keep it thus if I am out of humor at things that happen.”

Practicing premeditatio malorum allows us to be more prepared for life’s inevitable setbacks. Though it may be hard to admit, everything will not go our way. We might not get that job that we want. We might not win that game. But we will be ready for any obstacles that cross our path.

We’ll know that we made the right decision – and we won’t regret our choices.

If you want to hear Ryan talk more about this topic, check out The Stoic Secret Of Facing Failure To Achieve Success: Premeditatio Malorum on the Daily Stoic YouTube Channel.

10 Best Stoic Quotes on Regret

“Then remind yourself that past and future have no power over you. Only the present – and even that can be minimized.” – Marcus Aurelius, from Meditations

“He is a wise man who does not grieve for the things which he has not, but rejoices for those which he has.” – Epictetus, from Fragments

“External things are not the problem. It is your assessment of them. Which you can erase right now.” – Marcus Aurelius, from Meditations

“Give yourself a gift, the present moment.” – Marcus Aurelius, from Meditations

“The man who has anticipated the coming of troubles takes away their power when they arrive.”- Seneca, from Consolation to Marcia

“To shrug it all off and wipe it clean—every annoyance and distraction—and reach utter stillness. Child’s play.” — Marcus Aurelius, from Meditations

“Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all, – the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.” – Seneca, from Letters from a Stoic

“When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.” – Viktor Frankl

“There is only one way to happiness and that is to cease worrying about things which are beyond the power of our will.” – Epictetus, from Discourses

“Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not; remember that what you now have was once among the only things you hoped for.” – Epicurus

items.articleBody:
Electronic Materials Office is the brainchild of Andrew Emerson. Back in 2023 he launched the Altar I, a rather distinctive mechanical keyboard. Much thinner than most, very opinionated in its industrial design and keycap typography. I got one and I don’t regret it, but there was too much I didn’t like about it, so it’s mostly sat in a drawer.

Today on Kickstarter Emerson/EMO has launched a campaign for the Altar II. Same cool aesthetic, but with improvements that address everything I didn’t like about the Altar I. The Altar II has all new switches. It’s so thin it resembles the profile of Apple’s Magic Keyboard from the side. The dial — now called the M-Dial — now attaches magnetically, which means it’s easy to detach for putting the keyboard into a bag. And it has new features that never even occurred to me, like NiteLite — backlighting from “a long-wavelength amber-red light that won’t affect your body’s circadian rhythm, meaning you can sleep better at night.” The sleep benefits might be voodoo but red lights are undeniably easier on your eyes at night, and it looks cool as shit. (My favorite feature of Apple Watch Ultra is “Night Mode” — a handful of watch faces that switch to all-red in the dark.)

I love that mechanical keyboards have come back into vogue, and that the market for them is thriving. But most of them annoy me. Often because they aren’t really keyboards — they’re design-your-own-keyboard kits. Kits are fun, but I want someone else to do the hard work of making all the design decisions. Don’t make me choose between half a dozen (or more!) types of switches. You’re the goddamn keyboard designer, you pick the switches. That’s my thinking. Altar II is that type of keyboard — one that has been properly and thoroughly designed for you. You just choose the key layout — US or UK. That’s it.

Another thing I don’t like about most mechanical keyboards — that also makes them feel like a hobby, not a finished product — is that they’re designed for cross-platform use. If they’re customizable via software, the software tends to be confusing and poorly made. Altar II is designed for the Mac and is going to come with a native Mac app for configuration. Fuckin’-A right.

I haven’t tried the Altar II yet because it’s only at the preproduction stage. That’s why it’s on Kickstarter. You can wait and see what I think of it next year. But if you jump on the Kickstarter now, there’s a first-48-hours early bird price that will save you $70. Retail price is going to be $350; for the remaining 40 hours or so, you can book one for just $280. After tomorrow, Kickstarter pricing goes up to $300.

Learn how guided virtual shock and drop analysis helps engineering teams identify reliability risks before physical testing, reduce qualification iterations, optimize packaging designs, and accelerate electronics product development.

What you will learn about:

Why shock failures found during physical qualification are costly, and how coupled electrical, mechanical, thermal, and packaging effects make them hard to predict.

How running the full drop orientation matrix as one validation plan supports packaging optimization, and how correlation with physical tests builds confidence before hardware is committed.

items.articleBody:
Mackenzie Hawkins, reporting yesterday for Bloomberg:

Despite that stance, in the months after Teter’s initial call with
Kessler, Nvidia gave BIS an incomplete account of its business
with Megaspeed. After several visits to Megaspeed’s data centers — 12 facilities owned by eight companies across three countries
in Southeast Asia — Nvidia had sent inventory checks to the
agency and declared to Bloomberg News in mid-November 2025 that
everything was where it should be.

The company also said at the time that it had asked the US
government whether it needed to cut off business with Megaspeed,
and was told no.

But Nvidia’s tabulations, as relayed to the US government,
undercounted the number of chips it had sold to Megaspeed via
hardware partners by 50,000 units, according to trade records
analyzed by Bloomberg. That’s worth billions of dollars. After
being pressed about the gap, Nvidia told Bloomberg in December
2025 that it had checked additional Megaspeed warehouses that
contained the missing hardware, while declining to state exactly
how many chips it found in those facilities or provide any further
details.

items.articleBody:
5 min read

NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds

The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy.

Watch to learn how the presence of a planet modifies the gravitational wave signal from tightly orbiting white dwarfs. The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory could detect a Jupiter-mass planet in such systems up to thousands of light-years away. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center

Download high-resolution video from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio

“The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,” said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.”

Two papers published Tuesday in The Astrophysical Journal detail the findings. The first, authored solely by McGrath, examines the detection method and determines the planet masses and orbital periods where it would work best. The second paper, by McGrath and coauthors, investigates how such planets could be confirmed using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope.

The possibility of detecting exoplanets around LISA double white dwarf systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008.

Led by ESA (European Space Agency), the LISA mission is slated for launch in the mid-2030s. As a collaborative partner, NASA is contributing the telescopes, other critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support as part of its mission to better understand how the universe works.

The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars. As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it. This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us. The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect.

“Something similar occurs with gravitational waves,” said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the confirmation paper. “By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency. Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.”

For LISA, this modulation will appear as sidebands, secondary signals at both higher and lower frequencies than the primary one.

McGrath likens the situation to modern radio communication, where some of the energy of a main radio carrier frequency goes into forming sidebands at adjacent upper and lower frequencies that carry messages (like voices or music). For gravitational waves, the sidebands carry messages about the presence of a planet.

White dwarfs are the Earth-sized remnants of stars like the Sun. While exoplanets have been detected around a few isolated white dwarfs, none have yet been found around a binary white dwarf, which means the LISA detections would represent a distinct new exoplanet population.

NASA’s infrared-sensitive James Webb Space Telescope, shown in this artist’s concept, will be able to confirm planets detected by gravitational waves in binary white dwarf systems located within a few hundred light-years.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

Astronomers estimate that our Milky Way galaxy contains 10 million double white dwarf systems with orbital periods of less than an hour, which generate gravitational waves in the right range for LISA to find. They expect LISA will resolve about 10,000 individual systems, as well as around 100 mixed binaries — with white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes — orbiting in similar periods.

“Once LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,” said Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. “These joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.”

The team described a new method for confirming these planets by taking advantage of the Webb telescope’s infrared sensitivity. A planet in a double white dwarf system produces a larger portion of infrared light than what’s expected from the stars themselves. Webb’s instruments can easily detect this infrared excess out to a distance of at least 500 light-years.

Using this technique for a test case system at this distance, the researchers find that Webb could detect an exoplanet about five times Jupiter’s mass, while LISA could detect a sub-Jupiter exoplanet under ideal circumstances.

The LISA observatory will consist of a trio of spacecraft following Earth as it orbits the Sun. They will form a vast triangular array stretching 1.6 million miles (2.5 million kilometers) on each side. Each spacecraft will include two telescopes that will use infrared laser beams to simultaneously transmit and receive signals between adjacent spacecraft. Through these telescopes, the spacecraft will measure miniscule changes — smaller than the width of a helium atom — in their relative distances, the signals of passing gravitational waves.

This artist’s concept shows the LISA mission at work. Telescopes aboard each of the three spacecraft simultaneously transmit and receive infrared laser beams, measuring their mutual distances to extremely high precision across 1.6 million miles (2.5 million kilometers).

ESA

Gravitational waves were predicted by Albert Einstein’s 1916 general theory of relativity and first detected by ground-based observatories in 2015. The waves form whenever massive objects accelerate, such as two stars in orbit around each other. They travel through space-time, moving at the speed of light, and are unaffected by objects they encounter along the way. These properties make them a valuable tool for probing the cosmos.

Additional NASA contributions to the mission include the laser system, devices to manage the buildup of electric charge on the proof masses, data analysis for identifying and characterizing individual gravitational wave sources, and additional scientific and engineering expertise.

items.articleBody:
Actor Eric Rasmussen revealed this week that he had removed his contribution to an installation by Denniston Hill in the main exhibition of the Venice Biennale because the residency program appeared to support the “eradication” of Israel, in Rasmussen’s view.

In an op-ed published by the Jewish Journal on Monday, Rasmussen wrote that he had combined two drawings by his mother of Adolf Hitler drawn from a notebook she kept during her childhood. The resulting work, transferred to an acetate panel, was included Denniston Hill’s installation, an exquisite corpse–style work titled Chimera (2026) that is located in the Giardini section of Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition.

The piece features contributions by dozens of past residents at Denniston Hill, which was cofounded by artists kara lynch, Julie Mehretu, Paul Pfeiffer, and Jessica Rankin, along with art historian Lawrence Chua and curator Beth Stryker, and is located in Upstate New York. Rasmussen was a resident at Denniston Hill in 2019 through the DPAA Workshop.

Rasmussen said his submission to Chimera was a 1943 drawing by his mother that he had previously enlisted in a performance staged during his Denniston Hill residency. The piece is a drawing of a mustachioed man and some numbers, along with text reading, “Mister Hitler is invaded and his spitting.” For the Venice Biennale, he added a caption in red: “Mom’s childhood drawing 1943. The Toxicity of the Past?”

“I felt like the piece reflected the work I did at Denniston Hill while, at the same time, gesturing toward our current moment,” Rasmussen writes. “Neither the ‘toxicity’ of authoritarian leaders nor the rabid antisemitism called to mind by Hitler’s image remain in the past.”

ARTnews was able to confirm that the drawing did make it on view in time for the Biennale’s opening in May by examining installation shots of Chimera disseminated by the exhibition, which closes later this month.

It appears to have been taken away by Rasmussen at some point after mid-May, when, he wrote, Denniston Hill sent an email noting that the organization was more than 70 Biennale participants who had signed an open letter that objected to the Biennale’s claims of political neutrality. The signatories said this conflicted with the controversial decision this year to host pavilions for Israel, Russia, and the United States, all of which are “current regimes committing war crimes,” the letter said.

Moreover, according to Rasmussen, Denniston Hill wrote that it was “aligning with ANGA,” or the Art Not Genocide Alliance, a group that has repeatedly protested Israel’s presence at the Biennale while also noting that Palestine has no official pavilion in the show, and never has. (Palestine is not considered a state in Italy; only countries viewed as states by Italy’s government can have national pavilions at the Biennale, per the exhibition.)

Denniston Hill’s Chimera installation at the Venice Biennale featured a drawing by Eric Rasmussen’s mother, visible here at center as a transparency.

Photo Andrea Avezzù/Courtesy Venice Biennale

“ANGA clearly considers all of Israel to be occupied Palestine and its goal is not to oppose policies of the government of Israel but to destroy the nation,” Rasmussen claimed in his Jewish Journal essay, which alleged that Denniston Hill has “no problem blithely aligning itself with an organization that seeks that nation’s eradication without even asking for the opinions of its artists.”

His essay also labeled anti-Zionism “an assault on not only the Jewish state and Jewish history, but also on language itself,” and claimed that linking “Zionism with racism, colonialism and apartheid” was akin to “Cold War KGB propaganda.”

Without stating a precise date for the work’s removal, Rasmussen said he “wrote a lengthy email” to Denniston Hill seeking the return of the drawing. Denniston Hill obliged the request and gave back the drawing, he said.

Representatives for Denniston Hill and the Biennale did not respond to requests for comment.

items.articleBody:
Getty Images/Silver Bulletin illustration

 The latest on ELWAY

November 10, 2026

ELWAY has been updated with Monday night’s game and all of today’s trades. Yesterday, Buffalo beat Minnesota 23-6 in a matchup of 6-1 teams, improving to 7-1 and taking sole possession of the AFC’s best record. James Cook rushed for 107 yards and a touchdown, while Josh Allen threw for 234 yards and a score. The Bills’ defense held Minnesota to just six points and intercepted Carson Wentz twice, dropping the Vikings to 6-2. The Vikings will need an elite Kirk Cousins (he’s back!) to maintain their momentum if they want to stay in Super Bowl contention.

November 9, 2026

ELWAY has been updated with Sunday’s games. C.J. Stroud threw for 384 yards and five touchdowns as Houston beat the Chargers 44-22. Even at 3-5, the Texans now have a solid chance to make the playoffs, up from 24 percent entering Sunday. Jordan Love accounted for four touchdowns in Green Bay’s 45-27 win at New England, lifting the Packers to 6-3. In Madrid, Joe Burrow threw three touchdown passes and ran for a fourth as Cincinnati beat Atlanta 34-17. Brock Purdy’s 100th career touchdown pass helped the 49ers beat the Raiders 38-17 and move past Buffalo into first place in ELWAY’s team ratings.

-NS & JG, 11/10/2026

See also: QBERT quarterback ratings.

Despite football’s reputation for being less analytics-friendly than basketball or baseball, there is a lot of data to work with. The NFL is now in its 107th season. There’s now a quarter-century’s worth of reliable play-by-play data (since 2001) and 20 years (since 2006) of advanced quarterback tracking stats.1

But it can take a bit of creativity to use that data effectively. ELWAY2 is probably Silver Bulletin’s most unique model. You can read more about it on the methodology page, but let’s get to the numbers.

The best (and worst) teams in the NFL

Let’s begin with our topline team ratings. A team’s offensive and defensive ratings represent, respectively, their projected number of points scored and allowed on a neutral site against an average opponent3 and can be combined to form a net rating. The Bills’ net rating of +6.0 means that we’d expect them to outscore an average opponent by 6 points in Week 2, for example.

The comparison between offense and defense is also instructive. The relationship between offense and defense is complicated in the NFL because efficient offenses not only score more but leave their opponents with worse field position and take more time off the clock. Put another way, “the best defense is a good offense.” This means that teams that score more points tend to allow fewer points, and vice versa. However, there are some outliers on either side. The Texans’ strengths are particularly concentrated on defense, whereas the Cowboys have a great offense behind Dak Prescott but really struggle on the other side of the ball, as the Giants exposed last week.

The rest of this page contains:

Projected W-L records for each team, including a new, detailed chart that shows the probability distribution of each team’s win totals (how likely is it that the Ravens win 11 or more games?) across 20,000 simulations.

Playoff, division title and Super Bowl odds, including conditional odds showing the effect on a team’s playoff chances from winning or losing its next game.

Detailed projections for every game of the regular season, with projected point spreads, totals (i.e. over/unders) and win probabilities for each game. There’s also a separate chart showing a distribution of simulated margins: 3-point wins and 7-point wins are particularly common, for instance.

Finally, we’ll add a series of graphs that track each team’s ELWAY rating from week to week, though we’ve left these off for now since we’re so early in the season.

The remaining features are for paid subscribers. A paid subscription also includes full access to our 2026 midterm election forecast when you sign up for ELWAY.

ELWAY projected records and playoff odds

Here’s what you were probably waiting for: our simulated standings based on playing out the rest of the season 20,000 times, along with each team’s odds of reaching the playoffs, winning its division and winning the Super Bowl. You can also click over to the “playoff seed probabilities” tab to see a team’s likelihood of finishing with the #1 through #7 seed in each conference. The projected standings account for strength of schedule and both current and future injury risk.

items.articleBody:
“About Texas,” newspaper + marker, 2024

My Friday newsletter began:

Molly Ivins called Texas “the laboratory for bad government,” and that’s been the case my entire adult life. I was a 17-year-old in Ohio during the 2000 election, and since I couldn’t vote, I went around waving a copy of Shrub: The Short But Happy Political Life of George W. Bush at my family members, warning them that the whole country could become Texas. (Whenever other Americans joke that they wish Texas would go ahead and secede, I reply, “But then you’d lose your early warning system!”) 19 summers ago, Meg and I moved to Austin so she could go to grad school. We stayed. She gave birth to a couple of native Texans during the Obama administration (I was able to become a full-time writer thanks to the Affordable Care Act), and since then we’ve been raising them in a sunny city full of friendly people and great food, all the while knowing that just five miles down the road, some of the most corrupt men in the world do their best to wreck the place. So you can imagine how it felt on Tuesday night, when a good number of those creeps were sent packing by our fellow Texans. The vibe around here is: jubilant.

Filed under: Texas

items.articleBody:
KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.

Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.
Branchline in Katonah, New York (photo Denis Gutierrez-Ogrinc, courtesy Gochman Family Collection)
Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic. “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”

items.title: Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo reveal why they joined Andy Weir's sci-fi audio drama 'Exoplanet' (interview)
items.subtitle: In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "W…
items.feedText: Such is the case with "Exoplanet," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet. items.articleBody:
In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere.

Such is the case with "Exoplanet," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet. All is not as it seems, though, as each crew member arrives in a different era on the same world.

We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.View Deal

Mackie voices Chief Engineer Jeff Shaw. His attraction to the imaginative genre began at an early age thanks to some cool family friends while growing up in the Big Easy.

"My brother went to college at Morehouse," he tells SPACE. "I was like 8, and he was 18. He’d always bring friends home, because New Orleans is a party city, so they'd come over and get drunk. But one of his friends gave me a book by Walter Mosley and one by Octavia Butler, and I got hooked into sci-fi and the future."

"From 'Back to the Future' to 'Aliens,' the future was such an idea of what was going to be out there. Now we’re living it," reveals Mackie. "It’s very important to me as a human being to have that construct as a part of my career. The only thing more arrogant than wanting to be president is standing up and saying, 'Yeah, I can go to space.' That sounds crazy to me."

"Exoplanet" was released by Audible on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: Audible)
Leguizamo's New York City childhood was influenced by absorbing classic radio dramas of the past, which primed him for this special Audible project.

“It was Anthony and Ariana being in it that really pumped me up, and of course Andy Weir," he recalls regarding his portrayal of Science Officer Logan Bowers. "Then when I got the theme, that it was something relevant today and makes you think about computers and technology taking over and making us obsolete. It just hit me in that right zeitgeist, at that right little point."

"As a poor kid, there was no YouTube or cell phones, and we didn’t have computers," reminisces Leguizamo. "I used to go to the Broadcast Museum on 53rd Street and listen to old radio plays like The Shadow and these incredible detective radio plays. It's a different art form. With no visuals, your voice has to create the world. I thought that was an incredible challenge."

DeBose portrays the Wild Blue Yonder's confident First Officer Becca Bang, who’s stranded in a temporal mystery that might engulf her at any moment.

"I've yet to do anything like this, which is always exciting," she adds. "I was a little afraid of it, which told me I should do it. These gents are so talented. It's great company. It’s coming from brilliant minds who build worlds so impeccably. And it's about real stuff we’re dealing with today. I liked the idea that we could tell this story and make people listen and create a space for them to imagine themselves in it and see how they problem-solve to make the world a bit better."

Recording your character's lines is far more difficult than just stepping up to the microphone to read a script, and our ace "Exoplanet" trio delivered in every session.

"I just go in and throw myself at something," DeBose recalls. "I don’t really have a method. But I can tell you this: it is a full-body workout. I use everything at my disposal, whether it’s a chair or a pillow or running in place. I just do what the character does and end up sweating. And after three days, I have to go sit in silence. It's great. I love the idea of bringing back the radio play. The art of listening is such a thing. I don’t think people listen enough. Even for myself."

"Exoplanet" revives the lost art of full-cast audio dramas for a new geneation (Image credit: Audible)
Likewise, Leguizamo embraced his booth sessions with exuberance and authenticity.

"You have to cancel the rest of your day, especially if you've got to talk, because your vocal chords are fried," he admits. "And if they're not fried you're not doing your job. You really have to do the physicality. If you run you have to run like a maniac and be out of breath. If I'm getting hit I start punching myself. Then there’s a sexiness to doing these things. Your voice has to have a little mystery, a little naughtiness. It’s an interesting intersection where you pull it back a little and invite the audience in.”

For Mackie, who’s used to athleticism needed to play MCU superheroes like The Falcon and Captain America, recording dialogue offered a different type of opportunity.

“I look for reasons not to talk to people, so I love doing these," he jokes. "Once I’m out of the studio, I’m not talking to anybody for two days. At a certain point for me, I find mentally I get tired of hearing myself talk. I just have to come home at cut off. I’ve said enough words for the next month.”

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible.

items.articleBody:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.

The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

You had one job

Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

items.articleBody:
Apple nutzt den heutigen Abend, um ein frisches Firmware-Update für die AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods 5, AirPods 4 und AirPods Max 2 zu veröffentlichen. Konkret hat Apple das Firmware-Update 9B47 freigegeben, zuvor setzt das Unternehmen auf die Version 9A348 bzw. 9A359.

Apple veröffentlicht Firmware-Update für mehrere AirPods

Im September dieses Jahres und parallel zur Freigabe von iOS 27 und Co. hat Apple auch Firmware-Updates für seine AirPods-Familie veröffentlicht. Seitdem hat das Unternehmen mehrere Beta-Versionen seiner AirPods-Firmware freigegeben. Nun steht mit der Build 9B47 eine finale Version für die AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods 5, AirPods 4 und AirPods Max 2 bereit.

Bis dato hat sich Apple noch nicht zu den Neuerungen zur Wort gemeldet, auch das begleitende Support Dokument wurde bislang nicht aktualisiert. Da Apple allerdings keine neuen Funktionen für seine Kopfhörer angekündigt hat, gehen wir davon aus, dass das Unternehmen ausschließlich unter der Haube gearbeitet, Fehler beseitigt und die Leistung des Systems optimiert hat.

items.articleBody:
marumi house and its sculptural sauna

NIKO Design Studio has completed Umino Marumi, a two-story wooden guesthouse on a hillside overlooking the Pacific coast of Chiba, Japan. With its enormous circular facade opening and exposed timber structure, the house makes an unusual addition to the surrounding residential neighborhood. In the garden, a much smaller companion building takes shape as a sauna hut, its curved roof designed to accommodate the trees growing around it.

Completed in 2025, Marumi was conceived as a second home where the owners could gather with family and friends, while also creating a welcoming presence within the local community. The architects approached this ambition through an engawa, the traditional Japanese veranda, transforming it into a series of staggered outdoor platforms that climb through the house and connect to the upper floor.

image courtesy NIKO Design Studio

a giant circular opening frames the stepped veranda

The Marumi House’s most recognizable feature is the enormous circular opening cut into its dark facade, revealing a network of timber columns and raised walkways beneath the pitched roof. Around one-third of the covered building is dedicated to the semi-outdoor engawa, where visitors can sit, gather, or move between levels without entering the enclosed rooms.

With this layout, the architects at NIKO Design Studio give the house an unusually open relationship with its surroundings. From outside, the veranda offers glimpses of people moving through the timber structure, while its various levels accommodate both intimate gatherings and larger groups. The circular opening brings these activities into view, turning the facade into an inhabited space that faces the neighborhood.

timber flooring extends through the open-plan interior and onto the covered terrace

thick cedar logs and traditional joinery shape marumi house

NIKO Design Studio worked with substantial cedar logs measuring approximately 400 millimeters in diameter, assembling the structural frame using traditional kanuki joinery. Horizontal timber members pass through openings in the round columns, creating a durable structure that retains the natural geometry of the wood. The holes were cut using chainsaws, following an approach suggested by the carpenters and inspired by forestry techniques.

The same hands-on approach extends into the landscape. To address the sloping site, a stone retaining wall was assembled during a two-day workshop using nozumi, a traditional stone-stacking technique. The rough stonework sits alongside the large timber structure, which brings a sense of craftsmanship to a building designed for communal use.

curved brick steps lead toward the bathroom and its sunken bathtub

a tiny sauna hut curves around a neighboring palm tree

Beyond the main house, the architects faced a different challenge when designing a freestanding sauna for the garden. The owners initially wanted a cabin for three or four people, but commercially available models appeared surprisingly bulky when placed within a model of the site. Looking more closely at the surrounding landscape, the team noticed a neighboring palm tree extending over the property boundary. Its continued growth became the starting point for the sauna’s unusual curved roof.

Working with carpenter Murakami of Murakami Carpentry Workshop, the architects sourced naturally bent timber from trees that had grown along a hillside. These curved members formed the roof structure, allowing its profile to rise and dip around the surrounding vegetation. When the timber arrived thicker and longer than anticipated, the team decided to retain the excess length, leaving the beams projecting beyond the roofline. The unexpected detail gives the small building much of its character.

the freestanding sauna hut features a sweeping curved roof and arched wooden doorway

five square meters accommodate up to six people

Despite its expressive roof, the sauna occupies remarkably little ground. Its foundation measures just two by two meters, with a total floor area of five square meters including the stepped portion. Inside, timber-lined surfaces and a tall ceiling make the small space feel surprisingly generous. Although originally intended for three or four bathers, the completed sauna can accommodate five or six people.

The hut combines electric and wood-fired heating, while a skylight brings daylight into the compact interior. It connects with the surrounding terrace and the house’s bathroom, which can be a cold bath during sauna sessions. Marumi and its miniature companion together explore two scales of wooden architecture, with one opening itself toward the neighborhood and the other adjusting its form to the trees already growing in the garden.

the sauna’s roof rises and dips around the surrounding vegetation

naturally curved timber beams meet beneath a skylight in the sauna’s roof

sunlight enters through the skylight, illuminating the sauna’s timber-lined interior and tiered benches

thick cedar columns frame the elevated veranda and views of the surrounding neighborhood

items.title: Tuning giant surface potential in OLEDs can improve efficiency and lifespan
items.subtitle: Organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) power many display screens, but their efficiency can be limited by energy lost inside the device.
items.feedText: As organic layers are deposited, their molecules can align to create an internal electrical potential known as giant surface potential (GSP). When this potential draws excess positive charges, or holes, near the light-emitting layer, they can interfere with light-producing excitons. This process, called exciton–polaron quenching, reduces emitted light and can affect device performance.

items.articleBody:
Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

Drawings and photography

Previous

Next

Drawings and photography

Close

"Avándaro is a landscape that's been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation," Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,

"Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers' houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.

“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture."

The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.

From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.

To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.

The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical plans, though their place in the landscape differs.

Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.

A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.

Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.

The stepped arrangement of both floors, in plan and section, also operates as a device for privacy between the two houses, PPAA explained.

“The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.

The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.

Read:

PPAA "celebrates the qualities of wood" with rotating CLT pavilion in Mexico City

“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.

“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first "all-wood" mass timber structure in Querétaro.

Project credits:

Architecture: PPAA
Design Team: Pablo Pérez Palacios, Emilio Calvo, Miguel Vargas, Jonathan Reséndiz, Adriana Hernández
Interiors: Mariana Morales

items.articleBody:
The word “other” is also a verb.
To other is to treat groups of people as fundamentally different or inferior.

It’s in our nature, but leaders amplify it for scare-mongering.
Those immigrants.
Those Muslims.
Those Chinese.
They’re the problem.
They’re not like us.

That message is broadcast and echoes all around you, which intensifies feeling it’s a fact.

It builds a huge wall: us versus them.
It repels you from that wall, to make sure you can’t see them, because that would complicate the simplicity of polarizing.

We categorize the animal world into species.
Species are so different that they can’t mate, can’t switch, can’t be both a cat and a bird.

The problem with othering is thinking of people as so deeply different that they are like a separate species.

It’s an enticing belief because it helps you jump to a conclusion, so you can stop thinking.
Those people are just weird and bad, and that’s that.

I’m so interested in othering, because I noticed it in myself.
I grew up with the usual stereotypes that shaped my worldview.
Then I moved to the city, where you meet people from the other side of that wall.

Like a great story where the heroes oppose an evil enemy tribe, but then one person falls into enemy hands and realizes that tribe is not evil and is not the enemy, and you get the wow moment of understanding a conflicting point of view.
Stories tend to make only two sides, so they can take sides and switch sides.
But imagine a longer story that does this twenty times, so you can’t even think of them as sides anymore.
That’s what I’m trying to do with my life.

I’m on a slow background mission to reverse the othering in my worldview.

It’s a fun challenge.

When I notice I’m othering, I undo my conclusions, and cross that wall.
Understand and internalize a conflicting point of view.
I try to join every tribe, to show myself we are not separate species.

This year, I heard the word “other” as a verb, and it called all of this to mind.
So now I can give my mission a succinct term: de-othering.

items.articleBody:
Silent illumination is one of the two main methods of practice in Chan Buddhism. It is a subtle practice in which stillness and insight are cultivated simultaneously, and curious inquiry allows us to reconnect with the natural state of being fully human.

The practice was transmitted through the Caodong (Japanese: Soto) tradition of Chan in China and articulated in the writings of Master Hongzhi Zhengjue (1091–1157). In his poem “Silent Illumination,” he described the clarity and freedom of silent illumination, inviting and encouraging us to join him here. Silent illumination is only to be found here and now.

Master Hongzhi’s poems were often used by my late teacher, Chan Master Sheng Yen (1930–2009), to elucidate silent illumination. Master Sheng Yen often said the practice is letting go, referring to the fact that we are the one getting in the way of ourselves. Silent illumination is about releasing the pervasive and entrenched habits of self-centered attachment. We can drop these habits and, as my current teacher Simon Child says, slip into silent illumination right now—where everything is as it is, and there is no suffering. This is a different way of being from our usual habit of feeling that whatever is happening in the present is not how it’s supposed to be.

In silent illumination we reconnect with the true nature of existence, clearly seeing the interconnectedness of all things in emptiness. All is thus, and there is no suffering. Our innate wisdom and natural capacity for compassion manifest as we remain fully present in each unfolding moment, skillfully responding to what is needed with clarity to benefit sentient beings.

When we try to just sit and be fully present, we will likely find we’re either spacing out or sitting with a mind jumping all over the place while we attempt to make it “silent,” wondering if we’re doing it right. It is not uncommon to approach the practice with the idea of making the present moment different in order to get to “silent illumination.” This mentality is precisely what gets in the way of being with the present moment. The practice is to truly allow each unfolding moment to be fully experienced by learning to relax into each moment and to let go of attachment to the ideas we hold about the present.

Relaxation is the basis of silent illumination. In preparing to practice silent illumination in sitting meditation, we start with relaxing the body. After finding a posture that’s stable and comfortable, we relax the whole body by starting from the top of the head, directly experiencing the relaxation of the scalp. Then we allow the relaxation to spread to the forehead, eyeballs, eye muscles, and facial muscles, and we continue to directly experience the subtle changing sensations as we allow the tension to melt away. Next, we allow the relaxation to spread to the neck, shoulder muscles, down the arms, to the chest and abdomen, the upper and lower back, and down the buttocks and legs. Finally, we feel the relaxation of the entire body sitting right here, right now, in this space, maintaining clear awareness moment after moment.

“Unkai (Sea Of Clouds) May 22 2021 5:47 AM NYC.”

This is not a visualization exercise; we’re not creating a mental image of parts of the body. Rather, we are developing body awareness by directly experiencing the subtle changing sensations of muscles softening. When the body relaxes, the mind relaxes.

A student on a retreat once told me that she was trying very hard to relax, but the harder she tried, the tenser she became. I told her, “No need to try. Just let the body relax.” She then tried not to try, but this generated even more tension and frustration. This “trying” is a good example of our entrenched habit of self-centered attachment; habitually, we insist on controlling the process of relaxation instead of trusting the body to relax. When the student finally stopped trying, she was amazed that the body and mind could relax without her directing it. She clearly saw how she generated suffering for herself, and her confidence in the dharma and her ability to practice strengthened as a result.

Silent illumination is often called the method of no-method. A practitioner whose mind is still scattered and agitated needs to start with a method to settle the mind. After relaxing the whole body and becoming fully embodied, we maintain moment-to-moment clear awareness of the body sitting and notice the subtle changing sensations of the body breathing. Resting our attention gently on the subtle changing sensations as the diaphragm contracts and expands, we allow the body to breathe on its own, anchoring the mind gently to each emerging present moment. There is no need to hold to the breathing tightly; that will tense the body and mind. It’s not a problem when the mind drifts off; use that as an opportunity to practice remembering to come back and reconnect with the direct experience of the body breathing. Practicing this way, the mind will naturally settle.

When thoughts and feelings arise, there’s no need to chase them away or block them. John Crook, Master Sheng Yen’s first lay dharma heir, with whom I previously studied, articulated a helpful way to work with thoughts: let through, let be, let go. When thoughts show up, let them through. They are already part of the present. Blocking them will only tense and agitate the mind, perpetuating the habit of reacting to the present with aversion. Letting be is allowing the thoughts to be fully felt, seen, and heard as they unfold, moment after moment, without labeling, commenting, or trying to change them. Letting go is allowing the thoughts to leave on their own without being in a hurry to make them go away. In this way, there may be thoughts, but habitual reactivities to the thoughts are not activated, allowing the mind to relax and be still. This nonreactivity is silence.

As the mind settles, we subtly shift from resting our attention on the changing sensations of the body breathing to open awareness of the body sitting in this space. When thoughts come through, let through, let be, let go. When we notice our awareness dulling, gently sharpen it to stay with the moment. Maintaining this moment-to-moment clear awareness, we experience ease as the body and mind unify. We would be mistaken to believe a special state has been achieved. The mind and body are naturally interconnected and unified. It is only our entrenched habit of believing the mind and body are separate, independent entities that blocks us from realizing this. As these thought habits are released, the body/mind is experienced as it is. We experience unification with the environment. The usual sense of body/mind being in opposition to the environment disappears, and we feel a deep sense of connection with everything. Often practitioners grasp onto this experience, thinking “this is it,” believing they have achieved a special state, and try to hold on to it. Instead of activating this habit of reifying the moment and grasping, we let go of the urge to follow these habitual reactivities. There is nothing to attain. In silence, the mind is still and all is revealed as it is—illumination.

The transition from settling the mind to the method of no-method can be tricky. It is quite subtle and easily misunderstood. Silent illumination is called the method of no-method because we’re not directing our attention to any particular object. The practice is to be fully here, with this body and mind in this space, with total clear awareness. There’s no need to direct our attention to different parts of the body. We only need to be clearly aware that we’re sitting with this body in this space, moment after moment. It’s important to remember that we’re cultivating total clear awareness of body, mind, and the environment. If we direct our attention to bodily sensations only, ignoring thoughts and what’s going on outside of us, that is not yet the practice of silent illumination.

Similarly, practitioners may direct their attention solely to the mind, watching mental activities intensely, resulting in a kind of hypervigilance of thoughts and emotions. Meditating this way can generate tension and can even make us quite self-absorbed because we’re focusing inwardly on our own ideas and feelings rather than letting go of self-centered attachment. This is not silent illumination. The practice is to open our awareness to include body and mind and the environment simultaneously.

“May 10 2021 Kumo (Cloud) Diptych”

Other practitioners may cultivate clear awareness of the body and mind but dull their awareness of the environment. Doing so strengthens the mentally constructed boundary that separates self from other and blocks us from realizing our interconnectedness. Still other practitioners might interpret the instruction to open their awareness to include the environment as an instruction to direct their attention outward. It’s not uncommon for retreat participants with this misinterpretation to spend days listening to bird songs while forgetting full awareness of body and mind. This is also not silent illumination.

It isn’t necessary to busy ourselves with any directing. We can remain clearly aware, fully experiencing the body and mind sitting here in this space, moment after moment, without directing our attention in any specific way. Most of us are habituated to directing our attention to an object as a method to focus the mind. While that is a valid method when specifically intended, transitioning to the method of no-method involves recognizing this habit and releasing the urge to follow it. The practice of silent illumination is to allow each moment to be experienced as it is. As instructed by Master Hongzhi, “stay with that just as that, stay with this just as this.”

Many practitioners assume, incorrectly, that the practice is about entering a trance where nothing is happening. They may achieve this trance state by creating a foggy mind that gives an illusion of peace, but there is no clarity of the habits of the mind. Habitual reactivities of craving and aversion are left to operate without awareness. This is not silent illumination, and practicing this way will not free us from suffering.

For other practitioners, as the mind settles and becomes still, they mistake the state of stillness for silent illumination and try to dwell in this quiet state. To protect this sense of stillness they disengage from life situations for fear of being disturbed, often leaving loved ones feeling rejected or responsibilities unfulfilled. These are two of the common ways our habitual reactivities are revealed when practicing silent illumination. Recognizing them allows us to gain insight into our mind and realize the true nature of existence.

Years ago, when I attended a silent illumination retreat with Master Sheng Yen, I was quite new to the practice and was attracted to the beautiful imagery of liberation described in Master Hongzhi’s poem. I thought I understood what I was supposed to do after hearing the instructions to let go. My erroneous interpretation at that time was that I needed to make the body disappear since my job was to get rid of the self that’s attached to the body. So, I went about trying to do this in sitting meditation. At one point I believed most of my body had disappeared and only my hands were left. I tried to make my hands disappear, but to no avail.

I share this story to illustrate how easy it is to project our erroneous views onto the instruction to simply be here. The myriad ways we get in the way of ourselves were on full display: all I need to do is to get rid of the self (as if the self exists independently) to get enlightened (as if enlightenment is somewhere other than the present), then I will be happy (as if enlightenment can be possessed for one’s eternal satisfaction). I was inadvertently perpetuating habitual tendencies that generate suffering while believing I was following Master Sheng Yen’s instruction to “let go.”

Was it a waste of time? Not at all. The practice of silent illumination is the process of recognizing how our erroneous views and entrenched habitual reactivities show up and cause suffering. As we maintain clear awareness of these subtle habits and the urge to follow and perpetuate them is loosened and released, we are less likely to succumb to them. This is what Master Sheng Yen meant by “letting go.” We also see how these habits show up in daily life, causing suffering for ourselves and hurting others. As we release the compulsion to fall into these unhelpful habits, by working with ourselves gently and kindly, we can live more in accordance with wisdom and compassion.

This article is from the March 2024 issue of Lion’s Roar magazine.

items.articleBody:
The city of Baku, Azerbaijan, recently finished hosting a festival showcasing its heritage alongside local and international artists. The second annual Fly to Baku. Art Weekend concluded on November 1, 2026, highlighting the city’s culture. This included over 30 of Baku’s museums, galleries, palaces, and cultural institutions. It even featured Old City and UNESCO World Heritage sites like the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, built in the 15th century, and Maiden Tower, constructed during the 12th century. The incredible Zaha Hadid-designed Heydar Aliyev Center served as one of the weekend’s main venues.

Baku transformed during the art weekend, utilizing the city as an open-air stage for art and design. In its second year, the event featured several high-profile creatives. Judy Chicago and Michelangelo Pistoletto were on view, alongside Faig Ahmed, one of Azerbaijan’s most celebrated living artists, known for transforming traditional carpets into surreal installations.

International curators, artists, and collectors flocked to Baku, with the event drawing 10,000 attendees. In addition to the art on view, attendees could interact directly with artists and get creative themselves. The weekend included intimate studio visits, immersive technology installations, music and poetry performances, and walking tours through the 1,000-year-old Old City. Food is also an important and demonstrative part of any culture, and Baku Art Weekend featured exclusive dinners at some of the metropolis’s most acclaimed restaurants.

The city—with its mix of historical and contemporary architecture—hopes to become one of the world’s art capitals by turning Baku Art Weekend into a fair or biennale. “It will be a long journey to get there,” Emin Mammedov, who heads the event, told Conde Nast Traveller. “We think it will be a minimum of five to seven years to see how it [the art weekend] grows. Then we will be able to say yes, Baku is ready to be a place where every country comes to show their own art.”

Get a peek into what Fly to Baku. Art Weekend 2026 had to offer.
