items.articleBody:
Did comedian Dave Chappelle refuse to shake hands with Sen.-elect James Talarico at the end of an episode of Saturday Night Live that aired on Nov. 7, 2026? No, that's not true: Chappelle gave Talarico a hug during the closing credits. There were no reports from established news outlets of any kind of snub by Chappelle of Talarico during the SNL appearance.

The claim appeared in a post (archived here) made by the X account @thewakeninq on Nov. 8, 2026. The post included a clip from the SNL episode, with a caption that read:

The BEST thing to happen on SNL tonight! Dave Chappelle snubbing James Talarico and refusing to shake his hand. LMAO! 😂

This is what a still from the video looked like on X at the time of writing:

(Image source: post by @thewakeninq on X.)

The post is embedded below:

The BEST thing to happen on SNL tonight! Dave Chappelle snubbing James Talarico and refusing to shake his hand. LMAO! 😂 https://t.co/d8KYLrxxss

-- American Nightmare 🇺🇸 (@thewakeninq) November 8, 2026

The clip only shows one part of the closing credits. In a video (archived here) posted by @nbcsnl, the official SNL X account, it is clear that Chappelle did not ignore Talarico. At the ten-second mark of the video, the comedian Druski acknowledges Chappelle, and Chappelle steps in front of Talarico to come to the front of the stage. This is the only moment shown in the video posted on the X account @thewakeninq, which makes the claim.

(Image source: post by @nbcsnl on X. Red circle added by Lead Stories.)

However, at the 31-second mark, Chappelle turns around and hugs Talarico.

(Image source: post by @nbcsnl on X. Red circle added by Lead Stories.)

Searches on Google News (archived here) and Yahoo News (archived here) for the claim did not return any matching results from established news outlets.

items.articleBody:
Attention, skint artists of England! Phoebe Waller-Bridge—the Fleabag herself—is starting a side hustle: patron saint to creatives with rent woes.

Specifically, Waller-Bridge will be lending a flat to London based playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds. This is part and parcel of a pilot program helmed by Writers’ Block, a group that aims to level the playing field for disadvantaged writers in the United Kingdom.

A flat is no small thing in London, where daily life grows ever more cumbersome for the working class artist. As The Guardian reported, Waller-Bridge’s space seeks to ease the burden of the hustle. Selected writers will get a place to work in peace, and pay only bills.

Fleabag’s not the only one lending a hand. Jack Thorne, a peer playwright and co-creator of the show Adolescence, is also throwing some serious pounds into the program. As he told the BBC in a statement, supporting working class writers should be an industry prerogative.

“If we want stories told about our complicated world, we need writers of every background writing them,” he said. “If you’re from privilege, your biggest problem is what to fill a page with. If you’re not, so much of your struggle is about the need to survive.”

Other Writers’ Block backers include Crown creator Peter Morgan, Happy Valley creator Sally Wainwright, and Waller-Bridge’s partner, the prolific screen and playwright Martin McDonagh. (Because only wild horses could keep them apart, I guess.)

Writers’ Block grew out of the Adopt-a-Playwright Award, founded in 2008 by Sofie Mason and Diana Jervis-Read. And as these heroes noted, the model is mighty reproducible.

I nominate New York City for the next pilot scheme.

items.articleBody:
Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.

For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)

Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.

Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder, which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

items.articleBody:
Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space.

Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible. It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI, with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster.

The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5, which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal.

To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention.

NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog, this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate.

Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai

We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and then gave all three the same app-building prompts.

The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first.

Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter. Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding.

As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis. Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison:

Model Intelligence Index

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45

GLM-5.3-Flash: 43

Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available

Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench.

The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card, Naive AI – Research.

Model

NL2Repo-Bench

DeepSWE v1.1

Agent's Last Exam (ALE)

GLM-5.3-Flash

Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail.

Speed and verbosity experiments

Speed is the headline feature.1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly.2

We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500, 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond. That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K.

For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity.

The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind.

Graphic by Gabriele Beltramo

Key observations

Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput, approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash.

Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average.

The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models.

The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high), at 89.8 seconds against 79.7.

Two caveats apply. The sample is small, at 10 questions per difficulty level, and we did not grade answer accuracy. Short, fast replies are only useful if they are correct.

App experiments

We also asked the models to build the same web apps from the same initial prompt. We tested six combinations of model and thinking effort, with the thinking effort in parentheses:

Naive-N0.5-Flash (no thinking)

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (low)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

GLM 5.3 Flash (low)

GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

The gallery of apps is available online. In summary, the three prompts asked the six model variants to do the following:

Create an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System.

Grow a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures.

Do a browser port of the book Ray Tracing in One Weekend.

Below we’ve embedded results for the thinking variants of each model.

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

Earth and the Solar System; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

3D tree; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

Earth and the Solar System; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

3D tree; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Earth and the Solar System; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

3D tree; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Solar system

The first app is an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System. Viewers can orbit the camera around the scene and watch the planets circle the sun, with controls to speed up or slow down their motion. Every surface is drawn from generated textures, with no image files.

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) produced the best result of the three. Its sun shows sunspots, and the dark side of its Earth glows with city lights at night.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) came close behind. Its version lacks an asteroid belt, and its Earth has less textural detail.

GLM 5.3 Flash (high) stumbled on lighting, which makes the planets hard to tell apart. Its speed controls are also too sensitive, so a small nudge sends the planets racing or crawling.

Tree modeling

The second app grows a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures. Wind makes the branches sway and the leaves flutter, and the shadows on the grassy ground move with them. The tree stands under a sky gradient and light fog. A control panel adjusts the seed, branching depth, leaf count, wind strength and direction, and sun position. There’s also a switch to autumn colors and a frame-rate counter sits in the corner.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) and Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) both produced good results. The surprise was Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking switched off, which did not produce a usable app at all.

The good results still had small glitches in the wind animation. In the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) app, thin branches can detach from their parents in strong wind and appear to float. The effect is subtle, but it is there.

The problem is easier to see in the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) app. When the wind intensity is turned up, the whole tree starts to deform and wobble like a jelly sculpture in an earthquake.

Ray Tracing in One Weekend

The third app is a browser port of the book Ray Tracing in One Weekend. It renders the book's cover scene: a vast gray ground, a scatter of small matte, metallic and glass spheres, and three large spheres in the center. One is glass, one a brown matte and one a polished metal. Depth of field blurs the foreground and background. The image builds up progressively on screen, with a progress bar, elapsed time and a rays-per-second estimate. A menu offers the book's earlier milestone scenes. The user can pick a quality preset and download the result as a PNG.

In this more coding-focused scenario, all three models with thinking on produced a working app.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) wins because its ray tracer is the most efficient of the three. It also uses the full width of the screen to display the rendered image.

The Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) app is correct, but its JavaScript is less efficient.

GLM 5.3 Flash (high) is again the weakest. Its speed is similar to the Naive-N0.5-Flash app, but its interface is more basic.

Pricing

Naive positions N0.5-Flash as a capable, low-cost model. The target prices are $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.40 per million output tokens, and $0.01 per million cache-read tokens.

That puts it in the $0.20 to $0.60 per million output tokens band occupied by several capable Flash models, including the two we compared it against.

The final bill will also depend on how many tokens the model uses. That in turn depends on the thinking budget requested and the difficulty of the questions.

Takeaways

In ultrafast mode, Naive-N0.5-Flash can peak at around 2,000 tokens per second and sustain nearly 1,000 during thinking-heavy tasks.

In our tests, its median response time was several times shorter than those of GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at their high thinking settings. Mean times were similar to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017.

On complex tasks, it spent far more thinking tokens than the other two models. On easy and medium questions, it consistently replied faster.

In the apps, Naive-N0.5-Flash was much more consistent than GLM 5.3 Flash (high). With thinking on, it also holds its own against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. It built the most detailed solar system app, tied with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on the tree model, and came a close second on the efficiency of the ray tracer.

For developers who value fast iteration over token economy, that speed is the main reason to try Naive-N0.5-Flash.

1

The speed of Naive-N0.5-Flash depends on an efficient speculative-decoding drafter and a custom inference engine. The reported decoding speeds were measured on a single eight-GPU Blackwell node running speculative decoding in NaiveRT. The drafter was Naive-N0.5-Flash-FP8-Draft, and the setup is tuned for single-stream decode latency rather than batch throughput.

Realized speed depends on how many draft tokens the target model accepts per round. That varies with the checkpoint pair, the prompt, context length, sampling settings, and the content being generated. The reported numbers show this clearly:

- Acceptance rate: 70.6% with thinking disabled, but only 43.4% with thinking enabled.
- Decode speed: about 984 tokens/s in the thinking phase and 1,816 tokens/s in the answer phase.
- Peak rate: roughly 2,100 tokens/s over a single second. Treat this as an upper bound, not a typical rate.

The engine matters as much as the drafter. The developers report that a full speculative round (draft, verify, sampling and commit) takes 3.4 ms in NaiveRT versus 12.3 ms in SGLang, a 72.4% reduction. The thinking-disabled campaign measured about 3.45 ms per round. For the full measurements, see NaiveRT: Performance.

2

Implications for reinforcement learning: Generating autoregressive rollouts is the main bottleneck in large-scale reinforcement learning. Anything that cuts decode cost, such as the sparse attention (DSA) adopted here, makes rollouts cheaper. Adapting other models to DSA could make that loop considerably more efficient and speed up frontier research.

This fits Naive AI's larger promise: a self-improving AI that can optimize its own inference CUDA kernels and adopt the most efficient architecture for large-scale reinforcement learning training.

items.articleBody:
Cake or pie for dessert after the Thanksgiving feast? At my house, it depends on who's coming, what they ask for, or what they bring. Some families have the same dessert(s) every year. Door Dash keeps up with the statistics of what people order each year to be delivered from groceries, restaurants, or other stores. Their map above shows which states show a distinct preference that deviates from the national average. While more states show a preference for pumpkin pie, it's not the top dessert ordered. That would be chocolate cake, and pumpkin pie only comes in at number four! Of course, this is Door Dash, and all their stats are delivery orders. You have to take into account how homemade pumpkin pie is always way better than what you can get from a grocery store.

They also ranked traditional side dishes by state and overall preference, and report on holiday deliveries that aren't Thanksgiving food at all, like meat thermometers, condoms, and liquor. You'll also learn tidbits like the spike in pizza delivery on Wednesday night and T-bone steaks on Thanksgiving Day. Get all the stats on Thanksgiving delivery at Door Dash. And save a thought, and a tip, for the poor gig workers who deliver them. -via Mental Floss

items.articleBody:
Ethan Mollick at One Useful Thing:

I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch, and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers.

So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are.

More here.

items.articleBody:
Nach 15 Jahren wird der Schmidt Eightvoice eingestellt. Nur noch 20 Exemplare der limitierten „Final Series“ sollen gebaut werden.

UPDATE: Schmidt Eightvoivce wird eingestellt

Der Schmidt Eightvoice wird nach 15 Jahren nicht mehr hergestellt. Schmidt kündigt an, noch 20 Exemplare in einer limitierten Auflage mit dem Namen „Final Series“ bauen zu wollen. Wenn ihr also noch einen Schmidt-Synthesizer haben möchtet, ist jetzt die letzte Gelegenheit zuzuschlagen.

Im folgenden Test könnt ihr noch einmal nachlesen, was den außergewöhnlichen Synthesizer auszeichnet und ob es sich lohnt, ihm trotz seines stattlichen Preises eine Chance zu geben.

Der Schmidt Eightvoice Test

Zu behaupten, ich kannte den Schmidt Synthesizer nicht, wäre gelogen. Allein seine schiere Größe hat es unmöglich gemacht, ihn damals auf der Frankfurter Musik Messe 2011 zu ignorieren – nur richtig auf dem Schirm hatte ich ihn nie. Das kann intuitiver Selbstschutz gewesen sein, denn immerhin wusste ich, was das Teil kostet – aktuell: 26k.

Zur letzten Superbooth hab ich mich getraut ihn auszuprobieren. Und eh ich mich versah, durfte die Demo Unit für exakt ein Jahr in meinem Studio residieren – ein Wechselbad der Gefühle. Und davon handelt dieses Manifest, was mehr Feature als Test ist!

Details

Heavy Duty Facts

Da steht er vor mir. Was für ein Gerät, der „Schmidt Syntheszier – Eightvoice Polyphonic“! Handlich? Leider nein, leider gar nicht; und so brauchte es auch einen Volvo-Kombi, um ihn in dem Flight-Case überhaupt wegzubekommen: 48 kg ohne Case, zusammengeklappt 114 cm x 60 cm und ohne Knöpfe 13 cm hoch. Achtstimmig. Analog. Digital kontrolliert. Made in Germany. Kompromisslos.

SM57 für Größenvergleich

Der Schmidt Synthesizer ist ein feuchter Ingenieurstraum in Echtholz, mit zehnjähriger Entwicklungszeit. 2011 hat man ihn erstmals präsentiert: einen modularen Synthesizer, der gar nicht wirklich modular ist – denn das braucht er nicht.

Es fängt beim konsequenten Verzicht auf eine Routing-Matrix an. Jede Sektion kennt eigene Envelopes sowie zahlreiche, dedizierte LFOs und sehr viele Veloctiy-Amounts. Das alles gibt’s im direkten Zugriff, Doppelbelegungen hingegen nur sehr, sehr wenige.

Links außen findet man den Stereo-Out und die acht Einzelausgänge auf großer Klinke, rechts die Controller-Anschlüsse.

Mit Händen und Füßen

Als spielerische Ergänzung zur Klaviatur dienen ausgewählte „Realtime-Modifier“. Darunter das Pitch-Wheel, ein ebenfalls schick leuchtendes Modulationsrad, ein eleganter Joystick, sowie natürlich Aftertouch und fünf weitere „Externals“. Es handelt sich dabei um analoge Eingänge auf großer Klinke, die auf diese Weise rückseitig vier Anschlüsse für Expression-Pedale und vier für Fußtaster bereithalten. USB, MIDI Trio und IEC-Stromanschluss sind hier auch dabei.

Die Control-Inputs A4-A1, das MIDI-Trio, B4-B1 und USB2.

Die Realtime-Modifier weist man über die Bedienelemente neben dem Keyboard zu: Assign drücken, Zielparameter durch Drehen des entsprechenden Reglers an der Front festlegen – fertig, spielen! Und bei Bedarf als Teil des Presets speichern.

Das Übertragungsverhalten kann man auf vielseitige Weise beeinflussen, Mehrfachzuweisungen im Sinne von Makros sind allerdings nicht möglich. Und wo wie gerade dabei sind: Der Schmidt verfügt über zwei Bereiche, um Presets zu wechseln: einmal hier, links außen, und noch einmal „ganz da drüben“, rechts neben dem Display. Luftlinie 1 Meter.

61-Tasten-Fatar, bald mit Multi-Aftertouch

Zwei weitere Drehregler in der Keyboard-Sektion bestimmen die Farbe von LEDs und Display – für den kleinen Hippie-Moment zwischendurch. Das Keyboard stammt von Fatar und ist mit 61 halb-gewichteten Tasten inklusive Velocity und Aftertouch ausgestattet.

Modulators-Assign für die Real-Time-Modifier: X & Y für den Joystick, Aft.(ertouch), (MOD-)Wheel und Ext.(ernal). Keyboard-Transpose, Color-Regler für LEDs und Display, Master-Tune, Volume sowie Preset-Wechsel-Taster und Kopfhörerausgang kommen hinzu.

Eine Multi-Aftertouch-Klaviatur ist übrigens in Planung, von extern empfängt der Schmidt entsprechende Befehle aber bereits jetzt schon – nur eben nicht per MPE.

Kompromisslose Klangerzeugung

Beeindruckender als die Ausmaße des Synths und die Unmengen an „funky“ Bedienelementen ist am Ende allerdings der komplexe – aber eigentlich auch wieder gar nicht so komplizierte – Signal-Flow mit den vielen Modulationsmöglichkeiten. Denn diese sind fast immer direkt vor Ort.

Die dedizierten LFOs für die PWM für OSC2, OSC3 & OSC1 – warum diese Reihenfolge ? Keine Ahnung.

Der Schmidt zeigt sich dahingehend so einfach wie genial; nur in der detaillierten Umsetzung hier und da manchmal eigenwillig. Was ich sagen will: Einfach dran setzten und losspielen – das könnt ihr vergessen. Das hat weder bei mir noch bei irgendeinem meiner Synth-affinen Studiogäste geklappt; selbst Jean Michael Jarre scheint bei seiner knappen YT-Demo etwas angespannt.

Hands on, Hands off

Der Schmidt ist definitiv ein Synthesizer zum Spielen, aber gewiss kein Spielzeug. Die Macher sprechen von Kunst, und so überrascht der „initiale Verzicht“ auf einen Arpeggiator und Sequenzer wiederum nur so halb.

Finden Sie den Cutoff auf Anhieb?

Einige Kunden wollten aber selbst das nicht so stehen lassen und haben beim Programmieren die DIY-Initiative ergriffen. Der Dank gilt Dr. Robert Skerjanc, der nachträglich noch einen Arp und Step-Sequenzer ins Menü „assembled“ hat. Die Fußtaster-Eingänge dienen dann zur Steuerung von Rec/Play, sodass es sich schön improvisieren lässt.

Nice to have, der Schmidt braucht das aber eigentlich nicht.

Nur, so richtig sexy ist das Ganze fürs Detail-Programming nicht, was in Anbetracht des begrenzten Speichers und des „Von-hinten-durch-die-Brust“-Ansatzes auch nachvollziehbar bleibt. Viel wichtiger ist ohnehin, dass man irgendwann realisiert, dass der Schmidt den eigentlich auch gar nicht braucht – Stichwort: Envelope-Repeat.

Bevor man anfängt, muss man sich erst mal vollständig reindenken – und dabei ist das Handbuch besser immer in der Nähe. Das hilft mit seinen grundsätzlichen Erklärungen der technischen Möglichkeiten inklusive Fließtext und Blockschaltbildern zwar durchaus weiter, nur wie man das Ganze am besten in der musikalischen Praxis anwendet, entpuppt sich als Stop-and-Go-und-wieder-zurück-Prozess.

Oben links: OSC1 und OSC2 sowie die PWM-Sektion für alle OSCs.

Wie man das besser machen könnte? Keine Ahnung, aber Instant-Satisfaction steht hier nicht auf dem Speiseplan. Es sei denn, man konzentriert sich auf das reine Preset-Surfen und auf universelle Modwheel-Action. Das geht schon – und ist auch für sich schon mehr als beeindruckend. Hier und da gibt es Brot-und-Butter-Sounds, am wohlsten fühlt sich der Schmidt aber sicherlich als Solo-Artist.

Slow down, Bro

Manche Design-Entscheidungen bleiben mir wohl auch weiterhin ein Rätsel. „Weil Stefan das eben so wollte“, lautet die Lösung, zumindest musste ich mir das des Öfteren vom Vertrieb anhören und habe mir noch etwas häufiger auf die Zunge gebissen und das „ja, aber“ verkniffen – denn niemand mag Klugscheißer. Wer Stefan ist und welche wichtige Rolle er einnimmt, klären wir aber besser später noch. Ab in den Ring, äh in die Praxis!

# Boersengang anthropic preisspanne 1772810

Die Analyse zu „Boersengang anthropic preisspanne 1772810“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
(March 15, 2026) — The International Space Station orbits 267 miles above a cloudy Atlantic Ocean southwest of Cape Town, South Africa. The Kibo laboratory module’s External Platform and the Canadarm2 robotic arm highlight the top foreground above Earth’s terminator—the line between night and day—in this photograph taken at approximately 6:36 a.m. local time. Credit: ESA/Sophie Adenot

NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station.

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud‑Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev will share mission highlights at 6 p.m. CST Tuesday, Nov. 17, at NASA Johnson Space Center’s visitor center. An awards ceremony recognizing key mission contributors will follow the presentation.

The astronauts will be available for media interviews before the event. Media may request an in-person interview no later than 5 p.m. Monday, Nov. 16, by emailing the JSC Newsroom at jsc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov.

Williams, Kud‑Sverchkov, and Mikaev launched aboard the Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on Nov. 27, 2025. The trio returned to Earth on July 26, making a parachute-assisted landing southeast of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. The crew was in space for 241 days, orbiting the Earth 3,856 times and traveling more than 102 million miles. The mission was the first for Williams and Mikaev and the second for Kud-Sverchkov.

Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot launched aboard a Dragon spacecraft on Feb. 13 as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. After more than seven months aboard the space station, Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot safely splashed down on Oct. 8 in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles.

During their 237-day mission, the four crew members traveled more than 100 million miles and completed more than 3,792 orbits around Earth. The mission was the second for Meir and the first for Hathaway and Adenot. Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev also flew as part of Crew-12 but is unavailable for the event.

The Expedition 74 crew dedicated more than 1,400 hours to scientific research and technology demonstrations aboard the International Space Station. Its work advanced in-space manufacturing by testing metal and tissue 3D-printing technologies and supported human health studies examining the effects of long-duration spaceflight. Research included blood flow studies, assessments of piloting capabilities under changing gravitational conditions, and activation of a new compact exercise system. The crew also evaluated life-support and environmental systems critical to future exploration missions under NASA’s Artemis program.

In addition, the crew members conducted pharmaceutical research to crystalize proteins for cancer medications, advance tumor targeting treatments, and grow stem cells for therapeutics. They cared for the first set of plants studied outside of curated systems, upgraded an instrument used to advance our understanding of matter and develop new quantum technologies, managed visiting spacecraft, and performed essential maintenance to support the continued operation of the orbiting laboratory.

Beyond research and operational achievements, Expedition 74 engaged students and audiences around the world through live educational events, outreach activities, and the sharing of stunning imagery that highlights the importance of scientific discovery and international collaboration in space.

For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.

Learn more about International Space Station research and operations at:

https://www.nasa.gov/station

-end-

Anna Schneider / Shaneequa Vereen
Johnson Space Center, Houston

items.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
items.subtitle: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

items.articleBody:
This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur?

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

Does true zero-trust architecture exist?

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

items.articleBody:
In 1949, West Germany was debating the location for its provisional government. After lengthy back-and-forth—the mayor of Frankfurt, Walter Kolb, had even pre-recorded a victory speech—the choice came to Bonn. A university town known as little more than the birthplace of Beethoven, Bonn had seen little wartime damage, had few ties to the Third Reich, and lacked the gravitas that a larger city might have commanded to keep the government upon reunification. Yet while Bonn offered the fledgling Federal Republic a fresh start, it lacked the culinary infrastructure to satiate hungry politicians.

Enter the Bundesbüdchen. Erected in 1957 by the family of Christel Rausch, the “federal kiosk” served sausages, sandwiches, and pastries to the builders of the Bonn Republic. Every day, politicians, diplomats, and reporters drifted in and out of the Bundestag and associated offices nearby to break at the Büdchen for a quick bite or to catch up on gossip or news. As West Germany grew, the Büdchen evolved into a symbol of postwar democracy. Joschka Fischer, member of the Bundestag and eventual Vice Chancellor and foreign minister, supposedly loved to buy Asterix comics, and Vice Chancellor Hans Dietrich Genscher loved to pick up gummy bears for business trips. Former Labor Minister Norbert Blüm claimed the kiosk stood for Bonn itself; “That’s just how Bonn was like. Not pompous. A lovable republic.”

In 1990 came reunification, and nine years later, the Bundestag moved to Berlin. The United Nations and various businesses (Deutsche Welle, Deutsche Telekom) moved into or nearby the former government facilities along the Rhine. The Bundeshaus, the former parliament building, became the World Conference Center Bonn. In 2006, when the UN Campus was inaugurated, the kiosk was stripped of its colorful advertisements and moved to a storage facility.

But the Bonners persisted. With owner Jürgen Rausch, a group of stalwarts founded the Förderverein historischer Verkaufspavillon Görresstraße e.V., a society dedicated to preserving the historic structure. In 2018, they secured a city council resolution and a €55,000 grant from the Nordrhein Westfalen Foundation to re-establish the Büdchen within view of its original spot. In May 2020, it was wheeled from storage through the streets of Bonn to Heussallee and given a face-lift to restore its Cold War-era grandeur. Today, visitors to the UN Campus and World Conference Center—or anyone nostalgic for a whiff of the Fifties—can stop in for a quick bite or to peruse the headlines. With many of the buildings from the Bonn Republic now occupied, the Bundesbüdchen remains one of the most accessible, living pieces of the era.

And its history isn’t lost on the current seat of power. In 2025, a Bundesbüdchen restaurant opened at Hannovrische Strasse 2 in Berlin, a twenty-five minute walk from the Bundestag. While its Michelin-trained chef and menu featuring oxtail and filets represents a leap from the casual kiosk, the restaurant’s bar replicates the original Büdchen in Bonn.

items.articleBody:
Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, RMI.

In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.

Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.

For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.

“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.

With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.

Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth

Note: “Other” includes stakes in other publicly traded companies and accumulated dividends and investment returns. Sources: Forbes’ The World’s Billionaires, Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, SEC filings, StockAnalysis.com Chris Alcantara/ProPublica

While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.

One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.

Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.

“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.

As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”

Gates’ Climate Awakening

Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.

In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.

A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.

Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.

It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases, he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, right, then-U.S. President Barack Obama, left, and then-French President François Hollande applaud a speech during the United Nations conference on climate change in Paris in 2015. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but usually from agricultural sources (“cow farts,” in his words). He has rarely mentioned landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office, Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic’s board in 2009. Gates’ stake in the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about something I’m buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea what Cascade owns.” (Gates’ Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in securities filings.)

Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it generates methane. The Gates Foundation has funded research and advocacy aimed at solving that problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest methane into fertilizer. Its product was actually tested last year at a Republic landfill in California, where the pink liquid was sprinkled on the soil covering the top layer of trash.

Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but the startup reportedly ceased operations after a Department of Energy grant was canceled. (Windfall didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.)

On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In 2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science Based Targets Initiative, promising to cut its emissions by 35% by 2030. Not that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its pitch for garbage-collection contracts in progressive cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for businesses that meet certain environmental, social and governance criteria, attracting sustainability-minded investors.

Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates’ vision. As Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You can’t have sustainability without profitability.”

A Not-So-Model Landfill

Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to mention the occasional dead pet.

Dust is kicked up by trucks and bulldozers at Republic Service’s McCarty Road Landfill in Houston. Mark Felix for ProPublica

Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under 100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country’s 1,400 active landfills, where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out of mind.

People who live near landfills, though, describe smelling rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning eyes, headaches and nausea. And while methane itself has no scent, those odors indicate that the gas is being released, studies show.

Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before. Open dumping and burning remained widespread until the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like benzene).

Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures. Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to keep that gas from escaping. Managing such a beast is costly, which helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of scale.

Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s historic climate bill — the company invited the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian kind of project.

On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave a tour of the gas-collection system. Like at most other large landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below — five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue, snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it into a salable product.

A Republic worker stands next to a gas well at the company’s McCarty Road Landfill in Houston in 2022. Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers

Most landfills that are required to collect gas simply burn it off. But they can also process it into “renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from decomposing waste, it’s generally considered more climate-friendly. It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.

Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In fact, it may be just the opposite.

In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement alert” saying that landfills across the country were “violating monitoring and maintenance requirements.” While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities targeted belong to Republic.

McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It would soon earn Republic a formal “finding of violation” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” — methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection system as well.

And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with renewable natural gas facilities can actually emit more methane than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some operators may prioritize collecting gas with higher methane content, which is cheaper to process — allowing more of the remaining methane to leak out.

Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”

“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.

The issues aren’t exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since 2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39 of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than 1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells — spewing excessive amounts of methane.

In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.

Methane Bubbles at a Republic Services Landfill

Methane bubbles up through a pool of liquid drained from the trash at Republic’s Apex Regional Landfill in Nevada, documented by EPA inspectors in 2024. Environmental Protection Agency

What the Satellites Saw

Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan: “Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying away from true climate leadership.

In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets Initiative, the SBTI made its minimum climate goal much more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.

This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders. Republic has also spent more than $8 billion buying its own stock in the open market, ProPublica’s analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by investors.

The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024, this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime investment manager — whose “insight into sustainability issues” is cited in company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’ dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the corporate-governance expert.

Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is “not an immediate strategic priority.”

Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to submit an updated target. But when ProPublica asked if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.

The entrance to Republic’s McCarty Road Landfill in Houston Mark Felix for ProPublica

Garbage trucks pull in and out of the McCarty landfill. Mark Felix for ProPublica

There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.

In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already cut its landfill emissions by 20% since 2017. But that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports, Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.

This method is based on an industry study that, as the EPA has noted, excluded data from gas-collection systems that were “not working well.” The EPA’s own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to “erroneously report decreasing emissions,” according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year period.

The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the No. 1 and No. 2 emitters among the roughly 70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA. And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn’t in the study, but according to measurements by Carbon Mapper, it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)

In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said, “We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”

He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association, a major trade group, questioning the accuracy of satellite measurements. It is a tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for cleaning up landfills.

“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane emissions,” she said. “There’s a fire alarm going off and instead of getting out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector.”

Quietly Fighting Climate Policies

Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the “doomsday view” of global warming — a striking shift for someone who’d once warned of the failing ecosystems, mass migration and soaring mortality that could result from hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald Trump, to say that Gates had admitted he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to shift his resources, he remained a “climate activist,” he told one audience.

Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas companies because, he later wrote, “I don’t want to profit if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also called on other business leaders to “make sure that they’re not holding back” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into profits.

Bill Gates attends the groundbreaking for TerraPower’s nuclear power plant near Kemmerer, Wyoming, in 2024. Benjamin Rasmussen/The New York Times/Redux

Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according to securities filings, has never sold a share.

In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among other potential changes, the agency asked for comments on the newer technologies, such as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in monitoring and controlling methane pollution.

Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But they wanted almost all of it to remain voluntary, according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which have Republic executives on their boards.

“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,” the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”

The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes against its climate commitments.

“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.

Gates’ press representatives didn’t respond to questions about whether he’s aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated the source of a fifth of his fortune. But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy, Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity. They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.

“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him, I think he’s very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for him.”

“My theory is that he probably doesn’t have much involvement in those investments,” said another laid-off staffer.

Gates’ investment managers, at least, can’t claim total ignorance. Larson and Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in Republic’s board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level” reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “practices we could do better,” this director said. (Larson didn’t return phone messages left by ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn’t respond to a question about his and Handley’s involvement in Republic.)

It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen, methane is produced.

Properly managing the waste we’ve already buried is only the first step, said Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. “In parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”

This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started phasing out the landfilling of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health benefits would ultimately outweigh the costs.

In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.

A steady stream of garbage trucks flows through Republic’s McCarty Road Landfill in Houston on a recent weekday. Mark Felix for ProPublica. Aerial support by LightHawk.

But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with dumpster collection, as its most profitable segments. So when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company, along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should be left to the states to decide.

“It’s like you’ve got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard, a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the environmental justice movement. “You’ve got a landfill, and it makes money — big money. So why tinker with it?”

items.articleBody:
Wer ein neues iPhone im Apple Store kauft, bekommt dort meist auch gleich Hilfe bei der Einrichtung – und offenbar mitunter etwas mehr, als ihm bewusst ist. In amerikanischen Filialen sollen Mitarbeiter Kunden für Probeabos angemeldet haben, ohne deren ausdrückliche Zustimmung einzuholen. Nach Ablauf der Gratisphase verlängern sich diese automatisch kostenpflichtig.

Whistleblower bringt unangenehme Details ans Licht

Ins Rollen gebracht hat das Thema der Reparaturexperte und YouTuber Louis Rossmann. Nachdem sich zunächst ein anonymer Store-Mitarbeiter bei ihm gemeldet hatte, folgten nach seinen Angaben Schilderungen von 18 mutmaßlichen Beschäftigten und sechs Kunden. Im Mittelpunkt steht das Verkaufssystem „Connect and Personalize“. Verknüpft ein Kunde beim Kauf seinen Apple Account, sieht der Verkäufer auf seinem Dienstgerät vorhandene Geräte, gebuchte Dienste und verfügbare Probeangebote, etwa für Apple One, Apple Music oder das Creator Studio. Die Schaltfläche zur Zustimmung liegt dabei auf dem Gerät des Mitarbeiters. Einige sollen sie selbst betätigt und die Angebote als kostenlose Zugabe zum Gerätekauf präsentiert haben.

Eingebetteten Inhalt von YouTube öffnen

Hoher Verkaufsdruck

Als Hintergrund nennen Beschäftigte interne Zielvorgaben. Der Anteil zusätzlich abgeschlossener Dienste fließt demnach in Leistungsbewertungen ein, die Rede ist von Quoten um 40 Prozent. Zur Einordnung gehört allerdings auch: Rossmann räumt ein, einige der gezeigten Dokumente zum Schutz seiner Quellen nachgestellt zu haben, und andere Mitarbeiter berichten von einem korrekten Vorgehen. Eine Anweisung aus der Konzernzentrale ist nicht belegt. Apple hat inzwischen reagiert.

Eingebetteten Inhalt von YouTube öffnen

Die umstrittene Kennzahl ist aus dem internen Mitarbeitersystem Orchard verschwunden, außerdem wurden die Filialteams daran erinnert, dass Kunden Vertragsbedingungen selbst bestätigen müssen. Cupertino begründet sie allerdings mit dem Weihnachtsgeschäft, in dem viele Geräte als Geschenk gekauft werden. Ganz nebensächlich ist das Thema für den Hersteller nicht. Die Services-Sparte erzielte im vierten Geschäftsquartal 2026 mit 31,57 Milliarden US-Dollar zwar einen neuen Rekordumsatz, wuchs mit 9,8 Prozent aber so langsam wie seit 13 Quartalen nicht mehr. Für das laufende Weihnachtsquartal stellt der iPhone-Konzern ein Plus von 8 bis 9 Prozent in Aussicht.

So überprüft ihr das bei euch

Die bekannten Fälle stammen bislang aus Nordamerika. Wer trotzdem auf Nummer sicher gehen möchte, findet unter „Einstellungen > Apple Account > Abonnements“ alle aktiven Abos und Probezeiträume und kann sie dort direkt kündigen. Für bereits erfolgte Abbuchungen lässt sich über reportaproblem.apple.com eine Erstattung beantragen.
