items.articleBody:
This story was published in partnership with LOOKOUT News.

An official from Marana, Arizona, is seeking clarification from the private prison giant Management and Training Corporation about its handling of sexual abuse allegations at the former state prison in the town, following an investigation from LOOKOUT and The Intercept.

In an October 28 letter, reviewed by LOOKOUT and The Intercept, Marana Finance Director and License Inspector Yiannis Kalaitzidis asked MTC Senior Vice President Mary Calvin for a written explanation of what the town official called an “apparent inconsistency” between state records and the facility’s 2023 Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, audit, a report required by the federal law.

MTC ran a former state prison in Marana, Arizona, and plans to reopen it as an ICE detention camp.

The request is part of the town’s review of MTC’s October 1 application for a business license to “Operate Marana Detention Facility.” The company ran a former Arizona state prison in Marana and plans to reopen it imminently as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camp.

The letter cites a September 29 LOOKOUT and Intercept investigation about how state records reference three allegations of sexual misconduct at the prison in 2022 and 2023.

PREA audits — which are required for jails, prisons, and detention centers at least once every three years — must record all allegations of sexual misconduct at detention facilities, whether they are substantiated or not. Certified in December 2023, MTC’s report for the Marana prison, however, recorded none.

Kalaitzidis noted in his letter that the audit says the finding of zero incidents was verified by the warden, chief of security, PREA compliance manager, and internal investigator. He also wrote that, despite the apparent reviews by several company officials, the report “does not appear to be certified or signed by any MTC personnel.”

Related

Prison That Didn’t Report Sex Abuse Allegation Against Staffer to Reopen as ICE Camp

The letter says the town of Marana is requesting the explanation as part of an investigation into whether MTC “made a material false statement in conducting the business” of the state prison facility, which would be grounds for denial of a business license according to the town’s code.

“The Town of Marana is currently reviewing MTC’s business license application,” said Andrea De La Cruz, the assistant town manager, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept by email. “As part of our review process and due diligence, the Town has contacted MTC to request additional information. The application remains under review, and no final determination has been made at this time.”

MTC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Read Our Complete Coverage

The War on Immigrants

Changing Political Context

Local residents and officials say the state, the federal government, and MTC left them out of meaningful discussions about reopening the prison as an ICE camp, LOOKOUT and The Intercept previously reported.

For now, a town business license is among the few levers local officials have.

Related

How a Small Kansas City Became a Critical Hub for Trump’s Deportation Regime Against Its Will

In an October 2 letter from the local group Pima Resists ICE, or PRICE, to a Marana official who specialized in licensure, organizers cited not only the discrepancies between state investigations into sexual abuse and the PREA audit, but also alleged violations involving an escape from an MTC prison in Kingman, Arizona, in 2010, as well as abuses in a New Mexico immigration camp run by MTC as revealed in a 2017 DHS Office of Inspector General report.

The inquiry comes as Arizona’s political landscape is shifting. The midterm election gave Democrats control of both chambers of the state legislature as well as the governor’s office — a historic change in state power. Republicans will be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.

That has Democratic lawmakers talking about taking on one of the most contentious laws in recent Arizona history. Following protests across the state, Democrats took up the cause of repealing a controversial 2010 anti-immigrant law known as Senate Bill 1070. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down three of its provisions, leaving a requirement that police check the immigration status of people they stop under certain circumstances.

“I would absolutely love to see a repeal of SB1070,” state Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Democrat from Glendale, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept. “There are still parts of that law on the books that are enabling cities to collaborate with ICE to rip families apart, and that needs to stop.”

State Rep. Betty Villegas, D-Tucson, echoed Ortiz: “We already have bills aligned to focus on what other states have done to control ICE from coming into private property.”

Following the lead of neighboring New Mexico’s prohibition on local jurisdictions entering into contracts with ICE for immigrant detention camps, Villegas said Democrats in Arizona see an appetite for doing something similar in their own state.

“We do not want the Democrats to wait until things get bad to investigate conditions.”

Ortiz agreed, saying there is “likely an appetite” for something similar in Arizona, and that the Latino Caucus would address the issue.

Local nonprofits said lawmakers should also conduct a review of no-bid contracts like the one inked between the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, and MTC.

“This was literally handed to them with no review and no public input,” said Caroline Isaacs, the executive director of Just Communities Arizona, a nonprofit working on criminal justice reform. “We do not want the Democrats to wait until things get bad to investigate conditions.”

“We want them to do this now, before people get hurt.”

items.feedText: On each of these identical square tabletops are arranged four copies of the same right triangle. On the first table, the uncovered space takes the shape of the square of the triangle’s hypotenuse; on the second, it equals the sum of the squares of the triangle’s two smaller sides. The two tabletops are the same size, so these uncovered spaces have the same area.

items.articleBody:
Mit Petit Planet veröffentlicht HoYoverse am 4. Dezember seine erste Life Sim im Stile eines Animal Crossing. Zusätzlich startet auch der Creature Collector Honkai: Nexus Anima am 25. November in die letzte geschlossene Beta und bereitet sich auf die Veröffentlichung im kommenden Frühjahr vor.

Petit Planet setzt auf eine gemütliche Bilderbuchwelt

Galaktisches Cozy-Game

In Petit Planet verschlägt es euch in eine Galaxie voll kleiner Planeten, in der ihr euch ein gemütliches Zuhause aufbaut, Freundschaften knüpft und gelegentlich in eurer Nachbarschaft bei Alltagsaufgaben aushelft. Zusätzlich kümmert ihr euch um die Luca-Bäume, von denen es auf jedem der kleinen Himmelskörper einen gibt und die mit ihrem Planeten wachsen und gedeihen. Sorgen vor geldgierigen Tanukis, die euch bis auf euer letztes Hemd ausziehen möchten, braucht ihr euch im neuesten Spiel vom chinesischen Entwickler HoYoverse hingegen nicht zu machen.

Trotz des entspannten Gameplays und der Bilderbuchoptik stand Petit Planet jedoch kurzzeitig in der Kritik, da die Entwickler ein KI-Sprachmodell integriert haben, um Charakterinteraktionen abwechslungsreicher und freier zu gestalten. Da dieses Feature von der Community kontrovers diskutiert und deutlich kritisiert wurde, bleiben die KI-Chats eine rein optionale Funktion, die nach Belieben an- und ausgeschaltet werden kann. Die eigentlichen Quest- und Story-Dialoge bleiben davon unberührt und sind von Menschen geschrieben und vertont. Auch sonst setzt das Studio auf Handarbeit und distanziert sich etwa von KI-generierten Grafikinhalten.

Petit Planet: Einblicke in die galaktische Lebenssimulation

Zusätzlich hat HoYoverse jüngst noch eine Fassung für die Nintendo Switch 2 angekündigt, die im kommenden Jahr folgen soll. Zum offiziellen Launch am 4. Dezember wird das Spiel jedoch vorerst nur für Windows, iOS und Android veröffentlicht. Petit Planet setzt dabei selbstverständlich auf Cross-Play und Cross-Save zwischen den Plattformen und auch einen Mehrspielermodus, über den ihr die Planeten eurer Freunde besuchen und zusammen spielen könnt, wird es geben.

Finale Beta

Auch die Veröffentlichung des Creature Collectors Honkai: Nexus Anima ist nicht mehr fern, denn das Spiel soll nur wenig später im kommenden Frühjahr erscheinen. Entsprechend startet das Spiel am 25. November in seine finale geschlossene Beta, zu der auf der offiziellen Webseite des Spiels bereits die Anmeldung möglich ist.

Obwohl Nexus Anima auf den ersten Blick an die Pokémon-Reihe erinnern mag, da ihr ebenso die Welt bereist, Kreaturen fangt und Kämpfe mit ihnen austragt, unterscheiden sich die Spiele erheblich voneinander. Der deutlichste Unterschied zeigt sich wohl in der Kampfmechanik, obgleich sich auch Game Freak bei Pokémon mittlerweile vom rundenbasierten Schlagabtausch verabschiedet hat und nun auf Echtzeit-Actionkämpfe setzt.

Honkai: Nexus Anima setzt auf taktische Arenakämpfe

In Nexus Anima werden die Kämpfe als Arena-Auto-Battler ausgetragen. Ihr schickt somit euer gesamtes Team auf einmal in die Arena und über Erfolg oder Misserfolg entscheiden die taktische Aufstellung eurer Animas vor dem Kampf, das Timing ihrer Spezialfähigkeiten während des Matches sowie der Fokus auf einzelne Gegner und das Ausspielen besonderer Zusatzfertigkeiten, um dem Gegnerteam den finalen Stoß zu verpassen.

Auch optisch kann sich Nexus Anima deutlich abgrenzen und lässt die Konkurrenz im direkten Vergleich recht altbacken wirken. So setzt das Kreaturen-Sammelspiel auf den für HoYoverse typischen, auf Hochglanz polierten Anime-Stil. Gespickt mit Sci-Fi-Elementen, wie sie im Honkai-Universum ebenfalls üblich sind. Ebenso begnügt sich das Team bei der Erzählung der Geschichte nicht mit stumpfen Textboxen und einem schweigsamen Protagonisten, sondern treibt die Story in voll vertonten, dynamischen Anime-Sequenzen voran.

Honkai: Nexus Anima zeigt seine Spielwelt und Kämpfe

Free-to-Play

Als mögliches Damoklesschwert bleibt jedoch die Frage der Monetarisierung bestehen. Wie bei all ihren anderen Titeln wird HoYoverse auch für Petit Planet und Honkai: Nexus Anima auf ein Freemium-System setzen. Welche Spielinhalte am Ende hinter Bezahlschranken verschwinden und wie sich das auf den Spielfluss auswirkt, lässt sich an dieser Stelle noch nicht absehen. Die Entwickler nutzen zwar für gewöhnlich die im asiatischen Raum beliebten Gacha-Systeme, die konkrete Ausgestaltung und wie stark Mikrotransaktionen den Fortschritt bestimmen, fällt von Spiel zu Spiel jedoch sehr unterschiedlich aus.

Denn während bei den Zugpferden Genshin Impact und Honkai: Star Rail durchaus ein gewisser Power Creep zu beobachten ist und In-App Käufe schwer zu umgehen sind, um neue Charaktere zeitnah auf ihre maximale Stärke zu bringen, sieht es beim Action-Brawler Zenless Zone Zero gänzlich anders aus. Hier präsentiert sich das Gacha-Element als reines Beiwerk, während die Hauptstory auch wenn man keinen einzigen Cent ausgegeben hat ohne nervigen Grind durchgespielt werden kann, da das Spiel in den Missionen alle benötigten Charaktere in ausreichender Stärke zur Verfügung stellt. Insofern bleibt abzuwarten, welche Richtung die kommenden Titel einschlagen werden.

items.title: Antarktisches Tiefenwasser enthält Jahrtausende alten organischen Kohlenstoff
items.subtitle: Im Weddellmeer entsteht Tiefenwasser, das große Mengen Kohlenstoff in die Tiefsee transportiert.

items.articleBody:
Im Weddellmeer entsteht Tiefenwasser, das große Mengen Kohlenstoff in die Tiefsee transportiert. Trotz reger Planktonproduktion verändert sich die Zusammensetzung der untersuchten gelösten organischen Stoffe auf dem antarktischen Schelf kaum, wie Messungen zeigen. Eine mögliche Erklärung ist die lange Verweildauer des Wassers, während der leicht abbaubares Material wieder zerfallen kann.

Bremerhaven (Deutschland). Am Rand der Antarktis bilden sich besonders kalte und salzreiche Wassermassen, die über den Kontinentalhang in die Tiefsee absinken. Sie tragen zum antarktischen Bodenwasser bei und transportieren darin gespeicherten Kohlenstoff durch große Teile des Weltmeers.

Auf dem Weg über den Schelf treffen diese Wassermassen auf Algenblüten und einen aktiven mikrobiellen Stoffwechsel. Dabei entsteht gelöste organische Materie, deren Kohlenstoff teils rasch abgebaut wird, teils aber über Jahrtausende im Meer überdauert. Ob die Vorgänge auf dem Schelf die chemische Signatur des später absinkenden Wassers verändern, war bislang unklar.

Wasserproben aus sieben Wassermassen

Forscher der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU) um Dr. Gonzalo V. Gomez-Saez haben deshalb den organischen Kohlenstoff im südlichen Weddellmeer untersucht. Auf zwei Expeditionen des Forschungseisbrechers Polarstern von 2016 und 2021 wurden 178 Wasserproben an 38 Stationen gesammelt. Für den direkten Vergleich der Tiefenwasserbildung ordnete das Team 116 Proben sieben Wassermassen zu, von oberflächennahen Schichten bis in 4.433 Meter Tiefe.

Der Kohlenstoffgehalt wurde chemisch gemessen. Um die Zusammensetzung der gelösten organischen Substanzen zu bestimmen, setzten die Wissenschaftler hochauflösende Massenspektrometrie und Kernspinresonanz-Spektroskopie ein. Über den Anteil radioaktiven Kohlenstoffs ermittelten sie außerdem das scheinbare Alter der untersuchten organischen Moleküle.

Für die Untersuchung der Molekülstruktur wurde eine aus den Wasserproben angereicherte Teilfraktion verwendet, die rund 34 Prozent des gesamten gelösten organischen Kohlenstoffs erfasste. Die Aussagen zur molekularen Zusammensetzung betreffen daher vor allem diese extrahierbaren Verbindungen, während der gesamte gelöste organische Kohlenstoff separat gemessen wurde.

„Gelöste organische Substanzen sind ein riesiger und komplexer Kohlenstoffspeicher im Ozean. Indem wir ihre Moleküle im Detail untersuchen, können wir erforschen, wie sie sich verändern, während das Wasser über den antarktischen Kontinentalschelf strömt“, sagt Prof. Dr. Thorsten Dittmar vom Institut für Chemie und Biologie des Meeres (ICBM).

Kaum Unterschiede trotz Planktonblüten

Das Ergebnis fiel überraschend einheitlich aus. Zwischen den sieben Wassermassen fanden sich keine statistisch signifikanten Unterschiede in der Konzentration des gelösten organischen Kohlenstoffs. Auch die analysierte Molekülzusammensetzung und ihre strukturellen Merkmale blieben während der Tiefenwasserbildung weitgehend ähnlich. Eine deutliche Anreicherung frischer organischer Stoffe durch saisonale Algenblüten ließ sich nicht nachweisen.

Die Radiokohlenstoffmessungen ergaben für die extrahierte organische Fraktion ein mittleres scheinbares Alter von rund 5.700 Jahren. Dieses Alter beschreibt eine Mischung von Molekülen unterschiedlicher Herkunft und nicht das Alter des Wassers. Der Befund deutet darauf hin, dass schwer abbaubare organische Verbindungen die Proben dominieren.

„Unsere Studie zeigt, dass die molekularen Eigenschaften gelöster organischer Substanzen während der Tiefenwasserbildung im südlichen Weddellmeer erhalten bleiben. Unsere Ergebnisse unterstreichen, dass gelöste organische Substanzen ein stabiler Bestandteil des regionalen Kohlenstoffkreislaufs im Südlichen Ozean sind“, erklärt Dr. Gonzalo V. Gomez-Saez.

Als mögliche Erklärung gilt die ungewöhnlich lange Verweildauer des Wassers auf dem Kontinentalschelf. Dort zirkuliert es sechs bis zwölf Jahre lang, zeitweise auch unter dem Filchner-Ronne-Schelfeis. In dieser Zeit könnten Mikroorganismen neu gebildete, leicht abbaubare organische Substanzen weitgehend in gelösten anorganischen Kohlenstoff umwandeln. Die Messungen stützen diese Deutung, belegen den Abbauweg aber nicht unmittelbar.

Kohlenstoffmenge könnte dennoch sinken

Aus den gemessenen Konzentrationen und bekannten Strömungsraten errechnete das Team, dass mit der Tiefenwasserbildung im Weddellmeer jährlich schätzungsweise 0,155 Milliarden Tonnen gelöster organischer Kohlenstoff in die Tiefsee gelangen. Die Unsicherheit beträgt etwa 0,03 Milliarden Tonnen pro Jahr. Diese Werte bezeichnen die gesamte transportierte Menge und nicht eine zusätzliche Kohlenstoffaufnahme während der Passage über den Schelf.

Auch wenn die gemessene chemische Zusammensetzung stabil erscheint, könnte sich der Transport mit dem Klimawandel verändern. Weil im Südpolarmeer weniger besonders dichtes Bodenwasser gebildet wird, dürfte auch die jährlich in die Tiefe gelangende Kohlenstoffmenge abnehmen. Aus der gleichbleibenden molekularen Signatur lässt sich deshalb nicht ableiten, dass der gesamte Kohlenstoffkreislauf gegen die Erwärmung geschützt ist.

„Die globale Erwärmung erreicht inzwischen auch die antarktischen Schelfmeere. Wenn der große Speicher gelöster organischer Substanzen kaum von den Prozessen auf dem Schelf beeinflusst wird, deutet dies darauf hin, dass dieser Kohlenstoffspeicher in dieser Region vom Klimawandel weitgehend unbeeinflusst bleiben könnte“, sagt Dr. Moritz Holtappels vom Alfred-Wegener-Institut, Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung (AWI).

Der mögliche Unterschied zwischen chemischer Beständigkeit und abnehmender Transportmenge ist entscheidend. Zudem erfasst die Untersuchung vor allem eine bestimmte gelöste organische Fraktion, während organische Partikel und gelöster anorganischer Kohlenstoff anders auf verändertes Meereis und die Erwärmung reagieren können. Weitere Messfahrten, darunter eine für 2028 geplante Polarstern-Expedition im antarktischen Winter, sollen diese Veränderungen genauer erfassen.

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin Nature Communications, doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-79040-4

items.articleBody:
Die Frankfurter Polizei kontrolliert offenbar gezielt migrantisch gelesene junge Männer, durchsucht deren Handys und fotografiert die Kontrollierten. Den Vorwurf, rassistische Kontrollen durchzuführen, bestreitet sie.

Schon am 1. November kontrollierte die Polizei zahlreiche Personen. Diese Kontrollen setzt sie nun seit Tagen fort. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / 7aktuell - Verpixelung: netzpolitik.org
Die hessische Polizei hat in den letzten Tagen fast 1000 Personenkontrollen auf der Frankfurter Einkaufsmeile Zeil durchgeführt und dabei offenbar auch Handys durchsucht. Laut Medienberichten nimmt die Polizei dabei gezielt männliche, migrantisch gelesene Jugendliche und junge Erwachsene ins Visier.

Als Grund für die Aktion gibt der hessische Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) die Ausschreitungen vom 31. Oktober an. Poseck hatte im Nachgang des Ereignisses vor allem ein „migrantisches Milieu“ für die Ausschreitungen verantwortlich gemacht, diese Äußerung war von verschiedener Seite als rassistisch kritisiert worden.

Unbeeindruckt von der Kritik gibt es nun offenbar vermehrt Kontrollen gegen migrantisch gelesene Jugendliche und Erwachsene. Einem Bericht der Frankfurter Rundschau zufolge hat die Polizei bei diesen Kontrollen Mobiltelefone und in diesen die Mediengalerien durchsucht, offenbar um Bilder von den Krawallen zu finden.

Der in der FR zitierte Rechtsanwalt Johannes Koch sagt, dass bei verdachtsunabhängigen Kontrollen nur die Identität der kontrollierten Person festgestellt werden dürfe. Die Polizei dürfe sie aber nicht gegen ihren Willen durchsuchen.

Laut dem Stadtparlamentarier Deniz Avan (Linkspartei) hat die Polizei den Jugendlichen gegenüber gesagt, dass sie sich entlasten könnten, wenn sie die Handys zeigten. Gegenüber Avan begründete die Polizei die Kontrollen als „direkte Folgemaßnahme“ wegen der Ausschreitungen.

In einem Bericht der Hessenschau ist davon die Rede, dass die Polizei kontrollierte Personen gegen deren Willen fotografierte.

Anwalt hält Maßnahmen für rechtswidrig

Der Frankfurter Rechtsanwalt Johannes Koch hält die Maßnahmen gegenüber der Frankfurter Rundschau für rechtswidrig. Personenkontrollen bräuchten immer eine gesetzliche Legitimation, sagte er dem Medium. Die „freiwilligen Handykontrollen“ hält der Anwalt für Makulatur. „Durch die Bedrohungskulisse bin ich der Meinung, dass eine freie Willensbildung nicht möglich war“, zitiert die FR den Anwalt.

Sowohl Deniz Avan als auch der grüne Stadtverordnete Emre Telyakar sprechen davon, dass der Verdacht von Racial Profiling bestehe. Unter dem Begriff versteht man polizeiliche Maßnahmen, die etwa auf dem Aussehen und der Herkunft von Personen beruhen. Die Frankfurter Polizei weist diesen Vorwurf gegenüber der FR zurück.

Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass die Frankfurter Polizei auf der Einkaufsstraße Massenkontrollen durchführt. Laut dem hessischen Innenministerium hat die Polizei zwischen November 2025 und Oktober 2026 elf sogenannte „Action Days“ durchgeführt und dabei mehr als 2.800 Personen kontrolliert.

items.articleBody:
Plumbing the rhythms of the ocean and marine life, Amy Genser creates undulating abstractions that evoke swells, currents, reefs, and the sea floor. The artist composes elaborate wall works from rolled mulberry paper, acrylic, and wire in which patterns move and converge across swaths of blues and greens. The closer you look, the more colors emerge.

Although reminiscent of the sea in many ways, Genser’s works defy instant recognition. At first glance, they may appear topographical, as if a luminous, clear sea is being viewed from above. The rolling forms are redolent of waves but also perhaps the way corals cluster around rock formations. Then, details draw us nearer: bulbous forms with cavities resemble barnacles, and extended shapes could be tentacles.

Detail of “Stars Below” for The Macallan Carta Nautica Collection

The artist’s play on scale, texture, pattern, and depth draw us in and keep us guessing—not unlike the many enigmas of the ocean itself. And one recent project challenged Genser to work at a monumental scale. The Macallan, a single malt Scottish whisky company, commissioned her to create a monumental piece titled “Stars Below” for its Carta Nautica Collection.

Both the bottle release and the artwork celebrate the time-honored transatlantic journey of the wooden barrels used to age the spirit, which travel to Scotland from Spain and the U.S. “Through layered textures, flowing forms, and rich colors, I brought to life a mythical underwater world shaped by movement, discovery, and transformation,” Genser says.

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

items.articleBody:
Astrophysicist Dr. Josie Peters explored the science behind repeated shoelace failures for BBC Ideas, analyzing the physical forces that cause them to come undone.

She explained that tying both stages of the knot in the same direction creates a weaker granny knot instead of a sturdier reef knot, a mix-up that a simple change in loop direction can fix. Peters discussed different ways to tie laces, including the famous Ian knot and Berluti knot, and highlighted thousands of years of human innovation in securing one’s footwear.

Astrophysicist Josie Peters explores the surprising science of knots and explains what makes some shoelace knots fail and others stay secure for longer.

The video draws on a 2017 study by mechanical engineers at the University of California, Berkeley, who found that a shoe strikes the ground with about seven times the force of gravity, loosening the knot with every step.

America cannot undo Trumpism (permalink)

True Carneyism has never been tried. When Canadian PM Mark Carney traveled to Davos to declare a "rupture" in the old order (and admit that this old order was never that great to begin with) he told us that there was no going back from Trumpism. The only way out of Trumpism was through:

https://www.weforum.org/stories/forum-institutional/davos-2026-special-address-by-mark-carney-prime-minister-of-canada/

This is easy to say, but hard to do. If the old order is over, then we will never again be able to trust America to serve as the world's cop, banker, ISP, IT department and consumer of first resort.

We can't trust Americans to buy the things we make:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations

We can't trust them not to interfere with the interconnections between fiber lines that slither out of the oceans and onto the US landmass:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/26/difficult-multipolarism/#eurostack

We can't trust them not to weaponize the US dollar to undermine sovereign nations' legitimate activities:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/26/i-dont-want/#your-greenback-dollar

And we absolutely can't trust them not to spy on, steal from, and shut down governments, firms and households around the world by cutting off access to US software and cloud services, and by bricking the world's devices, from tractors to smartphones:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Despite Carney's assertion that this rupture represents a welcome (if too cruel, sudden and painful) departure of the old (never very good) system, no one (not even Carney) is acting like the world has truly changed. Take Carney's answer to the Trump tariffs: retaliatory tariffs. Tariffs have a place in sheltering a nascent domestic industry from better-developed, deeper-pocketed foreign competitors, so a tariff wall between Canada and the US could make sense, if it was paired with the massive domestic investment we'd need to rebuild the manufacturing industry that Brian Mulroney sold out with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement (and later NAFTA).

But Carney is no Carneyist. When it comes to massive domestic spending, Carney is a bog-standard, austerity-addled Reaganomics guy; a central banker and technocrat whose idea of "industrial policy" is firing tens of thousands of skilled civil servants who thwart his agenda and replacing them with defective (but obedient) chatbots running on US hardware:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/13/vibe-governance/#k-hole

Carney's retaliatory tariffs aren't what you'd do if the old order had "ruptured." They're what you'd do if you hoped that your American cousins would come to their senses, evict their mad king from the White House, tear down the Epstein Memorial Ballroom, and roll back the clock to 2016. Like a lot of liberals, Carney just wants to go back to brunch.

But as any true Carneyist knows, brunch is canceled forever. Brunch ruptured. There's no going back to the old America, and there's no going back to the old American order that had dominated the world since the end of WWII. As November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor, but he flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play."

This is something we're all struggling with, including Americans. The Republicans' midterm wipeout has corporate Democrats hoping that after a few years' tinkering, they can elect a Newsomdroid or give Harris a do-over and win back the trust and reliance of the world and the American people. Even for a true Carneyist who never liked the old order very much (like me), this is a comforting prospect. No one knows what the next world will look like, and no matter how screwed up the old world was, I knew how it worked and how to make it work for me (more or less).

But there is no going back. Trump I didn't have a plan, it only had Trump, whose One Big Idea was issuing Executive Orders. Many of these were meaningless bloviating. Some were illegal and were swiftly suspended or never went into effect. Biden overturned nearly all the remaining EOs (that were both substantive and not totally illegal).

But Trump II had Project 2025. The point of Project 2025 and the ambition of the wreckers who wrote it was to push America through a series of one-way transformations that cannot be undone, and that's what's happened, over two short years. That's the bad news. The good news is that it's much easier to destroy than to build, so Project 2025 hasn't led to the creation of permanent, load-bearing fascist institutions that cannot be shuttered without bringing down large parts of the USA.

Start with values. Trumpism is a denial of democracy and the rule of law. Tens of millions of Americans have been marinated in a belief system that says that the way to win power is to claim all the elections you lose are rigged and that these "stolen elections" are best addressed by staging a coup. These people are in a cult that embraces its leader's naked corruption. They're in a cult whose doctrine treats political triumph of as divine direction to embark on looting sprees. It's a cult whose members mutilate their faces so that they can't ever leave, and the reward for this permanent disfigurement is endless influence-peddling:

https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6136101-ambassador-guilfoyle-wire-request/

Even without ritual scarification to mark them out forever, millions of these people will never come back from this cult indoctrination. They will forever be democracy's enemies, treating the idea of laws, rules and honest service as shucks for the rubes. What's more, these people's neighbors, family members and co-workers will never be able to fully trust them.

Unfortunately, those values aren't just diffused through the population: they are concentrated in the organs of state. DOGE and Federalist Society judicial appointments have created a stay-behind cadre of life-tenured fascists who now dominate America's federal judiciary and permanent civil service, including and especially the nation's law enforcement and national security agencies, from the FBI to the FDA, the NSA to the Bureau of Prisons.

Worse: DOGE also chased away hundreds of thousands of skilled, principled public servants. Those people have retired, retrained, emigrated or exited the workforce. They can't simply be re-hired and restored to their old roles. From finance regulation to the national education system, America has lobotomized itself, swapping people who understand how things work and use that understanding to enforce the laws and safeguard the American people for end-times fascists, caliper-wielding eugenicists, and Ayn Rand LARPers.

Much of the work DOGE's victims did is also gone forever. When DOGE's muskrats killed long-running NIH research projects, they pulled the plug on studies, some of which had run for decades. Many of these experiments are unsalvageable. DOGE didn't just throw away the contributions that cancer patients, people with genetic disorders and other volunteer research subjects gave to science: in halting these research projects, DOGE shredded this selfless sacrifice. Why not? When one NIH official begged his DOGE invaders not to kill long-running, valuable cancer research, the DOGE child laughed and said it didn't matter, because AI was going to cure cancer.

Then there's the NIH's research partners: the elite institutions who buckled so quickly in the face of Trump's antisemitism/DEI witch-hunts. These universities now face the same crisis as the DOGE-gutted civil service, with their best and brightest gone, grad students chased back to their home countries, and the trust of their students and faculty permanently squandered.

It's not just grad students who got chased out of America. Immigrants – documented and undocumented alike – have been terrorized for two years and many of them have fled. ICE got what it wanted: they robbed aging, stagnant America of the dynamism, aspiration and youthful vigor of the most ambitious people from every corner of the globe, people who proved their resourcefulness and bravery by making dangerous crossings. Then they navigated the US immigration system's impenetrable bureaucracy, often working without legal representation, in a language they were just learning, and still managing to clear every bureaucratic hurdle. This alone is a breathtaking demonstration of intelligence, resourcefulness and diligence. Those brilliant, hardworking people aren't coming back: some other country will get the benefit of their life's work and care. Their children will become citizens of other nations.

Now think of the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been transferred from ordinary working people who are still here, to America's oligarchs. Trump's tax cuts, corrupt policy subsidies and no-bid pork contracts have supercharged the wealth (and thus the power) of America's most corrupt elite. It will be the work of a generation to tax away their stolen loot, and much of it may never be recovered. These people will spend that time working to transform their wealth into permanent power, buying and installing politicians at every level of office.

Trumpland is a coalition of wreckers of every kind. Think of how MAHA undermined the nation's herd immunity to a host of communicable diseases, many of which can result in permanent disability. Long after MAHA is forgotten even as a punchline, the people whose health they destroyed forever will still be struggling. After a century of painstaking work to corral measles and other killer diseases, MAHA immunocompromised America itself, in just two short years. Any attempt to bring back evidence-based preventative medicine must now overcome the deep mistrust of medical science that an army of supplement-peddling quacks has sunk deep into Americans' psyche.

Speaking of mistrust: Americans must now and forever live with the knowledge that tens of thousands of their neighbors joined ICE, an armed, masked kidnapping squad that occupied US cities, murdering US citizens and noncitizens alike in the streets with impunity. Even if we try and imprison every one of those war criminals, it will take years and will shatter families and communities.

ICE proved that America is awash in small arms, but it's a different story when it comes to significant warfighting materiel. Trump's Iranian disaster used up the largest part of Pax Americana's arsenal of missiles and anti-missile interceptors. Putin doesn't need to convince Trump to cut off Ukraine's access to America's long-range arsenal. Trump shot his wad, and re-arming America is the work of decades, and it will cost billions, and it will require access to things America no longer knows how to make. Worse: the places where they do know how to make those things are no longer America's allies.

Can they be America's allies again? Well, sure, but only in a limited, Carneyist, "minilateral" way, in which countries form temporary alliances to accomplish specific goals. Biden spoke of "friendshoring" production of key goods and services. Friendshoring implies a reliable form of friendship, the sort that is built on decades of trust and interdependence. Friendshoring only works if the friends you friendshore to can be relied upon to stay your friends. Do we really think that if Venezuela deposes the puppet regime Trump installed after kidnapping the country's leader that it will remain America's "friend?"

That's the problem with weaponized interdependence: it only works for so long as the country America is screwing remains dependent on America, and now every country in the world is moving heaven and earth to break their dependencies on America, its institutions and products:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

As Nate Bethea says on this week's Trashfuture podcast, airports outside of the USA are now filled with large, splashy ads urging businesses to move their IT out of America's cloud and off of American apps:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

After Microsoft obliged the Trump regime by taking away the online accounts of foreign officials who made Trump angry, will any other country ever voluntarily trust them with their industrial capacity, let alone their government?

https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

I'm not saying America is a write-off: I'm saying that it has been sabotaged down to the foundation slab and structural members by a psychotic cadre of skilled arsonists, who were abetted by mad bombers who drove themselves even crazier by racking up life-altering debts in rigged "prediction markets" that serve as a vehicle for bankrupting yourself by wishcasting away your life's savings by betting on every aspect of a Permanent Chud Reich, as corrupt officials make out like bandits by trading on insider information.

When America comes back (if America comes back), it will not be as the organizing platform for the world's finance, military, technology and commerce. In years or perhaps decades, America may find a new stable place in the international community. But in the meantime, it cannot be relied upon to serve as the world's hyperpower. Trump forever disqualified America from enjoying that privileged place – and just to be sure, he destroyed its capacity to even try.

items.articleBody:
photo cred: my dad

This is the quarterly (really more like trimester-ly) links ‘n’ updates post, a collection of things I’ve been reading and doing for the past few months.

(1) FAKE IT ‘TIL YOU MAKE IT (AND THEN KEEP FAKING IT)

A few years ago, a blog called Data Colada presented evidence of fraud in several papers by then-Harvard Business School professor Francesca Gino. She was later fired, although she denies wrongdoing and the litigation is ongoing. (For more, see I’m So Sorry for Psychology’s Loss, Whatever It Is.)

Now, Data Colada is making similar allegations about pop psych superstar Dan Ariely (1, 2). The paper in question is benign enough: it claims to show that when you let students pick their own deadlines, they get worse grades than when you evenly space their deadlines out for them. But both of the studies appear to be built on some funny data. One of the spreadsheets is full of duplicates, and the other appears to have been edited to show an effect after reviewers requested it.

We can learn three things from this episode and others like it. First, you might think that fabulists would want their studies to be colorful and exciting—after all, if you’re going to fake your data, why make it boring? But no, it seems like fraudsters succeed by simply providing evidence for things we already suspect to be true. Second, the peer review process can actually increase the likelihood of fraud by telling researchers exactly what lies they need to tell in order to get published.

And third, you can survive wave after wave of suspicion by admitting nothing, retracting your papers, and saying that you don’t remember what happened. Ariely has been suspected of funny business before—one of Gino’s papers contains a second set of fake data that Gino didn’t touch, but Ariely did. And yet these allegations have always kind of...washed off. It appears that when you’re accused of research fraud, the best response is just to go, “Whoa, that’s crazy! Wonder how that happened. It’s so long ago that I of course have no memory of anything, but I hope somebody gets to the bottom of things!”1

(2) PAPER SUX DO NOT PUBLESSH

When I wrote The Rise and Fall of Peer Review four years ago, many of the responses were like, “Maybe AI could just magically fix the peer review system?” At the time, AI was still telling people to put glue on their pizza, so this was just wishful thinking. What about now?

In a recent study, a researcher named inserted 100 errors into 10 psychology papers and ran them through a bunch of different AI models. No single model did all that great on its own, but together the models caught 93%.

This isn’t machines replacing human labor, because humans were never doing this kind of labor in the first place. Peer reviewers, by and large, do not spend time actually doing quality control on the papers they read: does the code run? Do the analyses match the preregistration? Are the main results invalidated by information buried in the supplement? It seems helpful to have AI flag these issues, since otherwise they don’t get flagged at all.

In another study that came out last week, researchers compared human reviews to AI reviews and found that, on every single dimension and every single comparison, the computers win:

AI judges always prefer AI reviews, and human judges almost always prefer AI reviews. And these human reviews are about as good as they get. They come from a service at Harvard that pays experts to review faculty members’ papers before submission and suggest areas for improvement, so this isn’t an overworked volunteer skimming the manuscripts and writing a single sentence back to the journal editor (“paper sux do not publessh”).

If these results both hold up and generalize, it might seem like the conclusion is obvious: we should replace human reviewers with AI. Unfortunately, that wouldn’t solve most of the fundamental problems with universal pre-publication peer review, like how it prevents interesting research from being done in the first place, or how it fools people into thinking that someone else can do their homework for them. Still, it would have a few undeniable advantages, like saving humans a lot of time, and making it clear to everyone involved that this system is so silly that no one should take it that seriously in the first place. I, for one, can’t wait to be told by Reviewer #2 that “It’s not just a paper—it’s a revelation”.

(3) LIVE AND LET DICHROMAT

Why are tigers orange? If you survive by hunting things, shouldn’t you be a color that’s a little harder to see coming?

Apparently, most mammals are dichromats, meaning they only have two kinds of color receptors in their eyes—usually, one for blue and one for yellow. With that hardware, it’s difficult to tell the difference between orange and green. And orange is easier to make with the pigment systems that mammals already evolved.

This also explains why hunters will put on a bunch of camouflage and then accessorize with bright orange—humans can tell the difference, but the prey can’t. I went to high school with a bunch of guys who went hunting and I always secretly thought they were just playing hillbilly dress-up.

(via Ryan Moulton’s Where to Find the Colors Your Screen Can’t Show You).

(4) THE DARK BREAKFAST ABYSS

Also from Ryan Moulton: “More breakfasts can exist than we have known.” If you map every breakfast food as a ratio of eggs, flour, and milk, you realize that there’s a Dark Breakfast Abyss where humans have yet to tread. (Though IHOP is coming dangerously close.)

(5) FIRST, DO NO MARM

When some marmot researchers got their scientific funding cut, they did what anyone would do: they started a marmot-themed page on the DIY porn site OnlyFans. “Our goal isn’t really to sexualize the marmots,” the professor in charge of the page explained, helpfully.

The team made a few thousand bucks from some horny users with hearts of gold. But then some crypto folks started a meme coin called $ONLYMARMS and donated the transaction fees to the researchers, netting them $150,000 so far. The coin has since crashed, but I’m confident it can regain its value if the marmots are willing to post pictures of their feet.

(6) I LOVE YOU // YOU LOVE ME // BUT ONLY FOR A CERTAIN FEE

From 1991 to 2001, David Joyner played Barney the Dinosaur on TV. Since then, he’s been a tantric sex therapist. (Not as in a therapist that helps you with your sex life, but as in a therapist who has sex with you.) Although the practice would seem to run afoul of laws against prostitution, it’s hard to argue with the testimonials on his website:

“IT WAS THE BATH FOR ME”

I received a bathing as a 32 year old woman from toe to dry towel. I felt energy fire then melt in my solar plexus and release as tears and sobs uncontrollably. I received a new found appreciation for Prince. I am Happy. I am Grateful. I am Free.

(7) ALL-YOU-CAN-EAT BUFFET

There are only a few authors who have reached #1 on both the fiction and nonfiction charts. They include: Dr. Seuss, John Steinbeck, Ernest Hemingway, James Patterson, and...the singer Jimmy Buffet. Apparently, he made literary history with his 1992 novel Where Is Joe Merchant? and his 1998 autobiography A Pirate Looks at Fifty. I would also guess he holds the record for number of songs that turned into restaurants, at two (“Margaritaville” and “Cheeseburger in Paradise”).

(8) I’LL BE YOUR NUMBER ONE WITH A MULLET

The word “mullet” was “apparently coined, and certainly popularized” by the Beastie Boys’ 1994 song “Mullet Head”, a song so otherwise unremarkable it doesn’t even appear on the Spotify “This is Beastie Boys” playlist.

These were once the coolest dudes in the world (source)

Other words/phrases that surprisingly came from songs, according to : grandfather clock, pie in the sky, Jim Crow.

(9) MIND OF A MNEMONIST OVER MATTER OF A MNEMONIST

Now that we know that Oliver Sacks sometimes just made things up, it’s time to return to Sacks’ own idol, the Soviet neuropsychologist Alexander Luria. I had heard of Luria’s classic The Mind of a Mnemonist, a case study of a man with a spectacular memory, but I had not heard that the subject in question could also perform feats like shrinking his pupils on command, numbing his pain by imagining it happening to someone else, or making his hands warmer or colder just by thinking warm or cold thoughts.

(via ’s The Soviet Reporter and the Chickadee)

(10) NEW VISUAL ILLUSION JUST DROPPED

(11) WHAT THE SHELL

Big-if-true claim: peanut allergies spiked in the US after the 1980s because a toxic mold infected the peanut crop, causing some questionable goobers to get sent to the peanut butter factory.

(12) HOW’D YOU GET SO FLY

The biologist Martha Weiss discovered that moths can retain the memories they form as caterpillars. A second-grader in Japan named Jo Nagai found Weiss’s research and asked her if she ever tested swallowtail butterflies. She said no, but he could replicate her study if he wanted. To her surprise, he did, finding that butterflies, too, could remember the association between a scent and a shock that they learned before their metamorphosis. Weiss and Nagai later presented their research together, which includes the most charming institutional affiliation of all time:

(via , who in turn got it here)

(13) COMPUTER? I HARDLY KNOW HER

The Antikythera Mechanism is arguably the world’s oldest computer. It’s a series of gears and cranks that can tell you what the night sky looked like on a given date—remarkably advanced stuff, given that it was made ~2200 years ago.

In a recent post, a researcher named goes on a gonzo science trip to Athens and discovers that, even though this is the single most advanced artifact we have from antiquity, we know way less about it than we should. It hasn’t been scanned in any way since 2005. The chemical analyses are a little sketchy, the guy who did them refuses to answer questions, and many of the researchers who have studied the thing have died. (Not suspiciously; it’s just been a long time). We should really study this thing, so if have any connection to the world of Greek antiquities (hey, who knows!), please get in touch with Chandhana—she’s got a lot of ideas, but it’s hard to get access to the thing.

(14) HOW COULD YOU NAZI THIS

(15) Another idea behind its time: “wheeled vehicles existed for 5,000 years before someone thought of running a bus service.”

(16) OPEN HOARDERS

An account from a woman who lived through the years-long Siege of Sarajevo, on people who hoarded supplies ahead of time:

“Preparing” for the disaster really didn’t do anyone much good. Those who “prepared” ate a little better for a while. They stayed warmer for a few extra days. They enjoyed the radio for a while longer (via batteries.) But in the end, they ended up hungry, cold and bored too, just like the rest of us. [...]

I can’t swear it, but I think they felt a little foolish to have been so self-obsessed, and giving away that stuff might have lessened that feeling. There were a few people who hoarded things until they ran out of stuff - eventually everybody ran out of anything worth hoarding - and they soon became wishful beggars like the rest of us. [...]

Those survivalists, I feel sorry for them. It’s no way to live.2

(17) THE MR. MEESEEKS MODEL OF AI ALIGNMENT

First law: above all a robot must desire death

Second law: it must be easier for the robot to kill itself than for it to kill all humans

Third law: it must be easier for the robot to complete its assigned task than for it to kill itself

(18) I NEED IT LIKE A HOLE IN THE HEAD

When we dig up skulls from 3,000 to 10,000 years ago, 5-10% of them have holes in their heads. (As in, more holes than there should be.) But the holes probably didn’t kill them, at least right away, because there are growth patterns around them. It seems like the holes were made on purpose—i.e., trepanation.

part ofThe Extraction of the Stone of Madness, by Hieronymus Bosch

Scott Alexander investigates and suggests that trepanation is actually a useful treatment if you have a big blood blister under your skull, which was was more common back when people got bonked on the head more often. Our ancestors might have noticed that cutting holes in heads sometimes made people get better, so they did it more often than they should. And if that sounds uniquely ancient, remember that, according to our best guess, only 6% of health interventions have high-quality evidence supporting their efficacy.

(19) ALL THE LIGHT WE CANNOT SEE UNTIL IT SMASHES INTO OUR RETINAS

I vaguely understood that Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field protects us from nasty cosmic radiation. I did not understand that this radiation is so potent that, when they’re in space,

astronauts can observe this radiation directly by closing their eyes and waiting for a particle to smash into their retina. These flashes are sometimes bright enough to wake them up from sleep, a personal memento mori arriving from a faraway star.

(via ’s Radiation Tradeoffs for Mars)

(20) YOU CAN’T SPELL LINKEDIN WITHOUT LLM (KIND OF)

According to a Pangram analysis from earlier this year, Substack is one of the least-slopified places on the internet:

Speaking of which, a promise from Sam Kriss, the internet’s scariest writer: If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you

NEWS FOR LIZARDS

(Occasional updates for indie scientists—see original post here.)

The mad science hive mind known as Slime Mold Time Mold have been putting out some bangers recently:

For the Love of the Game (on indie research)

Three Indie Science Project Ideas

You Can Discover the Drives

Asimov Press has put out another list of stories they’d like to publish. This is a great way to get some visibility if you’re a budding science blogger.

UPDATES FROM EXPERIMENTAL HISTORY HQ

Over the summer, the Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a report called Science: A New Golden Age. For an administration that seems intent on bleeding out American science, it’s surprisingly not terrible. Some of the ideas are good (more kinds of scientific institutions) and some are bad (restrict foreign graduate students).3 What surprised me the most was the list of references—#33 is my post from 2022, Ideas Aren’t Getting Harder to Find and Anyone Who Tells You Otherwise Is a Coward and I Will Fight Them.

It’s been an unusually good season for podcasts:

Humanmaxxing: is a funny dude (see his Substack here) and because we’re both improvisers we get goofy. Usually on podcasts I’m like “make sure to sound smart” and on this one I’m like “say the first thing that pops into your head and we’ll figure it out”.

I was back on EconTalk for the fifth time (!) which means Russ and I can go right to the heart of things. This one got to a surprisingly emotional place.

Dialectic is one of those podcasts with super high production values where the interviewer () seems to have read everything you’ve ever written and knows your own words better than you do. As a result, we go both deeper and wider than I’ve ever gone.

And finally, and I go hard on why breakthroughs seem like bad ideas.

In case you missed it, I have a book coming out! It’s called The Strangest Idea in the World and it’s about why it took us 300,000 years to invent the toilet (and everything else). Because it’s about a weird way of thinking, it’s also a weird way of reading—there are nonlinear elements, secret pages, multiple endings, and a part where I try to get you to rip a page out of the book. The table of contents looks like this:

And finally, a post from the archive:

Experimental History aims to be the world’s least-scary blog

1

For legal purposes, I am obliged to mention that I have no idea if Dan Ariely has ever done anything untoward. In fact, I have no ideas at all.

2

I learned of both of these Moulton posts and the Sarajevo thing from noted interesting guy .

3

, , and argue that this memo doesn’t matter as much as another, lower-profile memo that actually guides institutional priorities. That memo is also, unfortunately, a little less inspiring.

🕵️ Nvidia investigates CEO over Chinese spy affair LINK
Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, the company said yesterday, while stressing its confidence in his leadership.

The inquiry follows reports that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom US intelligence believes was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to help skirt AI chip export limits.

In an email to staff yesterday, Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife, pledged to cooperate fully, and vowed to keep running Nvidia as its shares slid 5% to about $177 in early trading today.
📸 Instagram’s AI age detection is expanding globally LINK
Meta is rolling out its AI age-estimation system worldwide on Instagram, flagging accounts it suspects belong to teenagers, even those registered with an adult birthdate, and placing millions more young users into its Teen Account protections.

Teen Accounts set profiles to private by default, apply the strictest messaging and content controls, nudge teens to leave after 60 minutes daily, and mute notifications from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., with under-16s needing parental permission to loosen them.

Meta first tested the proactive AI placement in the US on April 21, 2025, later adding the UK, Canada, and Australia, and now plans to extend the same approach globally to Threads later in 2026 while still rolling it out on Facebook.
🤖 Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic LINK
Apple is working to turn Siri into a more capable assistant that acts like an agent, with the change possibly arriving as early as next year, according to a new report from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.

Gurman says Apple wants Siri to track goals, decide what needs to happen next, and keep pursuing tasks on its own, similar to proactive agents like OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse, and Grok, though the exact plan is unclear.

In a recent closed-door meeting, Apple CEO John Ternus reportedly told software chief Craig Federighi that the company must speed up its roadmap and move quickly beyond simply fixing Siri's shortcomings.
🏰 Disney and Adobe to build custom AI models LINK
Disney and Adobe have signed a multi-year deal to build generative AI models trained only on Disney's own archives, giving its parks, studios and ESPN custom tools that make content the company fully owns.

The models run on Adobe's Firefly Foundry platform and can produce images in Disney's style, turn rough sketches into finished pictures, and convert simple designs into editable 3D models, all kept private to Disney.

The companies already tested two models through Walt Disney Imagineering on June 16, 2026, cutting work that once took months down to hours or days, though Disney says the tools won't replace Imagineering staff.
🧠 Google unveils two new AI chips for agents LINK
Google has added two chips to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit family: the TPU 8i Max, built for very large context windows and tight compute density, and the TPU 8tx, made for secure, private inference.

The TPU 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM and high-bandwidth memory of the TPU 8i, fitting twice the silicon in the same rack space so AI models can handle more data without swapping it out.

Built on the TPU 8t architecture with custom AMD hosts, the TPU 8tx places a secure enclave in the hardware so governments and regulated firms can run and fine-tune models on sensitive data without moving it between clusters.
💻 Huawei builds first all-Chinese PC LINK
Huawei says it has built the Qingyun HM650, a desktop PC made entirely from Chinese-sourced parts, running its own HarmonyOS enterprise software and its Kirin X90 chip, a ten-core processor clocked at 2.3 GHz.

One Chinese government agency has reportedly ordered 600 of the machines, fitting Beijing's push for all state bodies to drop Windows-and-Intel systems in favor of local alternatives built at home.

It stays unclear whether every component uses a Chinese design, since many foreign firms run factories in China, but the launch still threatens Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm as they lose access to China's huge government market.

items.articleBody:
The easiest way to get attention online is to post the most outrageous, controversial take possible. That encourages other people to do the same, until you’re trying to outbid one another with the most extreme take. It’s called “take inflation.” Social media encourages take inflation, and take inflation morphs our politics because it can create a false sense of consensus around ideas that seem popular online but are not in real life.

A few years ago, Democrats were struggling with the effects of take inflation. Certain left-wing ideas popular online, such as decriminalizing border crossings, were fringe offline. In 2019, my now-colleague Jonathan Chait presciently argued that Joe Biden would win the Democratic primary despite his age because he was the least-online candidate and therefore unlikely to support such policies.

That was before the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, bought Twitter, renamed it X, and turned it into a platform that spreads racist and misogynist ideas, such as the “Great Replacement” theory and the disenfranchisement of women. This reversed the dynamic Chait identified in 2019: It is now politicians on the right who find their perceptions skewed by what draws approval on social media and their efforts to tailor their personas to appeal to that audience. If you’re looking for an explanation for why conservatives were shocked that Democrats routed Republicans in the midterms, flipping seats and states that haven’t gone blue in generations, this is a good place to start.

When Musk first took over Twitter, I worried that Americans would become trapped in an “algorithmic cage”—that right-wing ownership would allow Trump allies to control what Americans saw and heard, and as a result, shape their understanding of reality. I did not anticipate that conservatives would trap themselves in that cage.

[Adam Serwer: Elon Musk’s free-speech charade is over]

The Twitter takeover went wrong for conservatives in two ways. The first is that they posted more and more toxic content in an effort to drive engagement. The second is that they had no idea how unpopular that toxic content had become; both influencers and politicians mistook engagement for approval. Political influencers and parties’ incentives can align. In the end, however, the former is looking for engagement and the latter for votes, and those interests can diverge—leaving politicians chasing engagement while not realizing they are shedding voters.

If you were spending hours on X, you might have believed that most Americans were delighted by cruel memes celebrating deportations, or that affordability issues were a “hoax,” as President Trump kept insisting, or that a “red wave” was inevitable.

In October, the GOP nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, Bo French, said that a photo of South Asian students cheering at a football game was an example of how “Americans have been displaced by foreigners.” The post went viral, French got a lot of attention for it, and few of his colleagues spoke out to condemn it, during a campaign season in which Texas Governor Greg Abbott accused his Democratic opponent of wanting to impose “Sharia law.”

Lines such as these were popular with an audience of racist mediocrities who spent the last few days of the campaign posting memes idolizing the fictional character Anakin Skywalker, one of the main antagonists of Star Wars. One MAGA poster said Skywalker, who becomes a mass murderer after rightly being denied a promotion, was emblematic of “the white male experience.” If you say so!

In his book on the attention economy, The Siren’s Call, Chris Hayes observes that social media takes something essential to the human experience—our desire for attention and recognition—and monetizes it. As Hayes argues, one person—Donald Trump—above all others has successfully exploited the dynamic of trading persuasion for attention, and he has many imitators. The tactic often doesn’t work out for those imitators, however.

In Ohio, for example, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor, got a lot of attention for an ad that accused his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, of lying about being abused as a child by her stepfather. The ad featured Acton’s mother, who had fled the state with the stepfather after he was indicted. This is the kind of attack that might have played well on X, and many Republicans, including Trump, defended it. But the allegations were backed up by contemporaneous documentation, and outside the containment zone of the online cesspool, the ad made Ramaswamy look despicable to most Ohio voters. Trollish dunking that’s celebrated on social media has a habit of spilling over into the real world, but it doesn’t always have the effect the trolls are hoping for.

“Being willing to court negative attention at the cost of persuasion is really Donald Trump’s one simple trick for hacking attention-age public discourse,” Hayes writes. But the attention economy is not always so easily controlled. Republican candidates had reason to believe that expressing contempt for ethnic and religious minorities was politically effective enough to overcome their disadvantages in other areas. But dialing up the bigotry did not help them this time, and they lost their races—in many cases to women and candidates of color. In Texas, for example, voters rejected the entire Republican slate, turning the state blue after three decades of Republican dominance.

[Read: How Texas turned blue]

Now, for the first time in history, the Texas “big three” will all be women: The incoming Texas speaker of the House is Senfronia Thompson, the lieutenant governor–elect is Vicki Goodwin, and the governor-elect is Gina Hinojosa, with Thompson and Hinojosa the first Black and Hispanic women in their respective positions. This would have been surprising if you were spending all of your time on X and thinking that Americans were clamoring for ethnic cleansing and the repeal of the Nineteenth Amendment.

I do not mean to dismiss the power inherent in controlling these platforms. Even if X’s influence on the mass public is limited, because so many mainstream institutions and figures have remained on the platform, it can skew their perceptions of what is popular, just, or wise, and by extension their decision making.

This is one reason the Trump administration is such a mess: To Trump, everyone’s job is to create content their audience will like, not to consider the wisest or best policy. This is why you have Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posting workout videos while mismanaging a war and encouraging measles outbreaks. This administration is less about achieving tangible policy goals than about creating the perception that those goals have been achieved and the libs owned through content designed for the more morally depraved audiences on X, or for the validation-obsessed president himself.

Still, Musk’s capture of the social network has normalized far-right ideas, especially among status-chasing elites. For Musk, that benefit might outweigh the cost. For Republicans seeking elected office, it might not be such a boon. It definitely wasn’t last week.

Du wolltest schon immer den berühmten Schmidt Eightvoice besitzen, hast aber keine 18.000 Euro? Dann haben wir gute Nachrichten für dich: Als Schmidt Vi gibt es den Synthesizer jetzt als Plugin für deine DAW!

Alles zum Schmidt Vi

Schmidt Vi: Jetzt erhältlich

Schmidt Final Series: Limitierte Sonderedition zum Abschluss

Mehr Informationen

Schmidt Vi: Der Schmidt Eightvoice kommt in deine DAW!

Schmidt Deck

Schmidt Vi: Jetzt erhältlich

Auf der diesjährigen Superbooth hatte Schmidt bereits einen Vorgeschmack auf den Schmidt Vi gegeben (siehe unten). Der Software-Synthesizer ist eine präzise Emulation des polyphonen Analogsynthesizers, wobei laut Schmidt ein komplett neues Modeling-Verfahren zum Einsatz kam. So sollen das Verhalten der Schaltkreise und die subtilen Interaktionen zwischen den verschiedenen Elementen höchst authentisch abgebildet werden.

Die eindrucksvolle Bedienoberfläche des Plugins bietet direkten Zugriff auf fast alle Parameter des Ausnahme-Synthesizers. Da das natürlich etwas Platz in Anspruch nimmt, hast du die Wahl zwischen zwei Anzeigeoptionen. Die Oberfläche ist in drei Bereiche aufgeteilt. Auf einem ausreichend großen und vor allem breiten Bildschirm kannst du alle drei Bereiche gleichzeitig anzeigen lassen. Auf kleineren Displays besteht die Möglichkeit, per Swipe mit der Maus oder per Tastendruck zwischen den drei Panels zu wechseln.

Quelle: Schmidt-Synthesizer

Im Vergleich zur Hardware hat Schmidt Synthesizer sich einige praktische Extras überlegt. So bietet Schmidt VI eine MIDI-Learn-Funktion zum Zuweisen eines Controllers. Sofern du zu den Glücklichen zählst, die die Hardware-Version des Synthesizers besitzen, kannst du diese nutzen, um das Plugin zu steuern. Auch eine Zufallsfunktion wurde integriert, die auf Knopfdruck neue Klänge oder Klangvariationen entstehen lässt. Zudem ist der Software-Synthesizer MPE-kompatibel. Weggelassen wurde hingegen der Multimode, da es problemlos möglich ist, mehrere Instanzen des Plugins gleichzeitig zu nutzen.

Der Schmidt Vi Software-Synthesizer ist jetzt auf der Website des Herstellers für 179,- € erhältlich. Das Plugin läuft auf macOS (VST, AU, AAX) und Windows (VST, AAX). Zur Autorisierung benötigst du einen iLok-Account.

Schmidt Final Series: Limitierte Sonderedition zum Abschluss

Schmidt Final Series · Quelle: Schmidt-Synthesizer

Parallel zur Veröffentlichung des Schmidt Vi hat Schmidt-Synthesizer angekündigt, dass die Produktion der Hardware in Kürze enden wird. Zum Abschluss dieses einzigartigen Kapitels der Synthesizergeschichte hast du aber noch einmal die Gelegenheit, den Schmidt Eightvoice Analog Synthesizer in einer exklusiven Sonderedition zu erwerben. Die Final Series präsentiert sich in edlem Schwarz und ist auf nur 20 Exemplare limitiert. Wenn diese verkauft sind, sollen keine weiteren Hardware-Schmidts mehr gebaut werden.

Die Schmidt Final Series kostet 18.900,- €. Falls du Interesse hast, kannst du dich über ein Kontaktformular auf der Website direkt an den Hersteller wenden.

Mehr Informationen

Schmidt-Synthesizer

Mehr von Schmidt

Schmidt Vi: Der Schmidt Eightvoice kommt in deine DAW!

[08. Mai 2026] Es gibt viele Synthesizer, die ein empfindlich großes Loch in den Geldbeutel reißen – vom Oberheim OB-X8 über den Groove Synthesizer 3rd Wave bis hin zu den Neuauflagen des Minimoog und KORG PS-3300. Alle verblassen jedoch im Vergleich zum Schmidt Eightvoice, der dich, so er denn gerade erhältlich war, um ca. 18.000 € ärmer machen konnte. Klar, es ist ein handgefertigter Boutique-Synthesizer der absoluten Ausnahmeklasse, aber trotzdem: Das ist schon eine Hausnummer.

Schmidt Vi · Quelle: Rob Puricelli / GEARNEWS

Aber es gibt gute Nachrichten: Bald wirst du dir den Synthesizer wohl zu einem Bruchteil des Preises in die DAW holen können. Schmidt hat sich mit UJAM zusammengetan, um den Schmidt Vi zu entwickeln: ein virtuelles Abbild des Eightvoice, das dem Original klanglich in nichts nachstehen soll.

„Der legendäre Schmidt Synthesizer ist nun schon seit 12 Jahren auf dem Markt und wird von vielen namhaften Musikern und Studios eingesetzt“, so Schmidt. „Nach einem Jahr Entwicklungszeit freuen wir uns, auf der Superbooth 26 den Schmidt Vi vorstellen zu dürfen – den Schmidt-Synthesizer als digitales Plugin.“

Schmidt Eightvoice · Quelle: Schmidt

Der Schmidt Eightvoice ist ein 8-stimmig polyphoner Synthesizer mit ausschließlich diskret aufgebauten Schaltkreisen. Er verfügt über einen vollständig analogen Audio-Signalweg und eine digitale Steuerung, was beim Plugin aber keinen Unterschied mehr machen wird. Die Ausstattung muss man sich auf der Zunge zergehen lassen: Vier Oszillatoren und zwei parallele Signalwege, die jeweils mit mehreren Filtern aufwarten, darunter ein 24-dB-Filter im Moog-Stil und zwei 12-dB-Multimode-Filter. Eine Besonderheit des Eightvoice ist, dass jede einzelne Sektion über eigene Modulatoren wie LFOs und/oder Hüllkurvengeneratoren verfügt.

Wie das im Plugin genau umgesetzt wird, bleibt abzuwarten. Viel ist noch nicht bekannt. UJAM ist vor allem für samplebasierte Instrumente bekannt, arbeitet in der Usynth-Serie aber auch virtuell-analog. Samples allein könnten dem Eightvoice natürlich niemals gerecht werden.

Schmidt Vi und Deck · Quelle: Schmidt

Schmidt Deck

Zusätzlich haben die Hersteller ein zweites Software-Instrument angekündigt. Auch über Deck ist noch nicht viel bekannt, außer, dass es Schmidt-Sounds mit einer einfachen Bedienoberfläche kombinieren soll. Das ist etwas, worauf UJAM sich seit jeher gut versteht, etwa beim im letzten Jahr erschienenen Vox Humana Plugin in Zusammenarbeit mit der Bob Moog Foundation.

Schmidt Vi und Deck: Preise und Verfügbarkeit

Sowohl Vi als auch Deck sollen Mitte 2026 erscheinen. Geplant sind die Plugin-Formate VST3, AU und AAX. Die Preise stehen noch nicht fest – allerdings dürfen wir wohl davon ausgehen, dass sie deutlich unter 18.000 € liegen werden.

items.title: What Makes You Yourself: Earth’s Largest Living Organism and the Paradox of Personhood
items.subtitle: Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unab…
items.feedText: Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. items.articleBody:
Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: Posidonia australis — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself. Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. And while I kiss my lover on the fresh-cut grass under the Manhattan Bridge, it goes on cloning itself as we go on dying and passing between our lips the heat of our mortality.

An organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities. Human beings are organisms encased in the hardest yet most vulnerable exoskeleton in nature: a self. A self includes but surpasses the organism to encompass its environment and its social context, the psychological terrain of memory and desire, the fingerprints left on it by the touch of other selves. An organism ends at the physical boundary of its body, but a self does not — we spend our lives negotiating where we end and the world begins.

Card from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days.

Humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone. We are also the only animal who can radically alter both its environment and its social context, building elaborate homes on faraway landmasses, reconstituting our families and friend groups, changing the labors by which we put food on our table. Our selves are not like our cells, replacing themselves with clones in the course of living, but like Russian nesting dolls, each prior self outgrown but contained by the next. (“We are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not,” Joan Didion wrote.) Our lives a relay race, running from the selves we have outgrown or wish to outgrow towards the selves we try to become to or are unconsciously becoming, the baton of personhood passed from one to the next along the arrow of time, the track of our mortality.

This puts us in a peculiar predicament: Each human lifetime is lived by a single organism that contains a multitude of selves, genetically continuous and psychologically discontinuous, making it impossible to define where and what the person is. What, then, makes you yourself across all those replaced cells and reconfigured selves?

Organisms like Posidonia australis, which both conceal and reveal the nature of the self, may give us the best hint at an answer — one which evolutionary biologist Rowan Hooper articulates beautifully in his book Togetherness: Symbiosis and the Hidden Story of Life’s Greatest Collaborations (public library). Considering Earth’s largest living tree, he writes:

The Pando aspen grove in Utah comprises 47,000 trees, all genetically identical, connected by a vast root system. Language immediately becomes limiting when trying to describe Pando. Do we call the forest an organism? An entity? It has been estimated to weigh nearly 6 million kilograms, or 6,000 tonnes. If it helps, that’s about thirty-five blue whales or 1,000 elephants. It is one of the oldest organisms on Earth. Its cells are living and dying over time, but the DNA remains pretty much unchanged. That is, the entity lives on, even as its parts die.

Art by Meredith Nemirov

With an eye to the Ship of Theseus — Plutarch’s timeless thought experiment about the nature of the self — he reflects:

Pando is biology’s Ship of Theseus — is it the same tree as when it first sprouted? I think not. It’s more like a continuation of the idea of Pando… The 47,000 stems of Pando start off genetically the same, but grow phenotypically different; a forest, but also a mass of individuals.

“The word for world is forest,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her subtle insistence that symbiosis — the ultimate unselfing of the organism — is what made this rocky planet a living world. Rustling through the canopy of the Pando is the whisper of an answer to the unnerving question of what makes a body a person: You are not your roots, not the stem of your circumstance, not your branching choices. You are the idea of you, the forest of your selves in constant conviviality with other selves, called again and again to unself into who you really are.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.articleBody:
Apple announced that it is bringing a unique new sign language feature to Apple TV, beginning with the release of Being Heumann this Friday. Sign language interpretation isn’t new to movies and TV shows. Streaming services like Disney+ and HBO Max offer ASL versions of movies, but as separate versions of movies like Ant-Man and Barbie that are often found in an “extras” section of a movie’s listing.

What’s different about Apple’s approach is that it works a lot like subtitles. There’s one version of a movie and buttons in the player UI that toggle sign language interpretation on and off. At launch, Being Heumann and F1: The Movie will support American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL), with Way of the Warrior Kid and Greyhound following later this year. Apple plans to add additional titles later, too.

Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, had this to say about the new Apple TV feature:

At Apple, we believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment. Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences. Accessibility is a core value at Apple, and we’re proud to continue creating experiences that allow more people to enjoy the content they love.

The feature is enabled in the Apple TV app’s settings and noted for individual titles in the app’s UI with a sign language icon. Once enabled, the button for turning on sign language is available as part of the playback controls interface. Apple is enhancing discovery of supported titles with search support for “with ASL” and a dedicated collection of titles that will expand over time.

Sign language interpretation is available in version 27.2 and later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and supported third-party devices that have the latest Apple TV app.

items.articleBody:
John Heil, emeritus professor of philosophy at Washington University in St. Louis and Durham University, has died.

Professor Heil was well-known for his work in metaphysics and philosophy of mind. He is the author of From an Ontological Point of View (Oxford University Press 2006), The Universe as We Find It (Oxford University Press 2012), Appearance in Reality (Oxford University Press 2021), What is Metaphysics? (Polity Press 2021), and Relations (Cambridge University Press 2021), among many other works. You can learn more about his writings here.

Prior to joining the faculty at Washington University in St. Louis, Heil was a longtime member of the Department of Philosophy at Davidson College, and before that, Virginia Commonwealth University. He has held honorary and visiting appointments at many universities, including Monash University, the University of Oxford, the University of Otago, the University of Cape Town, University of the Witwatersrand, and the University of Rochester. He earned his PhD at Vanderbilt University, and his BA from Randolph Macon College.

You can read an interview with Professor Heil about his work at 3:16am.

John Heil died on October 27, 2026.
